item.title: 10 undertouristed destinations where your travel spending will actually make a difference
item.description:
Source: Adventure Score: 2.89
Sometime, what’s hot is what’s ‘not hot’. That’s the thinking behind Intrepid’s annual Not Hot List, which highlights 10 places around the world that are undervisited, want tourism, have a great reason to visit in 2027, and have the facilities to welcome more travelers. Find out which cities, regions, islands and experiences made it into the Not Hot List 2027.

item.title: These 6 Gear Trends Took the Long Trails By Storm in 2026
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.46
(Photo: Zoe Gates) On long trails, gear and clothing trends can seem as fad-driven as they were in high school. Caps are out, bucket hats are in. Heavy boots are so 2005. And if you aren’t dressed in a hooded, collared shirt with donuts all over it, are you even a thru-hiker? Show up to the trailhead with the wrong setup, and just like when you were a teenager, you might feel like you risk being laughed all the way back to town for a resupply. Not that every trend exists across every trail, of course. Trail culture—and the gear that contributes to it—varies from place to place. For example, “Ultralight felt very ‘in’ out west in a way that it didn’t out east,” says thru-hiker Madelyn Dukart, who has trekked long trails across the country. When something is hot in the thru-hiker community, it’s only a matter of time before it trickles down to the rest of the backpacking world. And while some gear crazes only stay in vogue for a season or two, plenty of fresh gear and apparel becomes popular thanks to its practicality or innovation. Here are the trends that took the long trails by storm this past season. To say the ultralight material Alpha Direct swept the thru-hiking community off their feet may be an understatement. “Just a year or two ago [thru-hikers] were all about microgrid hoodies, but they definitely have moved on to Alphas,” notes Mary Pillsbury, owner of 2 Foot Adventures outdoor stores located along the PCT in Julian and Kennedy Meadows. It makes sense: Alpha Direct is lighter, more compact, breathes better, and still insulates well when layered under a windproof jacket. Hoodies made from the material have been popular for a few seasons, but this year’s hikers aren’t stopping there: pants, hats, socks, even gloves have been hot ticket items this year for their gram-consciousness and versatility. Head to any trail town and there’s one thing you’re practically guaranteed to find in every hiker box: a quarter-full IsoPro fuel canister or three. After all, no one wants to leave town with one day of fuel left in their canister then have to carry it empty to the next resupply. Enter fuel transfer devices. These pocket-sized wonders allow hikers to combine fuel from multiple partially empty containers into one. They aren’t new this year, but they were formerly built of hefty metal materials. But a 2.4-gram plastic version is becoming ubiquitous: “Almost every hiker carries a fuel transfer device thanks to Alpenglow Gear. They are so light and inexpensive; 3D printing is changing the market,” says Pillsbury. “This is the first year I’ve heard thru-hikers talk about microplastics,” says Pillsbury. Where Smartwater bottles were once the go-to, more hikers have made the swap this year to using reusable CNOC or M!Go bottles, she’s noticed. Smart, since studies have shown that reusing single-use plastic bottles results in ingesting more microplastics. Plus, reusable bottles are designed to last for years and are only marginally heavier. “Most people that get involved in outdoor recreation begin with their love for nature, and it can feel dissonant to preach respecting nature while relying on single-use plastics for such a crucial piece of gear. Seeing multiple brands with thru-hiker-friendly water bottles seems to alleviate some of that dissonance,” Dukart says. Long gone are the days of huffing and puffing into your inflatable sleeping pad every night thanks to the rise of ultralight pad pumps. In fact, the gadgets have gotten so small and light––thanks in part to the rise of 3D-printed gear and the cottage industry––that there’s little reason not to pack one. After all, there’s an option to suit every hiker, from the stupendously light Alpenblow that you plug into a power bank to the battery-powered Flextail Zero Pump. Wander into any thru-hiker camp this season, and you’re unlikely to see many people inflating their pad the old fashioned way. While Durston has enjoyed a loyal cult following for several years now, this past thru-hiking season brought an explosion in popularity. “It feels like you can hardly walk through a campsite without seeing an X-Mid,” says Amber Rae Hedman, a thru-hiker who completed the PCT in 2022 and 2025, among other trails. It makes sense: The unique offset design of the trekking pole tent offers a more spacious layout and for staggering low weight. Plus, while they were once difficult to get as limited batches were often released months apart, more regular production has allowed hundreds—if not thousands—more hikers to become instant die-hard fans. A more surprising piece of gear that’s made an appearance on long trails in the last year are standalone cameras. Be they digital, film, or disposable, more thru-hikers are ditching the photo capabilities of their phones for a dedicated image-capture experience. “Documenting the journey has become such a big part of the thru-hiking experience,” Hedman says. To do so, many modern hikers are turning away from their smartphones. Is it worth the weight? That’s a personal choice. But compact cameras take measurably better photos than phones (and without draining your battery).

item.title: “Bison Belong on This Landscape”: Judge Blocks Federal Order to Remove 1,000 Animals in Montana
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 5.04
Bison grazing on American Prairie (Photo: Courtesy American Prairie) Nearly 1,000 bison that faced removal from federal land in Montana will be able to continue grazing for now after a judge blocked a Bureau of Land Management order seeking to kick the animals out. The lawsuit stems from an order by the BLM this May that sought to remove the bison from public portions of American Prairie. The nonprofit preserve covers more than 600,000 acres of private land and public grazing leases on Montana’s shortgrass prairie, all of it open to the public, and features camping, wildlife-watching, and hiking. The BLM granted the permits for the animals to graze in the first place in 2005. Its new order is rooted in a reinterpretation of the Taylor Grazing Act, which allows the department to issue livestock permits for public grazing. The rewrite seeks to re-categorize the definition of livestock as “production-oriented.” U.S. District Court Judge Brian Morris objected. “No statutory language or judicial precedent exists that requires a livestock operation to focus exclusively on production and entirely ignore conservation, range improvement, preservation, or other values,” he stated in the decision. “Congress recognized livestock grazing and livestock management often includes and considers preservation, improvement, and thoughtful development, hand-in-hand with other uses.” The bison will now remain on American Prairie’s leases while the lawsuit proceeds. The decision will delay the BLM’s original removal order, scheduled for September 30. If that order had taken effect, the preserve would have needed to either cull or remove hundreds of bison from the land, as Beth Saboe, American Prairie’s director of public relations, told Backpacker in May 2026 shortly after the BLM announced the changes. “Worst-case scenario, we potentially would have to get rid of hundreds of animals. We don’t want to see that happen,” Saboe said at the time, adding that the organization planned to appeal any adverse final decision. Besides incurring major costs to American Prairie, Saboe said that removing the bison from the public range would have stripped a restorative species away from its native habitat. The uncertainty around the herd also led to the cancellation of American Prairies public bison harvest for 2026. While the permit revocation had support from the Montana Stockgrowers Association and many local ranchers, American Prairie’s tribal partners pushed back. In a January 2026 letter to the Secretary of the Interior, J. Garret Renville, chairman of the Coalition of Large Tribes and Sisseton-Wahpeton Oyate of the Lake Traverse Reservation, wrote that American Prairie had provided animals to and worked with a number of tribes attempting to grow their own herds, and that the organization’s methods of raising bison were “largely indistinguishable from the practices and techniques employed by tribal herd managers.” In his ruling, Morris wrote that he “struggle[d] to see” how the BLM’s choice to impose the new regulation while ignoring American Prairie’s evidence could be consistent with the law. With its redefinition, the BLM sought to limit grazing to animals “used as part of an operation to provide output for various purposes, such as meat, milk, fiber, or other products and any animals when they are being used to assist with management of other animals in connection with such operations (e.g. horses that are used to assist with cattle management).” The BLM itself concluded in 2022 that bison grazing would improve rangeland productivity and riparian health on the same lands it now seeks to remove the animals from. If American Prairie ultimately loses the right to graze bison on its leases, it could choose to replace them with cattle. There’s evidence that could compromise the land: Cattle herds often heavily graze one small area before moving on. Bison, on the other hand, tend to graze more gradually while constantly moving over the landscape, covering up to 2-3 miles per day. Studies have shown this can increase biodiversity and even drought tolerance on native grasslands. “These are the ungulates that evolved with the prairie landscape,” Saboe said in May. “They’re one of the main keystone species here and that’s because of how their presence on the landscape improves the rangeland.” The court’s preliminary injunction covers the three federal allotments where American Prairie bison are currently grazing. It did not grant the organization’s request to protect three other tracts where bison do not already graze. “Bison belong on this landscape, and today’s ruling gives them a chance to stay,” said Alison Fox, CEO of American Prairie. “For more than 20 years, our bison have grazed these lands under federal authorization and without grazing violations. The court recognized the concrete harm that removing them would cause, not just to our work, but to our Tribal partners and the broader effort to return bison to their native home.”

item.title: PCT’s Northern Terminus Reopens, to Thru-Hikers’ Delight
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 3.83
Monument 78 and the Canada/ US border marks the northern end of the Pacific Crest Trail (Photo: eppicphotography via Getty Images) The northern terminus of the Pacific Crest Trail is accessible again following a weekslong closure that foiled the plans of many northbound (NOBO) thru-hikers. The 50-mile stretch from Hart’s Pass to the Canadian border reopened on September 9 after having been officially closed since July 31 due to the Ptarmigan fire. Since then, finishing northbound thru-hikers have commemorated the finish line in a number of ways: In late July, some built a makeshift monument at the trailhead for Rainy Pass, just south of the closure. Others rerouted to the west, converging on a little-known obelisk at the Canadian border in the Mount Baker Wilderness. As of today, NOBO hikers still on the trail will be able to take the standard route to the border. “We’re overjoyed to know that the PCT up to the Northern Terminus is open again, as it is such an iconic and symbolic portion of the trail,” says Chris Rylee, Director of Marketing and Communication for the Pacific Crest Trail Association. “Appreciation and gratitude goes out to the Methow Valley Ranger District of Okanogan Wenatchee National Forest and all of the other partners, responders, and firefighters who coordinated massive efforts to keep PCT hikers and communities safe.” As thru-hiking season winds down on the PCT, the reopening comes at a difficult time for many hikers who recently left the trail. Last year, the average finish date for NOBO thru-hikers on the PCT was September 12, according to a survey by Halfway Anywhere. “For me it’s tough because all last month I’ve heard that there’s no possible chance they’d open to the terminus, despite the Ptarmigan fire being more and more contained. Because of this I changed my plans to skip that section and go east to the other monument,” says Reed “Steezy” Patricelli, a thru-hiker from Portland, Oregon who reached the Canadian border on September 6, just three days before the terminus reopened. “As much as it’s a bit annoying, to me its also not a huge deal,” he adds. On his reroute to monument 90, a spot on the Canadian border east of the official terminus, Patricelli says he spotted three black bears and 12 mountain goats: “I firmly believe that the trail is a different journey for everyone, and if the end of my journey had to be a different terminus, so be it!” For others still in the final stretch, the reopening means they’ll be able to cross the trail in the way they’d always imagined. Nicola “Sunflower” Whitbread, a NOBOer from England, is one of those hikers. Whitbread was on the trail in northern Oregon when she heard from another hiker that the terminus had reopened. “The PCT for me has always been about the journey and not the destination, but I won’t lie, I’m stoked that I’ll have the finish I’ve dreamed of for a decade.” In an Instagram post, the PCTA noted that lands east and west of the trail remain closed due to ongoing firefighting operations.

item.title: Colorado Bear Euthanized With Trash in Intestines as Food Scarcity Drives Record Conflict
item.description:
Source: Backpacker Magazine Score: 2.58
Unsecured garbage cans are a liability for both bears and humans. (Photo: CPW) Wildlife officials euthanized a black bear in Durango, Colorado, on September 9, after it was discovered moaning in pain in a residential yard. The bear had dug itself into a hole, and the homeowner who called Colorado Parks and Wildlife (CPW) said it was acting extremely lethargic and making strange noises. Arriving on scene, CPW Officer John Livingston and his colleagues immediately noticed the bear’s distended, bloated belly. They managed to get it to stand up, but couldn’t get it to move or leave the area. They tranquilized the animal, and as soon as they touched the bear’s stomach, Livingston says they realized something was very wrong. They made the tough call to euthanize and performed a field necropsy. “Immediately upon getting into the stomach, we just started pulling out cleaning wipes and full trash bags that still had the whole drawstring,” Livingston told Backpacker. “It was pretty rough stuff.” This incident comes as human-bear conflicts are peaking across the state. So far this year, Livingston says CPW has logged over 8,000 bear reports—the most they’ve ever dealt with. The agency has euthanized over 294 bears so far this year. In all of 2025, the number was just 98. “It’s definitely going to be a record year,” Livingston says. Between this year’s drought and a late Spring freeze that devastated natural food supplies, he expects human-bear conflicts to continue rising this fall. That’s why CPW is advocating extra caution among mountain residents—not just for their own safety, but for the bears’. Livingston is the CPW public information officer for southwest Colorado and the lead for the agency’s Statewide Bear Working Group. He says that CPW officers have been responding to bear incidents since June, working 18- to 20-hour days, often without weekends. Bear relocation incidents are up 3.5 times the 5-year average, and euthanizations are up 2.7 times, according to CPW. Livingston was preparing to head out on a bear call even as we spoke on the phone. “It’s been a busy year,” he says. “Across the state, we’re seeing more bears getting into homes and crossing lines that maybe, in most years, they’d be too timid or not quite bold enough to cross.” That’s largely due to two factors, he says: food scarcity and habituation. Livingston points to the record-low snowpack that has caused drought across the state and an early spring freeze in May that decimated natural food supplies in the southwest. That drove bears down into the towns early in the season. Now, Livingston says, they’re habituated to that food source. “As long as they are getting trash and human-provided food like bird seed, pet food, or whatever gets left outside, they don’t have the incentive to go back up and look for those natural foods,” he says. That creates a dangerous situation for these ursines. It’s much easier to make a fatal mistake, like breaking into homes or cars, or eating garbage that they can’t digest, when neighborhoods represent their main source of food. It can even mess with their biology. “Bears that get human-provided foods will continue to stay up looking to eat as much as they can for as long as they can,” Livingston explains. It isn’t cold weather that drives them into hibernation; it’s a lack of food. “In some places, there have been instances of a few bears never denning because they continued to access food year-round.” As winter draws nearer, CPW is asking residents across Colorado to exercise greater caution. Many towns and neighborhoods require bear-resistant trash containers, but Livingston points out that they do no good if they aren’t regularly cleaned, as bears will still be drawn to their scent. If they get broken, owners need to fix them, and make sure they’re secured every night. Failing to do so could result in a $100 fine for the first offense and a $200 fine for subsequent offenses. He also says that leaving windows or doors open, or your car unlocked at night, is asking for trouble. “It may not be a person you have to worry about coming into your house or trying to get into your car at night,” he says. “It might be a bear.” Finally, he says, don’t be afraid to haze bears who wander near your home. Livingston suggests yelling at them, sounding your car alarm, banging pots and pans, or using an airhorn. “If you’re going to take the time to take out your phone and record the bear, help send the right message and record it while you’re yelling,” Livingston says. “We shouldn’t want them being around our homes.” If there is any year to exercise greater bear caution, he says, it’s this one. The bears need our help.

item.title: Six US drive-ins where you can stay the night
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 5.01
Six places in the US where you can sleep at a drive-in From retro 1950s properties to modern glamping sites, these places are reviving one of the US's most enduring pastimes – and offering travellers one last classic summer experience. At the Frontier Drive-Inn, there are no televisions in the guest rooms. Instead, as the property rather cheekily puts it, the biggest TV in southern Colorado is right outside your door. That would be the outdoor screen left over from the Frontier's first life as a drive-in cinema, which opened in 1955 and went dark three decades later. Today, the former cinema anchors a retro-inspired hotel where guests sleep in Quonset-style yurts and vintage trailers, then gather outside for films beneath the famously dark skies of the San Luis Valley. As Labor Day (7 September) approaches, the Frontier and other properties like it are providing a fresh take on one of the US's most enduring warm-weather pastimes – and offering one last classic summer experience before the season winds down. For generations of Americans, drive-ins have been inseparable from summer. The country's first drive-in opened in 1933, but they exploded after WWII, when rising car ownership, suburban expansion and the baby boom helped push their number to nearly 5,000 by the late 1950s, according to April Wright, a drive-in historian and director of Going Attractions: The Definitive Story of the American Drive-In Movie in which she visits roughly 500 open, abandoned or former drive-in sites. "Going to the drive-in was just something you did every summer," Wright said. Though their heyday may have passed, Wright says the appeal of drive-ins isn't purely nostalgic. Plenty of younger visitors are experiencing them for the first time, drawn to the fact that a night at the drive-in is as much about the ritual around the film as the film itself. "What it's always been about, and what it is still about today, is spending time with friends and family, and creating an experience," Wright said. Now, a handful of hotels, motels and campgrounds around the US are turning that experience into an overnight stay. Some have revived long-shuttered drive-ins, while others let guests sleep within sight of giant screens that have been showing films for decades. At these properties, film night doesn't end with the final credits. Frontier Drive-Inn – Center, Colorado Luke Falcone, co-owner of Frontier, said the screen had survived decades of the San Luis Valley's harsh weather and was too important to the site's history to lose. "When doing historic preservation projects, if you come across something that isn't broken, you've hit the jackpot," he said. Despite the name, the Frontier is no longer a traditional drive-in: guests don't pull up in their cars, but settle into lawn chairs or onto blankets to watch fan-favourite films under the stars. "By bringing folks out of their rooms (and cars), we provide an entirely different experience that we can all bond over," Falcone said. The programming leans into nostalgic cult classics, while the accommodation is decidedly modern. Best Western Movie Manor – Monte Vista, Colorado The motel was built beside The Star Drive-In Theatre, which opened in 1955 as drive-ins were booming across the US, and many rooms face one of its two screens through large picture windows, with the film's audio piped inside. Each room is named after a movie star, from Cary Grant to Robert De Niro, and guests can also head outside and watch from their cars. More than 70 years after The Star first lit up, it still shows films seasonally (generally from spring to the end of September). Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday – Sutherlin, Oregon The Sutherlin/Umpqua Valley KOA Holiday campground occupies the former Cloverleaf Drive-In, where the original 100ft (30m) screen survived long after the cinema itself closed. When the current owner bought the property in 2006, they chose to keep the screen and eventually added a digital projector and FM transmitter, bringing films back to the site. Today, films are shown most weekends. Some RV sites sit directly in front of the screen (or have private patios angled towards it), allowing guests to watch from their rigs and tune into the film over their radios, much as they would at a traditional drive-in. Tent campers and guests in the rest of the RV sites can bring chairs or blankets to a grassy viewing area just in front of the screen, where the sound plays aloud. Hotel Caravana at Four Brothers Drive-In – Amenia, New York Unlike most of the places on this list, Four Brothers isn't a survivor from the golden age of the silver screen. The Hudson Valley theatre opened in 2013, reviving the format decades after thousands of its predecessors had disappeared. Since then, the family-run property has added mini-golf, fire pits and Hotel Caravana, where guests can sleep in vintage trailers within the drive-in grounds or even pitch their own tent. Ofland Escalante – Escalante, Utah Set along Scenic Byway 12 in southern Utah, Ofland Escalante occupies a former drive-in site within Grand Staircase-Escalante National Monument. Guests spend the day hiking, exploring slot canyons or visiting nearby Bryce Canyon and Capitol Reef national parks, then return in time for the nightly film. "The movie starts just after dusk and it anchors the whole evening," said Noah Ellis, CEO of Ofland Hotels. "It's a key amenity, not an add-on." The old drive-in comes with its own fleet of vintage cars – including a 1957 Chevrolet and Ford Thunderbird – that are parked facing the screen. Guests grab complimentary popcorn and classic sweets from the concession stand, choose a car and settle in beneath the desert sky. "The site was a drive-in long before it was a hotel, so keeping actual cars in the mix mattered to us," Ellis said. "There's something about a row of vintage cars, climbing in with a bag of popcorn, that stays with people." Overnight options range from modernised vintage Airstreams to a variety of cabins. Tiger Drive-In – Tiger, Georgia Tucked into the mountains of north-eastern Georgia, the Tiger Drive-In first opened in 1954, went dark in the 1980s and then sat abandoned for roughly two decades. It returned to life in 2004, and today guests can stay after the movie in one of three vintage 1960s campervans parked on the drive-in grounds (each with a private deck facing the screen), or camp in a tent or RV. --

item.title: The 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 3.79
Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita: An icy 4,554m hike to Europe's highest overnight stay You can sleep over at this historic mountain refuge straddling the Italy-Switzerland border – but only if you're willing to undertake a days-long, high-altitude icy mountain trek. I'm roped to four strangers, concentrating on the light cast by my headtorch, as I wend my way through the icy labyrinth of crevasses tearing across the Alpine Lys Glacier. We've been here since 05:00, tugging each other ever higher up the Monte Rosa mountain massif towards the highest altitude building in Europe. We've just reached a giant mountain bowl filled with clouds of snow. The milky blue twilight fades to the soft glow of dawn. Our guide squints into the distance. "Up on that ridge" he says, "Do you see it? That's the Margherita refuge." I can't see anything, but the peak he's pointing towards is so sheer sided that I'm convinced he must be mistaken. We press on and, by midday finally arrive at the summit, 4,554m (14,941ft) above sea level. The crystal frosted world of the Punta Gnifetti peak is revealed. I can see the refuge now. I gasp. Somewhat resembling a giant tin can, the narrow three-storey metal building is not so much built onto the mountain as it is balanced on the edge of a precipice. On one side is a steeply falling snow slope and on the other, there's just a vertical kilometre of thin air. A refuge fit for a queen Sharing the Alpine border between Italy and Switzerland, the Monte Rosa massif contains some of the highest peaks in the Alps, including Monte Rosa itself, which at 4,634m (15,203ft) is behind only Mont Blanc. Punta Gnifetti (also called Signalkuppe) comes in sixth. It's here where an Italian scientific research facility and mountaineers' shelter was constructed and named for the then-queen of Italy, Margherita of Savoy. The queen, famed for her adventurous, athletic nature, insisted on climbing to the refuge herself for its 1893 inauguration and spending the night. Plan your trip: When to go: The Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita is staffed only between mid-June and early September. This is a very popular hike, so make guided tour, accommodation and travel reservations well in advance. The refuge sleeps 70 in summertime. How to do it: Most people climb with a qualified local guide on organised tours, which depart daily in summer. To stay overnight at the rifugio, choose the three-day climb. What you need: Winter clothing, sturdy mountain hiking boots and crampons (not micro spikes). More than a century later, the refuge still supports scientific research while also operating as a mountain hut (rifugio) offering rustic accommodation and thrilling panoramic views. Hiking the massif's eternal winter landscapes has become a popular trek in its own right. Roughly 30,000 hikers summit the peak each year and 4,000 stay overnight, ready like me – and Queen Margherita – to say they've slept in the continent's highest beds. I opted for a three-day guided hike, which requires crampons and ropes. As a frequent hiker, this didn't faze me. If anything worried me, it was the altitude. The hike to the refuge involves a dramatic gain in altitude, from 1,200 to 4,554m (3937 to 14,941ft) in just two days, so steady acclimatisation is essential. More than 4,000m into the air My journey began a day earlier in the Italian mountain village of Alagna Valsesia, at the slopes of the Monte Rosa massif – the literal end of the paved road before the mountainous ascent. From here, a series of cable-car rides whizzed me uphill to Punta Indren, (3,275m/ 10,745ft) where I met my guide and the four other members of our climbing group. Since we were all still acclimatising, our first day involved little more than an hour's hiking across rock and ice to where we would spend our first night, the Rifugio Città di Mantova (3,498m/ 11,476ft), a large wooden mountain refuge set just below the start of the Lys Glacier. There was a marked difference in temperature from Alagna Valsesia, but by wrapping up warm from the biting wind, I could enjoy the panoramic terrace with views of the green valley far below. Despite the stunning setting, I slept fitfully – due, I suspect, to excitement about the coming day's 1,000m (3,281ft) ascent and my body adjusting to the altitude. It was almost a relief when the alarm went off at 04:00 and we crawled out of our beds. We strapped the crampons onto our boots to prevent sliding on the glacial ice and roped ourselves up together – just in case someone slipped into a crevasse. We set out over the glacier and, after an hour or so of hauling ourselves through a spiderweb of crevasses, cleared a ridge and trudged across the mountain bowl. Behind us, dawn clouds bubbled in the valleys and ahead stood the walls of 4,000m (13,123ft) peaks. Despite the drama of the Alpine scenery, this middle section of the hike was considerably easier than traversing the steep, ruptured and torn up glacier crossing. Before I knew it, we were starting the final haul up to the refuge. Although I've never suffered major ill effects from altitude, I do struggle with vertigo. As we zig-zagged sharply up the summit cone, teetering alongside a ridge that fell away into the haze, I began feeling the unmistakable dizzy sensation kicking in and, instead of taking in the view, concentrated on where I was placing my feet. But when I next raised my head, we had made it. The vertigo eased as I stepped out onto the snowy dome. Fold after fold of mountain peaks sparkling with icy crowns stretched out around me – and the refuge itself. I was exhausted. But would I be able to sleep in what was easily one of the most hair-raising buildings I had ever seen? The highest sleep in Europe Once inside, the refuge felt more like a safe cocoon, and it was easy to forget how precarious our situation was. A dining room took up almost the entirety of the ground floor while the upper two were filled with dormitory-style beds which, the night of my stay, were completely booked. I dropped my backpack onto one of the bunks and headed downstairs to order a frothy bowl of cioccolato caldo (hot chocolate) topped with a dollop of Chantilly cream. As I savoured the drink, I fell into conversation with Tommaso Bagnati, one of the refuge's four wardens, who told me how the weather conditions can bring the reality of living on the top of Europe into stark focus. "When there's a big storm the building shakes a bit and you can feel very small," he said. "If there's a thunderstorm it can feel like you're right in the middle of it. All our supplies are delivered by helicopter, so when the weather is very bad and the helicopters can't fly, you can feel a bit cut off from the world." As I sat down to dinner, a weather front rolled across the mountains. The refuge became blanketed in clouds and sleet splattered against the windows. Sitting next to me at the communal dining table was Chinese YouTuber Jianpeng Cui, who told me that despite the "end of the world" feel to the place, he was pleasantly surprised. "I thought there'd only be a bed," he said. "No toilet. No kitchen. But it's not at all like that. I can even buy pizza and juice up here!" I was relieved that altitude sickness had missed me this time. But not everyone was so lucky. Mikhail Morozov, whom I met on his way down from the summit, had suffered headaches and nausea. "Coping with the altitude was the hardest part," he said. "I wasn't acclimatised and you go up very fast. After a couple of hours, the altitude started to hit me hard." More like this: Life in the Rifugio Capanna Regina Margherita – as with all mountain huts – is very communal. Sleeping at high altitude in a cramped dormitory with seven or eight strangers, sharing two toilets with no shower, means you get far cosier than you perhaps want. But the shared effort of reaching the refuge also creates an easy camaraderie. "The best part for me has been meeting people from all over the world who have come here to climb the mountain," said Craig Shaw, a New Zealander living in Switzerland. "Seeing all these different nationalities together in this refuge is just phenomenal". Perhaps the real magic of this mountain is not just its ability to support a crazily positioned refuge. It's an ability to bring people together. --

item.title: Glamping on Vermont's newest bikepacking trail
item.description:
Source: BBC Travel Score: 2.43
The US's newest bikepacking trail is pioneering a whole new way to see Vermont The Heart of the Greens trail threads through Vermont's stunning Green Mountain wilderness, and is the first part of an ambitious bikepacking adventure that will someday span the state. My mountain bike tyres thud over pebbles and roots as I whizz through the darkening path. Dusk has fallen over Vermont's Green Mountain National Forest and nearly 400,000 acres of woods extend in every direction. In the distance, I spot pinpricks of light. The campsite is finally near. In the last fleeting moments of light, I arrive at the Chittenden Brook campground. As I wheel my bike past the welcome sign, I spy a slick, modern hut with pine siding. I'd planned to simply pitch a tent – to this weary bikepacker, the hut's glass windows and wraparound porch seem like the lap of luxury. Next time, I thought, I'm staying there. This hut is part of the Heart of the Greens Loop, a 38-mile (61km) bike trail loop and the first completed segment of an ambitious, continuous bikepacking network that, when completed, will stretch 485 miles (780km) and span the entire state. Plan your trip When to do it: Spring and summer are ideal, but tackle the trail in autumn to appreciate its stunning changing leaves. Most riders can expect to complete the loop in one to three days. How to get there: Rochester has limited bus service, so it's easiest to drive to the trailhead. Alternatively, park in Pittsfield and start your ride from there. What to eat: Bring your own provisions. The two villages anchoring the trail have a handful of eateries, like Rochester's farm-to-table Maple Soul and Pittsfield's Clear River Inn & Tavern. Sample dishes made with Vermont's famous maple syrup, like the iconic Creemee ice cream. Pittsfield has two general stores. Blazing a path for bikepackers My journey began that morning in Rochester, a picturesque village nestled in Vermont's mountainous White River Valley. I've driven through it dozens of times without stopping, but since it became the official start and end point of The Heart of the Greens when it opened in 2024, the tiny town has become a magnet for bikepackers. Like me, many are eager to blend the escapism of camping with the thrill of cycling through Vermont's glacial-carved wilderness and explosion of autumnal colours. The loop is a closed-circuit preview of the forthcoming Velomont, a bikepacking route through Central Vermont with a twist: it will be connected by 30 cleverly spaced off-grid huts allowing tired pedallers to bed down in protected forest shelter. On track to finish the first 200 miles (321km) within the next 10 years, the project echoes a larger trend in bicycle travel: statewide bikepacking routes are in development in Utah, Massachusetts and along the entire West Coast. I grew up near Rochester and have dreamed of such a multi-day bikepacking route. For now, I'm thrilled to take on the Heart of the Greens. Two huts are already placed along the trail, roughly 19 miles (30km) apart: the Chittenden Brook Hut, featuring simple bunks and a self-service kitchen, and Spikehorn Yurt. The yurt doesn't have electricity, and neither accommodation has running water. The route's huts will straddle a curious middle ground between camping and traditional stays, allowing bikepackers to carry lighter gear and immerse themselves in the wilderness. The Heart of the Greens may be considerably shorter than the Velomont, but with a cumulative ascent of nearly 6,000ft (1,830m) on largely unpaved forest roads and trails, it's no less intense. "It's a big walk on the wild side," says Doon Hinderyckx, owner of Green Mountain Bikes in Rochester, when I stop by before shoving off. Hinderyckx encourages visitors to hire e-bikes for navigating the steeper grades: "You're mixing mountain biking and the adventure of the challenging terrain. You're on and off the seat a lot." It also requires a bike with thick tyres and suspension, a water filter and provisions, since the current route passes through only two small backcountry villages – Rochester and, 9 miles (14km) south, Pittsfield. Like the huts, eateries and general stores along the trail itself are still in development, so I've packed several meals, plus rain gear and insect repellent, despite the beautiful late summer weather. Hinderyckx checks the air pressure in my inner tubes and oils my chain. He's the last mechanic I'll see for the next two days. Next door to Green Mountain Bikes stands the Stable Inn, run by Hinderyckx's wife, Anni MacKay. This handsome two-story guesthouse opened in 2023, with a range of rooms, Nordic-chic decor and rooftop solar panels, converted from a timber-frame warehouse from the 1840s. While not an official hut on the trail, the Stable Inn has become a base for many Heart of the Greens riders to unwind, or bookend their bikepacking journey with jaunts to the village's quaint art centres and shops. "[The loop is] a very strategic, positive thing," says MacKay. "People always want to have access to the backcountry, in a safe way, with the benediction of the community that is providing services. It's a complete win-win." Ups and downs in the Green Mountains I know Vermont well and have bike-toured widely, but this is harder than I expected. On asphalt, a 38-mile ride makes for a pleasant afternoon. The Heart of the Greens is far more demanding – and adventurous. Rugged roads lead to mountain bike trails, which scissor their way up the alpine forest. The first day, I coast south along Route 100 and turn onto State Garage Road, into a residential area. Houses disappear beyond the canopy, and I huff up one shelf of road, then another. All at once, the road transforms into steep gravel. I grind past the Spikehorn Yurt, the Loop's first hut, a rounded fabric enclosure with bunkbeds, a futon, homey furniture and a spacious terrace with views of the mountains. The route then devolves into two dirt tyre trenches cutting through the grass – what mountain bikers call "double track". My temples pound as I climb. Summer mosquitoes drone in the sultry air. After a couple of gruelling miles, the road finally descends, and so do the conditions. Logging lorries have shredded the ground into potting soil, my wheels sink into a mire of turned earth and broken branches. As I struggle, another cyclist pulls up behind me. "This is crazy, isn't it?" he wheezes. "I don't think I'd have made it if I wasn't on an e-bike." I can't help but agree. The grades are tough on my middle-aged thighs, and I frequently dismount and push. I got a late start to begin with, and as I reach the third major trail section of the day – a mile of switchbacks cheekily named "Perspiration" – my legs boil with lactic acid, and the Sun melts beyond the ridge. This is how I come to arrive at Chittenden Brook Campground after nightfall. I pitch my tent onto the cold ground and gaze longingly at the modern hut before me. Riding high After a decent night's sleep, I finally hit my stride. I sail down the smooth pavement of Route 73 and pedal through the pastoral scenery of the quiet, unpaved Bingo Brook Road. Dense trees all around, I pass occasional farmhouses and cottages, but most of this land is national forest. Fog lifts over a pond, and the air is cool and quiet. I try to imagine what the Velomont will look like in future decades. The Heart of the Greens now passes through just two village centres with a loose string of businesses straddling Route 100. As the Velomont expands, it will tether together more towns and country shops, making it easier for cyclists to resupply and interact with locals. Bikepackers will traverse ever-more-varied terrain and, like me, stop in towns they might never notice by car. "You're camping, but you're not really camping," says Georgia Grzywacz, a Maine resident who rode the loop and stayed at the Chittenden Brook Hut in June. She appreciated the kitchen, electricity and bunk mattresses, as well as the nearby brook. "You're without running water, but you have these creature comforts." Even the booking process was easy: "The [Vermont Huts] website is so navigable." I veer off Bingo Brook Road to find a final trailhead. Two mountains remain, totalling 12 miles (19km) and more than 2,000ft (609m) of climbing, but this time, I'm prepared. Teeth clenched, I grind my way up the switchbacks of Swan's Mill Trail, fighting for every foot of elevation. More like this: At last, my reward: Tunnel Ridge is a five-mile-long (8km) flow trail that snakes its way back down to Rochester, for a total of 110 switchbacks. My tyres shudder over washboard terrain and swerve around S-curves. I choke the brakes, my saddlebags bounce noisily over my rear rack. The forest becomes a wash of brown and green. Gravity lures me downward, into the valley. Endorphins flood my brain as I drift into The Stable Inn's parking lot, back to my waiting car. I'm euphoric but exhausted. For now, I'm closing the loop. But in time, there should be many miles, and many huts, more. And I'll be ready. --

item.title: Blueberry Protein Pancakes (No Protein Powder)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 5.04
Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. Tofu in blueberry pancakes?! Your eyes do not deceive you. Here, silken tofu acts as a binding agent in these protein-packed vegan blueberry pancakes. As there are no eggs in this recipe, you’ll need as much help with leavening as possible to cut through the density of the tofu. This means adding both baking powder and soda—and a lot of it. Baking powder (make sure to use the aluminum-free kind to mitigate any unpleasant flavor) will activate with the water and again when the batter hits the heat; baking soda will react with the water and the acid in the brown sugar. The result is a fluffy, crisp-edged pancake with a slightly chewy, almost mochi-like interior. Small wild blueberries are best, but whatever kind you find at the store will work. As is the case with most baked goods—even those that technically don’t go into the oven—these pancakes are most successful when the ingredients are measured by weight with a scale. If measuring by volume with measuring cups, it can be easy to pack in a little extra flour. If so, you may need to add about a tablespoon or so more water; you want the batter to be the approximate consistency of pourable whole-milk yogurt (not thick Greek-style). Discover more Good for You recipes here: Veggie Club Sandwich; Berry Protein Smoothie; Chopped Salad With Sardines and Preserved Lemon Read More: How I Make Protein Pancakes Without Protein Powder Recipe information - Total Time 1 hour 15 minutes - Yield Makes about 16 Ingredients 1½ ½ 3 2 1 1 1 5 ½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Whisk 1½ cups (188 g) all-purpose flour, ½ cup (62 g) whole wheat flour, 3 Tbsp. light brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. aluminum-free baking powder, 1 tsp. baking soda, and 1 tsp. Diamond Crystal or ½ tsp. Morton kosher salt in a large bowl to combine. Step 2Blend tofu and liquid from one 16–17-oz. package silken tofu in a blender until very smooth. Scrape down sides and add 1 Tbsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil and 1½ cups water; blend until mixture is very smooth. Scrape into bowl with dry ingredients and gently fold in with a whisk. Step 3Heat a dry large nonstick skillet over medium for 3 minutes. Drizzle in 1½ tsp. avocado oil or vegetable oil. Pour 2 scant ⅓-cupfuls of batter into skillet, leaving space around each. Top each pancake with about 1½ tsp. fresh or frozen wild blueberries. Cook pancakes until tops start to look matte, about 4 minutes. Gently flip and cook until golden underneath, about 4 minutes. Transfer pancakes to a plate or wire rack. (Alternatively, transfer to a wire rack set inside a rimmed baking sheet and keep warm in a 300° oven while you make the rest). Working in 7 more batches, repeat process with remaining oil, batter, and blueberries, adjusting heat as needed to keep pancakes from absorbing too much oil or burning. Step 4Serve pancakes with pure maple syrup. Do Ahead: Pancakes can be made 3 months ahead. Let cool, then stack between sheets of parchment paper and place in an airtight container or resealable plastic bag and freeze. Reheat in a toaster or toaster oven until warmed through.

item.title: 19 Margarita Recipes for Any Season
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.71
A great margarita is hard to beat: tequila, fresh lime juice, orange liqueur, and salt in sweet-tart harmony. But the classic margarita recipe is also an excellent starting point for experimentation. Small tweaks—swapping triple sec for agave syrup, say, or tequila for mezcal—can create a whole new drink. Perhaps even more compelling is the margarita's ability to veer into maximalism. Blend yours with frozen mango, muddle in fresh blackberries, or infuse the tequila with chiles. Below you’ll find 19 of our best margarita recipes, including frozen margaritas, spicy margaritas, fruit-forward riffs, and a few less traditional variations. There’s a salted watermelon margarita for summer, a blood orange version for winter, and an avocado margarita that blends up remarkably creamy. Whether you like yours on the rocks, straight up, or frozen, there’s a margarita here for you.

item.title: Spicy Chicken Lettuce Wraps
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.25
These lettuce wraps with spicy crumbled chicken, fresh herbs, and lime are a longtime favorite of Bon Appétit readers (and staff). Inspired by larb, the saucy filling gets its savory-sweet heat from a blend of soy sauce, fish sauce, brown sugar, and sriracha, with plenty of garlic and scallions. The combination of warm, spicy ground chicken, cool, crisp lettuce, fresh cilantro or mint, crunchy store-bought fried shallots, and bright citrus comes together in just about 20 minutes. It’s a high-reward dinner for very little effort. Chicken lettuce wraps FAQs What kind of lettuce should I use? Bibb lettuce is our first choice: Its leaves are tender and pliable enough to fold around the spicy chicken filling without tearing. Boston and butter lettuce are good substitutes, while romaine “boats” will give the wraps more crunch. Can I make these lettuce wraps with a different ground meat? Absolutely. Ground pork, beef, turkey, or lamb can be swapped for the ground chicken without otherwise changing the recipe. For fattier meats, like ground beef and lamb, you can start with 1½ Tbsp. oil. What should I serve with chicken lettuce wraps? These lettuce wraps make a complete light dinner on their own, but steamed jasmine rice or coconut rice will make the meal more substantial. You can also skip the lettuce and spoon the chicken, herbs, fried shallots, and lime over rice for an easy rice bowl. Recipe information - Total Time 20 minutes - Yield 2 servings Ingredients 3 2 2 2 3 6 4 1 Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Mix 3 Tbsp. low-sodium soy sauce, 2 Tbsp. light or dark brown sugar, 2 Tbsp. sriracha, and 2 tsp. fish sauce in a small bowl to combine; set aside.x Step 2Heat 3 Tbsp. vegetable oil in a skillet over medium. Add 6 scallions, thinly sliced, and 4 garlic cloves, finely chopped, and cook, stirring occasionally with a wooden spoon, until softened (a little color is okay), about 3 minutes. Add 1 lb. ground chicken and lightly season with kosher salt. Cook, breaking up meat with spoon and tossing occasionally, until cooked through, 5–7 minutes. Add reserved soy sauce mixture and cook, tossing occasionally, until liquid is reduced by half, about 2 minutes. Step 3Serve chicken mixture with Bibb lettuce leaves, mint leaves and/or cilantro leaves with tender stems, lime wedges, store-bought fried shallots, and more sriracha for making lettuce wraps. Editor’s note: This recipe was first published in 2019; it has been updated based on reader feedback to increase the sauce and reduce the saltiness. Head this way for more of our favorite weeknight dinners →

item.title: Listen to BA Bake Club's Podcast on Plum Karpatka (Polish Cream Puff Cake)
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 4.12
For the past six years, senior Test Kitchen editor Jesse Szewyczk has been trying to get a karpatka recipe published. Even though he’d never made one in its entirety before. But he knew BA’s Bake Club was the perfect place to showcase what he calls the drag queen of Polish desserts. “I’ve made every component before,” Jesse tells his cohost Shilpa Uskokovic. “I just haven’t arranged the puzzle pieces in this fashion.” “We hope that that's what people in Bake Club take away,” Shilpa adds. “That by having these building blocks, you can make all these things, even if they’re the first time you’re making them.” Jesse’s version has an American twist (a no-bake cheesecake filling) and a nod to his Polish roots (the plum compote). Listeners also weighed in with questions about and photos of their sky-high desserts, and we awarded our Baker of the Month. We also had a visit from a beloved star baker in The Great British Baking Show (a.k.a. Bake-Off for those in the UK). Season nine finalist Ruby Bhogal stopped by the podcast to talk about her new book Around the World in 80 Cakes. And yes, there is a karpatka in it! Find Ruby Bhogal @rubybhogal and on Substack. Shilpa Uskokovic: I'm Shilpa Uskokovic. Jesse Szewczyk: And I'm Jesse Szewczyk. SU: We're both senior test kitchen editors at Bon Appétit. JS: And this is BA Bake Club. SU: Bake Club is Bon Appétit's community of confident and curious bakers. JS: We're creating the nerdiest and most wholesome corner of the baking internet. SU: Every month, we publish a recipe on bonappetit.com that introduces a baking concept that we think you should know. JS: Then you'll go bake, and you can send us any questions you have or pictures of your finished creations. SU: And we get together here on the podcast to talk about the recipe. JS: The September Bake Club recipe for glazed apple pie fritters is live now on bonappetit.com, and we'll tell you a bit more about those at the end of the episode. SU: But today, today we're diving into Jesse's Polish roots with his recipe for a Plum Karpatka. JS: Listen, I've been pitching of Karpatka for years. SU: You have? JS: Okay, I'm going to be real. I didn't grow up eating Karpatka. And we'll explain to you what this is. I feel like I'm building suspense here. SU: Yes. JS: But it's this Polish cake that I stumbled across several years ago, and I was like, "This is cool." SU: How do you describe it in your text? I love the phrase that you use. JS: Oh, and they let me keep it. I called it the drag queen of Polish desserts because it's just big, boisterous, and kind of silly. SU: Showy. JS: Yeah. SU: It's a lovely dessert. JS: Thank you. SU: And you gave it a really nice ... In a way, it was almost like a very New York spin with a cheesecake. JS: Yeah, yeah, yeah. SU: That's the whole thing. Okay. The photos that our Bake Clubbers have sent in of the Karpatka have been absolutely incredible. JS: They're big. Yeah. SU: I feel like there were a lot of skills that came together in this one from past Bake Club bakes. JS: Yeah. Those of you who have been around for a while, we did a Paris-Brest, which is this big kind of tire of choux that you fill with a sweet filling. SU: And for those who are listening, it's choux, as in choux pastry. JS: Choux paste, yes. SU: Okay. Sorry, Jesse. Didn't mean to cut you off. JS: Not the gym shoes, a big tire of choux. And that was a traditional way to cook pâte à choux, you can make cream puffs, éclairs. And this is baking choux in a cake pan, which I feel like is a very unique way to bake it. So, it's like building upon that foundation we learned several months back to create something completely different. SU: I love that you did that, because that's what baking is about. It's like these few things that you have, and then you re-spin it in different directions. Okay. Before we go any further, let's take a moment to get a brief step-by-step tour of this recipe. Okay? And for that, we're going to need our jaunty Bake Club music. Here it is. Okay. Jesse, walk us through this recipe. JS: Yeah, and buckle up because it's a challenge. Not hard, but it takes some effort. Okay, let's start. SU: Sure. JS: So, you're first going to start by making plum compote, and that's very easy. You just cook some plums with sugar and salt. And then when that's nice and thick, you're just going to finish it with some lemon zest juice and some vanilla, and that's your jam. So, make sure you cool that though, because it'd be warm, you need it to be nice and cool and thick. So, as that's cooling, you're going to make your pâte à choux, which we might be familiar with. So, you're going to bring a stick of butter, cut into little pieces, some sugar, some salt, and water to a simmer. And with simmering, you're going to add some flour, and then cook that into this thick doughy paste, and then take that out, let it cool for a while, and then you're going to whip that in a mixer with some eggs. Divide that between two cake bands and bake them, and then watch as they dramatically turn into these giant wonky discs. So, cool your discs, and as those are cooling, you can work on your filling. So, this is like a no-bake cheesecake. So, you're going to start by blooming some gelatin in some cold water, let that sit, then heat up just a tiny bit of cream, pour that over that, so it dissolves the gelatin. And then, to that, you're going to add some cream cheese, some powdered sugar, some vanilla, some salt, and then you're going to beat that all together while adding some more heavy cream to kind of lighten it. And then that's your filling. So, you can assemble everything at this point. So, those two choux puff discs you have, you keep one in a cake pan, and then you put your filling in, you swirl it with the jam, put the other on top like a sandwich, let it sit overnight, and it sets into this beautiful Karpatka. And that's that. SU: The drag queen of Polish desserts. JS: The drag queen, that's how the drag queen gets her beat on, the full beat. SU: Have you ever made Karpatka before this? JS: I'm being called out, and the answer is honestly no. SU: I love that. JS: So, this was a learning experience for us all. SU: Yes. JS: Yeah, and it was really fun. SU: I want to get philosophical here and be like, just because we've never made something before doesn't mean we don't have the authority to make it. Do you know? JS: Well, I've made every component. SU: Exactly. JS: I just haven't arranged the puzzle pieces in this fashion. SU: Exactly. JS: Yes. SU: And we hope that that's what people in Bake Club, our members, take away, that by having these building blocks, you can make all these things, even if they're the first time you're making them. JS: Shilpa, that's beautiful. SU: Thank you. Okay. What occasion do people ... Well, it's a cake. You can eat it at any time. But traditionally, I wonder when a Karpatka is usually served and eaten. JS: I think traditionally in Polish culture, it's for holidays, like Easter, Christmas, and I guess this was my summer version. The flirty summer version of a Karpatka. SU: And I think something, the Easter connection, I'm thinking about ... My husband is Serbian, and they do- JS: Yeah, my husband. SU: And they also have a lot of choux-based pastries, especially around- JS: Like what? SU: They have something called a Princes Krofne, which is éclairs. JS: Sure. SU: Actually, they're cream puffs, to be honest, but no chocolate top. I'm not sure why they call it Princes Krofne, but they are. But I think Easter and Christmas, especially Easter, I think it's after that fasting period, and then you're able to use all these rich ingredients like eggs, which the defining factor of choux, I think, is how many eggs there are in the pastry. JS: Yeah, it's like eggy. It's like doughy, eggy in a nice way, like custardy. SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: Okay. So, I want to talk more about the pâte à choux, because it is really deeply fascinating. But let's start with the first component that you named, which is the compote. Why did you decide to go with plums? JS: Well, a few reasons. I guess you can kind of use any jam you want. If you want cheap, you can buy a thing of jam, that's fine. But I was thinking, "Oh, what is a late summer produce?" Because it's not quite the peak of summer anymore, nor is it cold weather. And I feel like stone fruit is kind of that transitional fruit, but also plums are very traditional in Polish cuisine and baking. In American culture, we have all these sayings about apples, like, "An apple a day keeps the doctor away," or, "A good apple," or various things. The Polish equivalent is plums. There's all these different sayings about plums, and it's just ... And also, when you use red plums and you make a compote, that color is crazy saturated. SU: Yes, it's very dramatic. JS: It stains your hand saturated, and I thought that would just be stunning. And I don't know, stone fruit's so underrated. Yeah. So, I really wanted to give it a moment. SU: How chunky do you like your compote? JS: Nah. SU: Not at all? JS: A little bit. SU: Yeah. Does it matter for the Karpatka, how chunky it is? Can people leave it a bit chunkier, or make it a bit smoother? JS: They can leave it chunky, but just make sure you cook it down enough that it's not wet, because you want it to thicken up enough that it doesn't seep out. SU: So, you want to dry enough moisture, so when you slice it, it doesn't just weep all over. JS: Yeah. SU: It's thick and jammy. JS: So, if you're able to keep chunks while cooking it out, that's cool. SU: Sure. JS: But I think it might be hard. SU: Got it. JS: Yeah, yeah. SU: And plums are pretty high in pectin. JS: They are, yeah. SU: They make a good jam. JS: Yeah. When it's warm, it can feel a bit loose, but then after overnight in the fridge, it does thicken up quite a bit. Yeah. SU: Is that your recommended amount of chill time for the compote? Can anybody chill it for less and still manage to get away with it? JS: I think you could. If you chill it for an hour, and it's a shallow metal bowl, you're fine. Also, you can, if you're in a rush, which I was many times making this, I'll put it on a sheet tray, so it's a very thin layer, and then that chills in, I don't know, 20 minutes. SU: Smart. JS: Yeah. SU: So, you just don't want it to be so warm that it will melt like the cheesecake filling. That's all we're trying to do, really? JS: Yeah. SU: Okay. JS: Yeah, pretty much. SU: Okay. Okay, that's great. Okay. We'll move on to the second component, which is our star. JS: The choux. SU: The choux. I remember this is when you had a bit of a eureka moment. JS: Yeah. I mean, honestly, looking back, I'm like, maybe I'm stupid, but- SU: Stop. Don't say that about yourself. JS: Okay. I'm sorry. SU: Apologize to Jesse, my friend. JS: Okay, let's move on. So, okay. When you make choux, you bring your water to a simmer with your butter, and then, in that, you can add salt and sugar if you want, and then you add your flour, and you cook it in the pan till it kind of sticks. And then, that glob, you mix with eggs, and people mix it by hand. They just add the eggs. Sometimes they even crack the eggs right in the pan once it's cooled a bit. Some people do it in a mixer, and I thought that incorporating the eggs was just mixing them in. That's that. The first couple tests, it got some nice height, sure. But then, one day, I'm like, "I'm just going to mix it crazy. When I add the eggs, I'm going to put it on high, and I'm going to let it go for five full minutes." I could tell that the batter was aerated. It felt and looked different. Then I baked it, and it was like- SU: Dramatic. JS: It was like a hat. SU: Yeah, it was. JS: It was like a little gnome hat. It puffed so much. I'm like, "That's it." So, just you need to literally mix the shit out of your choux, and incorporate that air physically, mechanically, and it's going to expand and give you two times the puff. SU: Does it matter if you use a stand mixer versus a hand mixer? JS: I don't think so. I think the stand mixer probably works better in this case, but you could use both. SU: Yeah. The trick is to just keep going. JS: Just keep going. SU: With the crap out of it. JS: Yeah. So, you get a lot of air incorporated in there, which makes sense because it's egg-based. SU: Yeah, and the egg is trapping all that air. JS: Yeah. So, it was really fun though to watch it expand. I remember some, we'll get to this later, but someone was like, "Oh, because it expanded too much." I'm like, "No such thing." SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: And then how ... Because choux, in many ways, is a very unique sort of dough. You're really cooking, you're pre-cooking the flour into this weird, as you said, glob. JS: Yeah. SU: How do you know when it's ready to come off the heat? JS: Sure. For me, when I'm cooking this dough, when I see a very thin kind of ... They say film, I guess is the word, a thin film start to develop on your pan, that's a good sign typically that you've cooked it long enough. SU: Oh, got it. JS: Yeah. SU: Because there's enough moisture, I guess, gone, so it starts sticking to the bottom. JS: Yeah. I think it's, at that point, the starches are pre-gelatinized and you're good to go. SU: Sure. JS: Yeah. SU: Okay. So, you make a choux, and you said one of the secrets to getting a really dramatic puff is to really beat it aggressively. JS: Yes. SU: Then you're putting it in the oven, and this you bake it in two cake pans. JS: Yes. SU: Which unlike your Paris-Brest, which you bake on a sheet tray. JS: Yeah, like freeform. SU: How do you get these two discs out of the pan? Is it easy to flip out of the pan? JS: Yeah, because you have a parchment round in the bottom of each one, so getting them out is not the hard part. I would actually say that getting the batter in the pan is slightly difficult because it's very sticky, and it's lined with parchment, so it moves around. I would suggest taking a little bit of your choux and making little blobs, and then use- SU: Goo dots. JS: Goo dots, and then gluing your parchment down, and then smearing the choux on top. SU: Got it. JS: And if it's not perfect, it's fine because I found, say, it's uneven, it kind of just adds to the uneven whimsy texture that you're going to get. So, you don't have to be too precious. SU: And what about greasing the sides of the pan? Do we have to- JS: No. SU: Got it. JS: Nope. SU: Not at all. JS: I learned that the hard way. It's kind of like a souffle, when it needs to climb on something, like the sugar. I think that greasing the sides made it too slippery, and it didn't want to expand upward. Yes. SU: Can we extend the same logic to the pan, if somebody uses a non-stick pan? JS: I would not recommend a non-stick cake pan here. Put them on mute, and I was furiously typing away on Google like, "Oh my God, please help me. What is this? What are they talking to me about?" Sorry, Bake Off if you hear this, but yes, I did cheat my way for the- JS: Fraud. RB: Loud and proud, can I just say? And then next thing I know, I was in the tent with people who had been baking since they were five, or been baking with their granny all their life. And everyone was like, "Oh, so how long have you been baking for?" And I was like, "About a year." But I think my inexperience actually really helped me in the tent because I had no expectation. I had none of this. I want to get to halfway point, or I want to get to the final, or I want to win. I was like, "I'm just counting my lucky stars that I made it into the tent." So, it was wonderful. I've made some incredible friends from there. I've had an incredible experience, and it's given me such a wonderful, joyful platform, that it will always be one of my most cherished memories, I think. JS: Are you still in touch with your fellow bakers? RB: There's one in particular who, no matter what I do, I just can't get rid of him. This guy is invited to my family weddings. He came to my cousin's wedding. He baked a cake for my own wedding. He's my best friend, and I couldn't see my life without him. Antony, he was only in the tent for about three weeks, but we bonded from the minute that we first met. Very, very grateful for that. JS: I'm like, "Damn, I need to fill out an application." SU: I know. RB: It's an incredible experience. SU: Is it safe to say that Paul Hollywood doesn't get invited to any family weddings? RB: Oh, absolutely not. That guy will be lucky if he gets a hello here and there. JS: Damn. SU: Okay. We'll move on to a rapid fire question. JS: Yeah. Are you down to answer some? RB: Oh, yeah, absolutely. Let's go for it. JS: What are you bringing to a bake sale? RB: Oh God, this is like asking someone who their favorite child is. This is terrible. Chocolate cake, something like my Brooklyn Blackout from my book. JS: Crowd pleaser, yeah. SU: Yeah. Who do you call in a baking emergency? RB: My friend Antony, for sure. I mean, very rarely will he give me good advice, but he will calm me down. JS: That's me for Shilpa. RB: Yeah. SU: That's both of us. JS: What do you think the best baking smell is? RB: Oh God, laminated pastry, for sure. It's just that waft of butter in the kitchen that really just gets me every single time. Just nothing but butter. Fantastic. SU: Do you have a motto or words that you live by in the kitchen? RB: What's the worst that can happen? JS: Fair enough. Yeah. RB: Literally, every time I have a disaster in the kitchen, I take it as a lesson and a step closer to perfecting something that I wanted to. So, yeah, definitely that. JS: I like that. SU: A great lesson for life. What is the best compliment you've ever received on something you've baked? RB: I remember on Bake Off, everyone would strive for getting a Hollywood handshake, or some praise from Paul, but for me, Prue was a tough cookie to crack. And there was one cake that I made, and she said that she wanted the recipe for it afterwards, and then she came up to me afterwards and said, "Please send that to me." And that for me was a huge compliment. Someone who I've admired in the food industry, she's a strong, fierce woman, who's really made a name for herself in the food industry. And so, to get a compliment like that so early on in what I didn't know then was my baking career was phenomenal. JS: That's a good one. SU: Did you send her the recipe? RB: Well, I sent it on to the production company, so whether she got it or not- JS: Who's going to say? RB: I don't know. But you know what? I did my bit, girl. SU: Yeah, yeah. You certainly did. Okay, that's the end of our rapid fire. Ruby, we really loved having you. JS: Yeah, thank you so much. RB: Thank you. SU: This was such a good conversation. JS: Where can our listeners find you if they want to follow you? RB: You can find me on Instagram and TikTok @rubybhogal, where you can keep up to date with the latest cakes. Hopefully, by the time you hear this, I've finished the cake series, but you never know. We could have another three years in it. Or you can also grab a copy of my new book, which will be out in the States towards the end of September at your local bookstore, on Amazon, at Barnes & Nobles, or your local independent. JS: Beautiful. Thank you so much. SU: Thank you. RB: Thank you. Thank you so much for your time today. JS: That's it for this month's edition of BA Bake Club. Shilpa, do you want to tell our bakers about the September Bake Club recipe? SU: Okay. September's Bake Club recipe is probably the one recipe that we're not actually baking. JS: Oh. SU: September's recipe is for glazed apple pie fritters, because I'm thinking of state fair fritters, and I've never been to a state fair, and I've always wanted to go to one. JS: They're fun. SU: Oh my God, I'm so jealous that you've been to one. How many have you been to state fairs? JS: A handful. SU: Oh my God. JS: Yeah. SU: Anyway, I've always been thinking about these state fair fritters and how they have these big chunks of fruit in them, and I wanted that same sort of chunkiness, but in the texture of a cider donut that you get at the farm stand. JS: Oh, yes, yes, yes, yes. SU: So, this is my version of that. JS: I can attest to their deliciousness. And is there any special equipment or ingredients that bakers should have on hand? SU: Ingredients, I would say get some nice ricotta. I generally like the ones that are in a tin with some holes. JS: Oh, with a big bulbous top? SU: Yeah. JS: Yeah. SU: Can I just name the brand? JS: Yeah, sure. SU: It's Calabro. Calabro has the best ricotta that I had. JS: Yeah, sure, sure, sure. SU: So, that's as far as ingredients go. Get yourself some nice apples. Jesse and I are very partial to Honeycrisp apples, after a few failed attempts with Granny Smith, and you should be good. JS: Yeah. SU: Yeah. JS: Cool. Well, Bake Clubbers, once you bake through the fritters, send us your pictures and questions. There are so many different ways to get in touch. SU: You can comment on the recipe on the Epicurious app, or on the Bon Appétit website. You can comment on our Substack, or you could email us at [email protected]. And if you've made it and loved it, please rate and review the recipe on our site. JS: Or you can tell a friend. If you have a buddy that should be in the Bake Club, share this episode. SU: Oh, good. Are we buddies, Jesse? JS: Oh, baking buddies. We got a package sent to us that said Shilpa and Jesse today. SU: I know. That was our first joint package. JS: Yeah. SU: I'm so touched. JS: Okay. Well, we're your hosts, Jesse Szewczyk. SU: And Shilpa Uskokovic. JS: This month's episode was produced by Emily Elias. SU: Pran Bandi is our studio engineer, and we had editing by Rhiannon Corby. JS: Research editing by Ryan Harrington. SU: This episode was mixed by Amar Lal at Macro Sound. JS: If you like this show, leave us a rating and review, and hit that follow button so you never miss an episode. SU: And if you're not already part of the club, head to bonappetit.com/bakeclub to find all the information you need to join. JS: Thanks for listening to BA Bake Club, and we'll see you next month.

item.title: Magical Midnight Margarita
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.81
Fans of the cult classic film Practical Magic may recognize some version of this cocktail. The “Midnight Margarita” is inspired by a scene in which two characters blend up a witchy brew to the soundtrack of Harry Nilsson’s “Coconut.” Some fans even start the movie at exactly 11:12 p.m., so the pivotal moment arrives at the stroke of midnight. While the movie’s cocktail appears to be a standard standard frozen margarita—no eye of newt or toe of frog, (maybe hair of the dog if you prefer tequila and lime in the morning)—but our version leans into the magic. Blackberries give the drink its deep purple color, while coconut water adds a subtle sweetness and makes the frozen version especially refreshing. Serve it on the rocks or blended. If serving on the rocks, garnish with a torched rosemary sprig for a smoky, spellbinding flourish. More tequila drinks to cheers to at midnight: Paloma; Citrus Slushy; Aperol-Kombucha Cocktail How to make a frozen version: Because freezing can dull flavors, adding a little extra lime juice perks this version up. We’ve also increased the coconut water so you won’t have to dilute the drink with plain ice. | Yield: Makes 1 | Total time: 10 minutes plus chilling | Ingredients - 1 cup coconut water - Flaky sea salt - 3 limes - 5 blackberries - 2 oz. tequila blanco - 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or triple sec) - ½ tsp. sugar Method - Pour 1 cup coconut water into an ice cube tray. Freeze until solid, at least 2 hours or, ideally, 12 hours. - Pour some flaky sea salt on a small plate. Halve 3 limes and rub a cut side of 1 half around rim of a rocks glass; dip rim into salt to coat. Squeeze juice from limes into a small measuring glass or bowl (you should have about 3 oz). - Place 5 blackberries in glass and muddle berries just to break up. - Blend coconut water ice cubes, 2½ oz. lime juice, 2 oz. tequila blanco, 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or triple sec), and ½ tsp. sugar in a blender until smooth. Pour into glass with blackberries. (Save any remaining lime juice in an airtight container in the fridge up to 3 days.) Recipe information - Total Time 10 minutes - Yield Makes 1 Ingredients 2 5 2 2 1 ½ Need to make a substitution? Preparation - Step 1Pour some flaky sea salt on a small plate. Halve 2 limes and rub a cut side of 1 half around rim of a rocks glass; dip rim into salt to coat. Squeeze juice from limes into a small measuring glass or bowl (you should have about 2 oz). Step 2Place 5 blackberries in glass and muddle berries just to break up. Step 3Combine lime juice, 2 oz. coconut water, 2 oz. tequila blanco, 1 oz. orange liqueur (such as Cointreau or Triple Sec), and ½ tsp. sugar in a cocktail shaker filled with ice. Cover and shake until outside of shaker is very cold, about 30 seconds. Step 4Fill glass with blackberries with ice cubes. Strain cocktail over and garnish with a rosemary sprig, briefly singed over a flame, if desired.

item.title: 26 High-Protein Breakfasts for Any Day of the Week
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 3.51
There’s more to high protein breakfast than protein bars and cottage cheese egg bites. (No offense intended, bars and bites: I love your work in a pinch.) When one is not at the airport, though, there are many more options. A high-protein breakfast should give a long-lasting sense of mesatiety and keep energy levels high, of course; but it should also taste good. That’s where our vast Bon Appétit recipe archive comes in. Before we get to the good stuff: What the heck makes a meal high in protein, versus one that simply contains the macronutrient? Depending on who you ask, it should contain about 15 to 30 grams of protein—a rough range based on your body type and activity levels. I’m not going to give you a full macro breakdown of each meal (I’m sure you have an app for that). I will, however, share some suggestions to turn up the protein-dial in these recipes, so you can adjust them to what feels best for you.

item.title: How I Make Protein Pancakes Without Protein Powder
item.description:
Source: Bon Appétit Score: 2.11
Healthy cooking doesn’t have to be complicated. In fact, often the simpler it is, the better it tastes. In Good for You, Test Kitchen editor Rebecca Firkser shares feel-good recipes for any day of the week. The thing about protein powder is that it doesn’t taste good. And that makes sense—it wasn’t designed to be a joyful culinary experience. As with many dietary supplements, it began with nutrition in mind, and morphed into an athletic performance enhancer. For this, we can thank two so-called “fathers” of their time and industries: German bodybuilder Eugen Sandow, a 19th-century proponent of neutral-tasting milk-based protein powderPlasmon, initially used to fortify packaged food products like porridge and cookies; and Bob Hoffman, a 20th-century American weightlifter who’s credited with the first successfully marketed soy- and whey-based “Hi-Proteen,” which was eventually flagged by the FDA for misleading health claims. Decades later, the supplement has become steadily more mainstream, from an almost-fatal smoothie on The White Lotus to Ballerina Farm’s viral Farmer Protein. Show me a person in 2026 who has never consumed a protein-powder-enhanced shake, bar, or “dessert,” or at the very least, wondered if they should. Whether made from whey, soy, peas, or beef, I find protein powder chalky and synthetic-tasting, only valuable in hangry emergencies. And with most powders costing well over a buck per serving, I’d rather just get my protein from food I’ve already purchased. Meat and fish are well-known sources, but plenty of meatless options—like eggs, beans, yogurt, and quinoa—can provide the body with ample protein. Today, I want to highlight one of my favorites: tofu. A beloved vegan protein, pressed soybean curd has graced plates for centuries. You’ll often see American recipes highlight firmer varieties of tofu (which are also the highest in protein), like stir-fries and nuggets. But just as, if not more, versatile is silken tofu. It can be the star of a dish, like this five-minute dinner or an eggless scramble; or sneakily blend into the background, like in this nutty dressing. Thanks to its neutral flavour, it can be even further camouflaged into sweet dishes, like 2-ingredient chocolate mousse or my new Blueberry Protein Pancakes. When blended with usual pancake ingredients, like flour, sugar, and leaveners, silken tofu acts as a binder, much like eggs in a standard recipe. The result is a thick, accidentally-on-purpose-vegan batter, creating fluffy pancakes that fry up with crisp edges. Studded with tart blueberries, they’re hearty and flavorful, and yes, protein-rich. On mornings when I’m craving something more fun for breakfast than my usual bowl of yogurt and muesli or boiled eggs on toast, I’ll reach for a couple of these. Pancakes take a little longer to make, of course, so I’ll whisk up a batch on a weekend and freeze the extras. (Stack between squares of parchment and tuck in a zip-top bag or airtight container.) A quick trip in the toaster and I’m ready to eat. Do tofu pancakes pack the same protein-punch as a powder-fortified shake? Of course not. And that’s okay. We can all stand to remove some of the pressure of optimizing every meal to the highest degree.
