But if you’re really in it for the gains, you still have the rest of the day to keep chipping away at that protein goal. In the meantime, pass the maple syrup.

item.title: TSA’s New PreCheck Perk Allows Non-Ticketed Visitors to Accompany Friends and Family at the Gate
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.44
TSA’s newest PreCheck perk is intended for people who aren’t flying at all. Gateside by TSA PreCheck, which began rolling out this month at 13 US airports, allows eligible non-ticketed visitors to pass through security after receiving advance approval. That means they can accompany someone to a departure gate, meet an arriving traveler airside, visit a friend or relative during a layover, or access the restaurants and shops beyond the checkpoint. The program marks an expansion of an idea that several individual airports have experimented with in recent years: allowing some people without boarding passes back into the secure side of the terminal. But Gateside also raises a more practical question—who actually wants to go through airport security on their own volition when they don’t have a flight to catch? Jennifer Yellin, managing editor at travel rewards platform Points Path, expects the answer to be mostly people helping or meeting someone they know. “I think families will be the ones to use this the most,” Yellin says “I foresee this being the most beneficial for parents accompanying their child for an outbound flight as well as welcoming home family members.” She also sees potential for older travelers, nervous or infrequent fliers, and people navigating unfamiliar airports with the help of a friend or relative. In those cases, Gateside could make it possible for someone to stay alongside a traveler all the way to the gate, rather than saying goodbye before security. “If you have a child, parent, spouse, or even friend who is a nervous flier, being able to walk them to their gate and see them off could help put their nerves to ease,” Yellin says. “It can also be useful to help the same younger or older family member navigate an airport, which might otherwise be challenging. For some travelers, having someone there with you to the very end can put them at ease.” That doesn’t mean Gateside will replace existing assistance available to travelers who need it. Airlines already issue escort or gate passes in certain circumstances, including unaccompanied minors, and airports and airlines offer assistance for travelers with disabilities. Gateside is broader: A visitor doesn’t need to be escorting someone who qualifies for one of those services. Instead, access is based primarily on the visitor’s eligibility for TSA PreCheck screening and approval for Gateside. How Gateside by TSA PreCheck works Gateside is currently being offered as an “operational assessment” at 13 airports, including major hubs such as Dallas Fort Worth International Airport, Los Angeles International Airport, and Salt Lake City International Airport. To use it, visitors need to be eligible for TSA PreCheck screening and have a Known Traveler Number. That includes TSA PreCheck members as well as eligible members of trusted traveler programs such as Global Entry, NEXUS, and SENTRI. The pass itself is free, but visitors have to apply online one to three days before their intended airport visit and select the participating airport they plan to enter. Those who are approved bring an acceptable form of identification to the airport and go through a TSA PreCheck checkpoint; they are still subject to normal security screening and restrictions. An approval is valid for the designated calendar day and allows the visitor to leave and re-enter the secure area that day. Gateside isn’t the first way for a non-ticketed visitor to get beyond airport security. Airports including Seattle, New Orleans, Orlando, Tampa, Palm Springs, and Tulsa already operate their own visitor-pass programs, each with its own rules. Detroit and San Diego have existing visitor programs in addition to being among the first Gateside airports. The distinction with the new TSA program is that Gateside is tied to PreCheck eligibility and gives approved visitors access through the PreCheck screening lane. For the average traveler, Yellin says, the program is still likely to remain fairly niche. “While it's a meaningful change, it's only beneficial for a small group of travelers,” she says. “For the average traveler, it won't change the airport experience since this is limited to a very small subset of airports and advance approval is required.” Seeing off a family member is perhaps the most obvious use for the program, but Gateside could also make it easier to spend time with someone who isn’t beginning or ending their trip in your city. “If you have a friend or family member traveling with a long layover in your home airport, meeting them during their connection is the perfect situation,” Yellin says. “This allows the traveler to stay near their gate without having to leave security.” Currently, meeting a connecting passenger generally requires the traveler to leave the secure area of the airport, then go through security again before continuing their trip. That may not be practical on a shorter connection, particularly at a large airport where getting between the gate and terminal exit can itself take time. With Gateside, the local visitor goes through security instead. Still, Yellin doesn’t expect non-ticketed visitors to start heading to airports simply because they now can. “The airport experience today is tiring for many and extremely different than what it once was,” she says. “Because of that, I do not believe too many people are going to choose to park their car and navigate their way through security, without actually traveling that day, unless they have a very real reason.” The program’s arrival also comes 25 years after the September 11 attacks transformed who could access US airport gate areas. Before 9/11, people without tickets could generally accompany passengers through security; afterward, access to the secure side of terminals became largely limited to ticketed passengers and those with specific authorization. However, Yellin doesn't believe Gateside is a signal that TSA is returning to the old airport model. “Now that it's been 25 years, TSA is experimenting to see how the overall experience can be better for travelers, while still keeping safety in mind,” she says. Airports offering Gateside by TSA PreCheck - Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Arizona - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) in Ohio - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) in Texas - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) in Michigan - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) in Indiana - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) in Nevada - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) in California - Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Arkansas - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma - Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Nebraska - San Diego International Airport (SAN) in California - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) in Utah

item.title: A New Museum, Cruise Haute Couture, and Gorgeous Glassware: Here's What's Exciting Us in Travel Right Now
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 5.40
Whether you're on land or at sea, in a bar or in Bahrain, there are myriad reasons for design lovers to get excited about travel right now. In the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler, we went long on a number of these stories—how Como's enduring craft traditions help make it one of the planet's most luxurious destinations, why Fort Worth is the sartorial epicenter of the rise of ranchcore in fashion. But we also collected a few juicy morsels worth sharing in brief. There's a new museum in the Middle East to earmark if you're interested in the intersection of craft and history, and a French cruise line has launched a new itinerary that will bring haute couture to the high seas. Read on for all we think you should know. A gem of a new museum on Bahrain's pearling path “Inside an elegant home formerly owned by a wealthy merchant family in Bahrain's coastal city of Muharraq sits the two-year-old Siyadi Pearl Museum. The space is the latest addition to the Pearling Path, which connects important structures from the city's pearling history. Along its two miles are 17 significant sites; public squares shaded by flame trees; and a pedestrian bridge that reconnects Muharraq with its original shoreline, which has been mostly lost to development. Terrazzo lampposts topped by pearl-shaped light bulbs double as trail markers. Tales of wealth are told in the grand living quarters of merchants and traders; those of hardship in the display of the simple tools pearl divers relied on (nose clips, stone weights, leather finger covers) during arduous months aboard dhows at sea.” —Nicola Chilton High fashion comes to the high seas “In September 2027, French line Ponant will sail a commonly traveled route along Italy's coast with an entirely unique agenda: placing the country's fashion maisons at the center of the passenger experience. Sailing down the coast from Tuscany and then up to Venice, guests on board the intimate Le Boréal will experience five major haute labels. They will chat with a Brioni tailor about making the perfect alterations; observe a master craftsperson cut precious gemstones at iconic jeweler Pomellato; and explore two historic sites in Florence tied to Gucci via the Palazzo Gucci and the 15th-century Palazzo Settimanni, home to the Gucci archives. Think of this as high fashion on the high seas.” —Erin Florio Drinks wear designer around the globe “Striking, artisanal glassware that upstages the concoction it holds is the coolest thing in cocktail culture these days. Here, bars around the world and the gorgeously unique vessels you may just encounter while there.” —Michelle Tchea This article appeared in the September/October 2026 issue of Condé Nast Traveler. Subscribe to the magazine here.

item.title: Thousands of Flights Disrupted at UK Airports Due to Air Traffic Control Issue
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.84
Several major UK airports are continuing to experience delays and cancellations following an air traffic control technical failure on Tuesday, September 8. The National Air Traffic Services (NATS) has now resolved the issue, which affected its flight processing system, but the disruption is expected to continue through Wednesday as airlines and airports work through backlogged flights. The failure caused widespread disruption across the UK on Tuesday, with FlightRadar24 reporting around 1,300 cancellations to and from UK airports. Heathrow, Gatwick, Manchester, and Stansted were among the airports affected, while the disruption also had knock-on effects at airports across Europe. NATs boss Martin Rolfe has apologized for the disruption, telling the BBC there would be a full investigation into what had gone wrong, after the firm said resolving the issue had taken “longer than hoped.” An official statement on the NATs website reads: “This has been a very complex recovery and has created difficulties for the whole aviation network, from which it will take time to recover.” London Heathrow was particularly impacted. Arrivals were suspended for the remainder of Tuesday, while departures resumed later in the day. The airport has warned that disruption will continue and is advising passengers to check directly with their airline before traveling. A statement on the airport's X account on Wednesday morning reads: “Following yesterday's NATS technical issue, flights are operating today, but some disruption may continue as airlines reposition aircraft and crew. Please check your flight status with your airline before traveling to the airport and only travel if your flight is confirmed to be operating.” FlightRadar24 is currently reporting that 177 flights scheduled for Wednesday, September 9 have already been canceled, with the vast majority at Heathrow, while further delays and cancellations are expected as aircraft and crew displaced by the disruption are repositioned. Can I get a refund if my flight was disrupted? If your flight was delayed or canceled following Tuesday’s air traffic control issues at NATS, you may be entitled to flight compensation. According to the UK Civil Aviation Authority, passengers can claim compensation ranging from £220 (approximately $300) per person to £520 (approximately $700) per person if the delay causes you to reach your destination airport more than three hours late. If the delay is more than five hours, you can choose not to travel and receive a refund. Because air traffic control issues are typically considered “extraordinary circumstances” outside the airline's control, cash payouts aren't likely in this scenario. However, many airlines will still provide food and drink vouchers, airport transfers, and hotel accommodations for overnight delays. If your flight is canceled, the airline is required to provide an alternate flight or full refund. Flight delay compensation in the UK is not automatic, and the procedure for submitting a claim varies by airline. Because the UK is no longer part of the European Union, EU passenger rights only apply to UK flights if it arrives in an EU country and is operated by an EU airline (for example, if you were flying from London to Paris with Air France). Or, if your flight departs from an EU country and arrives in the UK (operated by either an EU or a non-EU airline). Passengers should check the status of their flight and compensation policies directly with their airline and monitor the NATS website and X account for further updates. UK airports reporting disruptions: - London Heathrow Airport - London Gatwick Airport - London Luton Airport - London Stansted Airport - Manchester Airport - Birmingham Airport - Belfast City Airport - Edinburgh Airport - East Midlands Airport - Jersey Airport This is a developing news story and will be updated with more information. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Shoulder Season on Paros: Ceramicist Christiane Smit Finds Inspiration at a Slower Pace
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.51
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to ceramic artist and owner of Moonhouse, Christiane Smit. For Netherlander and artist Christiane Smit, a holiday on Paros in 2008 rerouted the course of her life. “It wasn’t a carefully planned life decision, it was something I felt instinctively,” she says of her unplanned move to the Cycladic island. “I listened to that feeling, stayed, and started building a completely new life on the island.” Having lived all over the island since then, she now operates a ceramics atelier in the village of Lefkes and owns the stunningly minimalist clifftop villa rental Moonhouse—both of which are open to visitors. She is currently completing the restoration of a nearly 100-year-old stone house in the village of Kostos. Here, the now-local shares the shoulder-season delights that keep her on-island year-round as well as her favorite hotel-slash-taverna for a warming meal and stay. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? For me, the sweetest time in Paros is late spring or early autumn. The island feels wonderfully balanced: Everything is open, but life is still unhurried. I love walking through the villages in the morning, when the streets are still quiet. The air smells of jasmine, fresh bread from the bakery, and the sea. You hear church bells, neighbors greeting each other, and the wind moving through the olive trees. The light is what inspires me most. It changes constantly, making the whitewashed houses glow and bringing out every texture in the stone. As a ceramic artist, I find myself collecting those colors, textures, and moments every day. They’re as much a part of my work as the clay itself. What do you love most about being there during this season? The season allows me to slow down and notice everything. The colors of the landscape, the textures of old stone walls, the shifting light on the sea—those details naturally find their way into my ceramics. I don’t have to look for inspiration here; I simply have to pay attention. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? It’s mostly locals. The cafés are filled with familiar faces, fishermen are heading out in the morning, and shop owners have time to stop and chat. You also meet a small number of travelers: The people who aren’t looking for the typical summer vacation, but who want to experience the island more slowly and authentically. There are also Greek visitors escaping the city for a long weekend or visiting family. It’s a lovely mix, but the locals set the rhythm, and that’s what gives Paros its real character. What’s notable about the locals in Paros; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What I’ve come to appreciate most about the people of Paros is their warmth and sense of community. Even though it’s a popular island in summer, life outside the season is very local. People know one another, and there’s a genuine willingness to help each other. As someone who lives here year-round, that’s something I’ve really come to value. There’s also a deep respect for craftsmanship—from marble carving, for which the Cyclades are famous, to fishing, farming, and handmade work. Where would we find you eating during this time? One of my favorite places is the family-run taverna at Hotel Julia in Drios. I love it because it feels authentic and unchanged—a place where generations have welcomed people with simple, honest food and genuine hospitality. My perfect day always starts with a swim in the crystal-clear waters just below the taverna. Afterwards, I walk up for a long, leisurely lunch. There’s something so special about sitting there, the sound of the waves below and nowhere else to be. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? Winter on Paros is the season for revithada (slow-baked chickpea stew), hearty bean soups, and goat or lamb braised with local wine—dishes that are more like daily specials rather than menu staples. But if there’s one meal that defines the island’s quieter months, it’s whatever is cooking in the pot that day (mageirefta). That’s what locals order, and every taverna has its own depending on the day. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? I wouldn’t say any one area suddenly comes alive in the off-season; it feels more like the island returns to its natural rhythm. While Parikia is the social hub for year-round residents, it’s the villages—Lefkes, Marpissa, Prodromos, Kostos, and Dryos—that reveal the character of Paros through seasonal festivals, religious celebrations, and community events. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? You get cooler temperatures; crisp, sunny days; and the occasional rainstorm, which turns the landscape unexpectedly green. The island feels softer and more vibrant. For me, one of the greatest advantages is the sense of calm. Of course, there are a few trade-offs. Stronger winter weather systems can occasionally disrupt ferry schedules, and many seasonal businesses close until spring. But these are minor inconveniences. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect Saturday begins slowly with a coffee in my house, catching the first sunlight. From there, I’ll often wander through Lefkes, Marpissa, or Prodromos before a long lunch at a traditional taverna. In the afternoon, I usually head back to my ceramic studio. The quieter months are when I’m most creative. Without the intensity of the summer season, there’s space to observe, reflect, and create. At sunset, I love taking a walk along one of the beaches or coastal paths. Even in winter, there are many clear, sunny days, and the light over the Aegean is extraordinary. I usually end the day with friends over a simple meal and a glass of wine. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love walking the ancient Byzantine paths that weave between villages. With few people on the trails, the silence becomes part of the journey. This winter is especially meaningful, as I’ll be putting the finishing touches on a small renovation project in the village of Kostos, a space I’ve been shaping with the same care and intention that I bring to my ceramics. Creating a home is, in many ways, another form of making, and I find great joy in both! This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: 'The Gentlemen' Season 2 Takes Us From English Country Estates to Italian Palazzos in Mob Territory
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.28
On Location peels back the curtain on some of your favourite films, television shows, and more. This time, we ask: where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The second season of Guy Ritchie’s hit Netflix series, The Gentleman, is here. The first series introduced us to Eddie Horniman (Theo James), a young British aristocrat who had inherited his father’s grand country estate, only to discover that behind the family money was a secret cannabis empire. In Season 2, Horniman, now the Duke of Halstead, is keen to expand the operation, alongside his business partner, Susie Glass (Kaya Scodelario). This will take them out of the English countryside and subterranean criminal worlds of the East End and Liverpool, and thrust them instead into the world of the Mafia, as they attempt to go international and do business with the dangerous Capo dei Capi, Marco Moretti (Sergio Castellito). “The madness of Italy’s beauty, its culture, its history and its traditions was something I felt would fit perfectly into our show,” says Ritchie. “I had wanted to expand the canvas of The Gentlemen in this season. Italy was just an obvious choice. British gangsters colliding with the Italian Mafia just feels so right for our world. Some fruit hangs low and looks so tasty you just can’t resist for very long.” Here are some of the key locations used in the filming of The Gentleman Seasons 1 and 2, from Ritchie’s Ashcombe Estate to Lake Maggiore in Italy. Is The Gentlemen based on a real-life story? Both the film of the same name and the two seasons of The Gentlemen are not based on a true story, though of course, they borrow elements from the criminal underworld and its cast of characters. The situation that Eddie Horniman and his family find themselves in – of having to find new ways to monetise their vast aristocratic estates – is a reality, however. There are no real life examples of aristocrats running cannabis empires that we know of though. The main thrust of the action in Season 2 of The Gentlemen takes place in Lake Maggiore, connecting Horniman and his business partner Katie Glass to Italy’s criminal gangs – the mafia. Historically, the area has not been known as a mafia heartland – unlike regions like Sicily, for example – but it does have a relationship with organised crime. In particular, the ’Ndrangheta, the Calabrian mafia, have reportedly used the area for cocaine and weapons trafficking, thanks to its close proximity to the Swiss border. Where was The Gentlemen Season 2 filmed? The Badminton Estate, Gloucestershire While some scenes of The Gentleman were filmed on stage sets at Alperton Studios in Wembley, London, the exterior of Halstead Manor, the fictional home of the Horniman family, is The Badminton Estate. The real-life home of the Duke and Duchess of Beaufort is a popular filming location and wedding venue in the south Gloucestershire countryside. Viewers with a keen eye may recognise the property from Netflix favourite Bridgerton and movies including Pearl Harbour and 28 Days Later. The sprawling estate has been occupied for thousands of years, and the remains of several Roman villas surround the main home. The medieval property was owned by the Boteler family before Edward Somerset, fourth Earl of Worcester, purchased the manors of Great and Little Badminton in 1612. It’s his son, Sir Thomas Somerset, who made significant alterations to the original house, and the property has captured the imagination of high society and even the royal family over the centuries – Charles II stayed in the house, and the late Queen Elizabeth II was a regular visitor to the annual Horse Trials. “Badminton felt immediately right for Halstead,” says supervising location Manager Iggy Ellis, “because it’s a proper, lived-in home rather than a National Trust museum. So inside, there’d be some walking sticks by the door or a few shotgun rounds from where they’d been out shooting. There were cracks and tired bits, as you’d get in every family home. But there was also oil painting and history and majesty. It felt perfect for our story.” Ashcombe Estate, Wiltshire In episode one, Ritchie made his own country estate, Ashcombe Park, available for filming a shooting party scene. “That was a lot of fun but tricky at times too,” says production designer Martyn John. “You’re in the middle of nowhere with no phone signal or internet. We had to take everything in; so, flowers, food, dogs, guns and also… frozen partridges.” Ashcombe is a working farm set in 1,100 acres of rolling chalk land, and is named after the ash trees and the valleys (‘combes’) that monopolise much of it. It has been the family home of Ritchie since 2001 (when he bought it with ex-wife Madonna for £9 million), and was previously the home of photographer Cecil Beaton. Loseley Park, Surrey Much like in season one, some of the exterior and interior scenes at Halstead Manor were filmed at Loseley Park, a historic home just outside of Guildford that is now used as a wedding venue. “Where possible we tried to maximise every location because when you move around it costs money that could be on the screen,” explains supervising locations manager Iggy Ellis. “So we used a cottage in the grounds of Loseley for the exteriors of gamekeeper Geoff’s cottage and built the interior in the studio because we needed lots of camera space and somewhere for Geoff’s menagerie of animals.” Swakeleys House, Ickenham Another multi-purpose location was Swakeleys House, a 17th-century mansion in Ickenham. “It was a great find because we were able to use it for so many things,” explains Ellis. “From the rehab centre where Freddie is recovering from the cocaine habit he acquired in the first series to the interior of the prison where Bobby Glass is meant to be serving time.” Built in 1638, it is an excellent example of the ‘Artisan Mannerism’ architectural style, a form of Jacobean architecture that features decorative classical flourishes such as gable ends. It was the home of Sir Edmund Wright, Lord Mayor of London, and was visited twice by the famed diarist Samuel Pepys. The Adelphi Building, London The Adelphi Building off The Strand was transformed into an auction house for a scene in which Susie Glass bids millions for a Botticelli painting, which is later snatched by a gang on e-bikes outside. “I wanted to use that network of streets around the Savoy Hotel, including a secret little tunnel that cuts between John Adam Street and the riverside,” explains Ellis of the chase. “It takes at least three months’ notice to get London streets closed for filming, and there were some careful negotiations with everyone from Westminster Council to building owners and the Savoy Hotel itself. But that amazing chase really is one of the things I’m most proud of.” The Grade II-listed Adelphi has retained many of its original 1930s Art Deco features, including its impressive stone facade, classic columns and Gilbert Ledwood sculptures. Today it is predominantly used as an office space, and houses the publisher Condé Nast, whose titles include not only Condé Nast Traveler, but also Vogue, Tatler and GQ. Villa Rusconi Clerici, Lake Maggiore Villa Rusconi Clerici became the glamorous palazzo home of Mafia heiress (and Eddie’s love interest) Contessa Isabella Savanza de Parme, known as Bella. “We spent three full days looking at several amazing palazzos, including one on Lake Como,” shares John. “But as soon as I saw the one at Lake Maggiore, I knew this was the one. It was in a much less touristy area and it had such great light and glittering water. You could point the camera anywhere and it just looked beautiful.” The interiors too were perfect for Bella’s home. “I wanted a house or a villa which reflected the taste – if not the scale – of Eddie’s country estate, Halstead Manor” says Ellis. “I wanted these two aristocratic families to merge, stylistically. So, you have all the antiques and the paintings that reflect tradition and ancestry, but also modern pieces because, despite the centuries-old history of both families, there’s a new generation in charge now.” Villa Rusconi Clerici is a beautifully preserved 19th-century palazzo on the Piedmont shore of Lake Maggiore, and unsurprisingly is popular as a wedding venue. The villa that exists today was built for a Hungarian colonel and revolutionary, Stefano Türr, who was married to one of Emperor Napoleon’s cousins and became intrinsic to the unification of Italy. The interiors are Art Nouveau in style, including a grand staircase featuring a wrought iron balustrade. Grand Hotel Majestic, Lake Maggiore The Grand Hotel Majestic stood in for the fictional The Grand Hotel, where a wedding takes place later in the series. First built in 1870, it was one of the finest examples of luxury hospitality in the area, and was immediately popular with the international elite. Unsurprisingly, considering its location on the shores of Lake Maggiore, it is often chosen as a wedding venue for modern couples, much like in the show. One of its chief assets is the view across the lake to Borromeo Island, with actor Theo James pictured standing on one of the balconies looking out across the water in one scene. While the interiors are French in style, with parquet flooring and chandeliers, the grounds are also particularly lavish, with centuries-old trees and flowers, and there’s even a small private beach. Chiesa San Leonardo, Lake Maggiore The 16th-century church Chiesa San Leonardo also features in the new season. Located in the lakeside village of Pallanza, the church features striking columns of pink Baveno granite, as well as 17th-century wooden sculptures and altars. There’s also a 65-metre high bell tower, as well as access to the lake from a dramatic staircase. Where was The Gentleman Season 1 filmed? Stoke Court, Buckinghamshire The Badminton Estate gets much of the credit for appearing as the exterior of the fictional Halstead Manor, but some of the interior scenes used Stoke Court in Buckinghamshire. Stoke Court is home to the study, where Freddie shoots Liverpudlian drug dealer Tommy after a memorable scene featuring a chicken costume, Halstead Manor’s boot room, drawing room and orangery. The real-life property is best known for its association with mid-18th-century poet Thomas Gray, who holidayed there during his childhood. Wrotham Park, Hertfordshire Wrotham Park in Hertfordshire plays the part of the home of extravagantly wealthy drug lord Stanley Johnson, aka Bridgewater House. The neo-Palladian English country house was designed by Isaac Ware in 1754, and it’s where we see Susie Glass and Stanley engage in a polite-ish war of words over his desire to take over her father’s empire. London The Gentleman’sfilming locations depict two sides of the coin: lavish country houses owned by the landed gentry and hideouts used by the criminal underworld. For the latter, the locations team looked to London. Locations used across the capital include The Reform Club in Pall Mall, which doubled up for Pinky’s Club, and Billingsgate Market, which is mentioned by name in the series as the headquarters of the Liverpudlian drug group. The exterior shots of the Croydon Tower Block were taken at Brandon Estate, while the boxing ring is the now-closed party venue Printworks in Rotherhithe.

item.title: You Can Now Book the 'Sterling Point' Cottage on Airbnb—and the Inside Might Surprise You
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.02
Great news for anyone who fell in love with Muskoka after watching Sterling Point but didn't inherit a lake house from their estranged grandfather: Gordon Bay Cottage, the actual property at the center of the hit show, is officially coming to Airbnb. In the Prime Video series, protagonist Annie Rubin makes a pilgrimage to the property—located on a fictional island called Sterling Point—after finding out it has been willed to her after the death of her grandfather, Gordon. Now, fans will be able to call this same cottage home, at least for a few nights, thanks to an Airbnb sweepstakes allowing guests to request one of three special stays at the five-bedroom lakeside lodge this fall. Bookings open on September 15 at 9 a.m. ET, and the stays will take place October 2 to 5, October 9 to 12, and October 16 to 19, with a price tag of $180 a night. If you're looking to cosplay as Annie, Ellis, Connor, or Ramona, set your alarm now—these dates are going to go quick. While Gordon Bay Cottage serves as the façade for Gordon's cottage, interior scenes were filmed on a soundstage in Toronto, about two hours south of Muskoka. That means while the outside of the home will look familiar—cedar-shingled gables, wraparound porch, stone steps leading down to the water, Muskoka chair–dotted dock—the interiors aren't what you'd expect. In fact, they're way more upscale. While Gordon's place in the show looks like it hasn't been updated in a few decades, the property up for grabs on Airbnb appears fresh and modern, with hardwood floors, bright white walls, and contemporary but comfortable furniture. Probably not Ramona's style, but definitely ideal for a luxurious long weekend on the lake. The real Gordon Bay Cottage also sits right on Lake Joseph, one of the most popular and sought-after lakes in the Muskoka region, which means a stay here will come with all the trappings of a classic Canadian summer getaway. Sweepstakes winners should come with their Roots sweatpants and be prepared to “shower” in the lake, drink some Steam Whistles around the firepit, drive their boats to dinner, and gulp down some fresh air while staring at the stars. Ready to experience all that cottage country has to offer but afraid you won't be able to score a stay at Gordon Bay Cottage? Lucky for you, there are plenty of other incredible rentals in Muskoka, and we've found the best of the best. Between Sterling Point, Heated Rivalry, and Every Year After, this stunning slice of Ontario is more popular than ever (no, really, Airbnb searches from outside Canada for check-ins through November 2026 are up nearly 110% year over year, according to the vacation rental brand), so if you want to secure a lakeside spot for next summer, you'd be wise to start looking—and booking—now.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: Fall in Santorini Through the Eyes of Winemaker Michael Kouloglou
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 4.01
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to winemaker Michael Kouloglou. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, the decision to move from the mainland to Santorini 11 years ago was a simple one. “It is the mecca of Greek white wine,” he says. Since relocating here from the Athenian Riviera town of Piraeus, he’s worked with a number of local wineries before launching Orycton, his small-batch Assyrtiko featuring grapes grown on old vines from all over the island. It was a winner at the 2023 Decanter World Wine Awards. On top of the siren’s song of Santorini’s prized volcanic terroir, however, Kouloglou says he appreciates that the region’s windy conditions allow him to pursue his other passions: surfing and kitesurfing. He’s currently settled in Monolithos, a quiet seaside village in the east—but has historically lived all over Santorini, which has offered him great insight into the rhythm of the island. “Each village has its own unique character,” he says, “far beyond the image [of Santorini] that most visitors see.” Here, the longtime Santorini local shares why autumn is his favorite time of year—and all the treasures of the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit—when the travelers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? If I had to choose the best time to visit, I would choose the entire off-season, from late September until around May. Every part of [offseason] has its own personality: Autumn brings relief after harvest, winter offers complete peace, and spring fills the island with optimism as nature comes back to life, just before the new season begins. What do you love most about being there during the off-season? Santorini has two completely different lives. One is the island that millions of visitors experience during summer. The other begins in October and lasts until spring. That is the Santorini only the people who live here truly get to know. By the end of harvest [in September], both the vineyard and I are exhausted. After weeks of living on adrenaline, my body is desperately asking for rest. Around the end of September, the evenings become cooler; you need a sweater after sunset, the days grow shorter, and the strong summer meltemi (the Aegean wind) gives way to a gentler, northern wind. Everything feels softer. All the locals are tired after another demanding [tourism] season, but at the same time, there is a feeling of optimism. Restaurants and bars begin to close for the season, and that's when the closing parties begin. Friends you haven't seen for months suddenly reappear. You don't even need to make plans; you know you'll see them somewhere during a closing party. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travelers at all? During autumn, you'll still find some travelers, but they are completely different from the summer crowds. They usually come looking for a quieter side of Santorini. They enjoy walking, hiking, discovering wineries and small villages, instead of rushing from one attraction to the next. By the end of November, even the last seasonal workers have left the island. We have a saying here that the last boat has sailed. From that moment on, Santorini belongs almost entirely to its locals. Conversations become longer, people have time for each other again, and everyday life feels calmer. I think that's the Santorini most visitors never get the chance to experience. What’s notable about the locals in Santorini? Do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? One thing that has always impressed me about the locals is how deeply everyday life is connected to the Orthodox Church and its traditions. Almost every small chapel on the island has its own patron saint, and every saint's feast day is celebrated with a panigiri, a traditional village festival. During the summer, many of these celebrations continue late into the night with traditional music, dancing, and plenty of local wine. What I also find fascinating is that many of the locals still organize their year around the feast days of the saints. They won't say, "I'll start pruning in late November." They'll say, "I'll start after Saint Philip's Day and I have to finish before Saint Alexius's Day." That's how they measure time. It's a tradition that has been passed down from generation to generation, and it's still very much alive today. Where would we find you eating during this time? During the off-season, you will most likely find me at Pentozali, a traditional taverna that serves authentic mezze from both Santorini and Crete. I absolutely love it for its relaxed atmosphere, its genuine food, and its people. What I appreciate most during this time of year is that it becomes a gathering spot almost exclusively for locals. It is very common for me to run into someone who has just finished a hard day's work in the vineyards. We’ll sit down together for a glass of wine and a little chat, with absolutely no rushing around. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? If you are lucky and the spring timing is right, the dish to order is definitely an omelette with wild asparagus. It’s a rare treat because you can't just find it every day; it completely depends on whether someone woke up early in the morning and gathered the wild asparagus fresh from the countryside. Another staple that is almost always on the table is our traditional Santorini fava topped with sautéed onions. It is incredibly simple, but when cooked properly, you truly don't need anything more. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? As the summer venues close, the life of the island doesn't disappear; it just shifts to the places where people actually live year-round. Areas like Karterados and Messaria become the real hubs. They are central points on the island that stay busy and full of life all year. The local closing parties of fall range from wild gatherings by the beach bars to more laid-back evenings in traditional cafés and small local hangouts. Later, in the winter, as people begin gathering more at homes, these central areas remain the heart of our social life. But if you want to talk about a completely hidden side of Santorini that comes alive in a very quiet, spiritual way, it’s the Askitaria. These are old stone monk lodgings perched right on the edge of the cliff on the mountain between Perissa and Kamari. In the spring, you will find many locals sitting there for hours, doing nothing in particular but gazing out at the endless blue, the passing ships, and distant islands like Anafi, Ios, and Anydro. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Autumn and winter are much warmer and sunnier than most people expect. They bring a rare, beautiful peace. For us winemakers, even the rain is a blessing, not bad weather. It’s a relief to see the vines finally get a drink after months of summer drought. The main disadvantage—if you can call it that—is the unpredictability. March, for instance, is a strange and stubborn month with strong winds, cold snaps, and constant weather shifts. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect off-season Saturday starts slowly, without checking my watch—perhaps walking through the narrow paths of the caldera in Fira or Oia. Later, I would meet up with friends. There is always an excuse for an impromptu barbecue, either with meat or, even better, fresh seafood; almost every group of friends here has at least one good fisherman. We would share a coffee or wine, talk without any rush, and if we are lucky, someone might randomly pick up a lute, a tsampouna, or a violin. No big plans or appointments needed, just letting the night unfold naturally. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? My favorite activities are tied to the water. The Aegean is ideal for kitesurfing due to its consistent winds, and as paradoxical as it may sound, specific weather systems often generate great surf here during the winter. We have a small but tight-knit community of surfers on the island, and when the conditions are right, we all head out into the water. Even though the water is still cold, the feeling is incredible. Sometimes you might even catch people paddleboarding inside the Caldera with absolutely no sea traffic, no cruise ships or catamarans, just you traveling parallel to the old quarries and rusty iron piers that hold the island’s history. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: Boston’s Best Lobster Rolls Include a Secret Off-Menu Pick
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.62
New Englanders grow up on unfussy seafood like lobster rolls the way other people grow up on tacos or barbecue—foods so embedded in the way of life of a particular place that you don’t realize how special they are until you start traveling. Now, when I’m away from home, I find that lobster rolls are seen as an expensive delicacy. Yes, lobster rolls are special; they exist in the city’s glitzier and fine-dining restaurants, and their prices have skyrocketed in more recent years. But they’re also just as common at fast food counters in the suburbs and fishmonger docks up and down the coast. And just like paying $6 a gallon for gas on a California road trip, or $43 for a martini at Bemelman’s Bar in Manhattan, having a lobster roll in Boston is a worthwhile investment every once in a while. It's simply what you do when you’re here. That being said, not all lobster rolls are created equal—and many (sometimes controversial) variations exist. A purist will say that a proper one must—must!—be served on a split-top bun that’s been griddled until golden brown, while others make compelling arguments for fancy swaps like brioche rolls. Then there’s the lobster meat itself, served either as a simply dressed cold salad (Maine style) or warm and buttered (Connecticut style)—but that’s more of a personal preference. The good news? There are many, many lobster rolls to experience in Boston, ranging from textbook classics to more chef-driven interpretations. Here's where to find the best. Row 34 Chef Jeremy Sewall knows a thing or two about good fish, and his popular Row 34 restaurants (with locations in Fort Point and in Cambridge’s Kendall Square) are where you go for excellent beer, interesting wines, and a chef’s sensibility. Here, the lobster roll is surprisingly personal, with lobster sourced from chef Sewall’s cousin Mark, who captains a boat in York Harbor, Maine. There are two versions here: a warm buttered roll with steamed tail, claw and knuckle meat and tucked into a traditional split-top bun; and the other, the Ethel’s Creamy Lobster Roll, named for Sewall’s grandmother and folded together with celery, red onion, pickles, mayonnaise, crème fraîche, lemon, celery salt and black pepper. The cold, creamy one comes on a rosemary brioche bun that is griddled to order and is nothing short of heavenly. James Hook & Co. James Hook & Co. is the alpha and omega of Boston lobster rolls; a platonic ideal of what a lobster roll should be. The family-run seafood business operating on the Boston waterfront for over 100 years is an adorable, unassuming shack on shiny, transformed Atlantic Avenue downtown—this is where any good lobster roll tour of the city should begin (or end). The company ships over 50,000 pounds of lobster daily, both online and to wholesale distributors nationwide, so they know a thing or two about quality. The rolls here come in two sizes and two styles, either chilled or warm with butter. While you’re here, don’t overlook the other seafood specialties; the double-stuffed scallop, clam chowder, and lobster mac and cheese make for a perfect shared side. Saltie Girl If James Hook is the lobster roll in its natural habitat, Saltie Girl is its glamorous, city-slicker cousin. This stylish Back Bay restaurant slings some of the best seafood on Newbury Street, in an elegant yet playful dining room overlooking the boutiques of Newbury Street. Its classic New England-style lobster rolls arrive perfectly coiffed, alongside a charmingly branded bag of Saltie Girl potato chips (add some caviar from the raw bar if you like). But the real insider move here? Ask your server about the secret, off-menu version of the lobster roll: the meat comes fried, sprinkled with Korean chili flakes and sweet corn butter, resulting in something richer, spicier, and considerably more decadent than a traditional version. It’s a sterling reminder that, even in a historic city like Boston, we don’t have to take our classics so seriously. The Banks Seafood and Steak The Banks is a crowd-pleaser of a restaurant—a perfect location in Back Bay, a lively bar scene, and an elevated menu of New England classics. The lobster roll here is an example of a perfectly adventurous recipe where the chef has improved on the original with a few tweaks, but none so heretical that they feel like a major departure from tradition. It comes on a house-made brown-butter bun, sprinkled with sea salt and chives, and served with Old Bay potato chips. The hot lobster roll is a standout—it’s par-cooked, then warmed in a “lobster beurre monté,” a classic French technique that glazes the meat and also helps infuse more lobster flavor into it. The result is a roll that is deceptively simple, yes, bursting with flavor. Eventide Fenway Originally from Portland, Maine, Eventide brought its contemporary take on New England seafood to the Fenway neighborhood as a seafood counter in 2017 before evolving into a full-service restaurant in 2023. The experience here is decidedly more Boston than Maine—it’s a bustling, popular spot for pre-Fenway Park drinks and snacks, less of a cozy, James Beard-recognized eatery than its progenitor in Portland—but Eventide did one key invention with it for the Hub: its brown butter lobster rolls. They come on a fluffy, bao-style steamed bun, drenched (in a good way) with browned butter and flecked with sliced chives. The Sail Loft Nestled on the fringes of the North End within steps of the Freedom Trail, Faneuil Hall and the restaurants of Hanover Street, this institution feels like it’s been here forever. The Boston Sail Loft’s lobster roll is classic, with chilled lobster salad lightly dressed with mayonnaise and piled generously into a toasted bun. The thick, crispy fries that accompany it are a departure from the canonical bag of chips, but they’re a nice touch. There are fancier lobster rolls in Boston—but with perfect execution, stiff drinks and waterfront views, what else would you need? Red’s Best at Boston Public Market A great, no-frills option for travelers who want to understand where their seafood actually comes from, this counter inside Boston Public Market is dedicated to small, independent New England fishermen. And that direct connection to the local fishing community is what makes this experience special. The market itself—just steps from the Freedom Trail—is an easy stop while sightseeing, especially if you’re in the Faneuil Hall, North End, or Beacon Hill areas. The lobster rolls fresh and unfussy. While there’s no waterfront view or white tablecloth, there is something very Boston about enjoying solid seafood in a bustling public market surrounded by Bostonians going about their everyday lives. Plus: Save room for a doughnut from Union Square Donuts, or a popover from The Popover Lady. The Barking Crab Right across Fort Point Channel from James Hook & Co., you’ll find The Barking Crab, another old-school spot where the lobster rolls are classic, but the atmosphere is decidedly more festive. This ramshackle seafood restaurant feels like a relic from the old Seaport, before the neighborhood redeveloped into an epicenter of glass towers and luxury condos. The location makes it especially appealing on warmer days, and the vibe is a little rowdy (in a good way). The lobster roll here is a straightforward expression—toasted roll, available either tossed with mayo or “naked” with warm, butter-poached lobster meat—but if you’re really feeling like splurging, opt for the “One and Done”: whereas most rolls come with about one-fourth a pound of meat, this one comes with a solid one pound, for a whopping $150. Worth it? After a few beers or cocktails, you bet. Yankee Lobster Co. Venture into the Seaport, keep cruising past all the newfangled developments, and you’ll eventually find yourself at Yankee Lobster Co., which has been serving seafood here for roughly 75 years, making it one of the increasingly rare links to the city’s working waterfront in this part of town. That history is part of the appeal, and the lobster roll is comfortingly old-school: generously portioned, straightforward, crafted from the freshest lobster. Come here if you want a classic Boston seafood experience without the polish or price tags of the Seaport’s flashier restaurants. Sullivan’s Castle Island A visit to Castle Island—which is actually not an island, but the tip of the peninsula known as South Boston, or “Southie”—is a beloved Boston ritual. You walk or bike to the far edge of Southie, go for a waterfront stroll around Fort Independence, the oldest continuously fortified site in British North America, then stop for a refueling at Sullivan’s, so much a part of the fabric of Boston life that it received a James Beard Foundation America’s Classics Award. This is not the lobster roll to choose if you’re looking for culinary drama—it’s the one you choose when you want to eat seafood like a Boston local.

item.title: The World’s Most Beautiful Libraries Worth Traveling For
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.61
The most beautiful libraries have long been more than places to check out books, though some make a particularly compelling case for lingering. As a demand for third places to gather outside of home or work continues to grow, libraries are having a moment as prime spots for idling, browsing, and simply taking a break from the bustle beyond their opulent doors. Libraries have taken on an array of forms around the world, as reading rooms that have been tucked into former monasteries, designed as futuristic cultural hubs, and constructed in the heart of the California redwoods. While the books are still the main attraction, it certainly doesn’t hurt to be surrounded by ornate frescoes or unexpected nooks that make you want to stay a while longer. From Colombia to Qatar, these 11 libraries are worth building into your next trip, whether you are architecture-obsessed or longing to sit down in a picturesque setting with a new read. This article has been updated with new information since its original publish date.

item.title: The Quiet Magic of Greece in the Off Season
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.58
Few eras of Greek history compare to the ancient times that the country has become so synonymous with—the cinematic fables of Odysseus, comic-book lore of Leonidas, and philosophic creeds of Socrates are ever-present in pop culture. But anyone who’s been to Hellas in the past few years can tell you that something new is brewing here—current-day Greece is coming close to a similar precipice, one that could be nearly as definitive as the Bronze Age, as visitors arrive in droves higher than ever before. Arrivals to the nation of 10 million people were up by 38% in the first few months of 2026, the highest increase on the continent for that period by far (Italy was second, with a 21% rise). Now, more than ever, it feels like everyone is planning a seafaring escape or mountain adventure to Athens and the islands—or, if you’re in-the-know, to the serene coastal towns of the Peloponnese peninsula or the northern Aegean’s sparkling Thermaic Gulf. One decade after the country’s financial crisis peaked, and a half decade since the pandemic-era halt in tourism that had so many here pleading for the long-despised cruise ships to return, you would think this is good news for a state as tourism-dependent as Greece. And you could be right—but the unfortunate reality, according to the Bank of Greece, is that the crescendo coincides with mounting climate disasters that threaten the infrastructure of a nation still in the throes of recovery; a particularly harrowing warning ahead of this year’s El Niño; not to mention during their Mediterranean neighbors' unprecedented fire seasons. The seasonal pressure has become a balancing act. The good news, though, is that summer is far from the only time to visit. Outside the grip of sweltering summer heat lies some of Greece’s most delicious adventures: tasting early spring’s olive oils straight from the groves right after harvest; fall parties with small-island locals celebrating another season of panigiria wrapped; perusing the treasures of Athens’ open-air ruins in the soft, pre-winter light. There is so much more to Greece than the postcard islands—and the packed ferries to get to them—and with the mainland about to have its moment in the sun (we’re looking at you, Christopher Nolan), there’s no better time than the off-season to uncover every corner’s most spectacular self—the one without the heaving crowds. To prove it, we’ve tapped the best local creators to share how they do it, and how you can, too, siga siga (more slowly). —Shannon McMahon, senior destinations editor Over the last 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has made Ammos Hotel (and its beloved on-site Red Jane Bakery) one of Crete’s most talked-about hotels. Born and raised in Chania, the owner’s joyful, design-led approach to hospitality is rooted in his hometown, with 80% of his staff also locals. From its high-quality cuisine to its warm, home-away-from-home atmosphere, Ammos reflects Tsepetis’s deep connection to Chania. Here, he shares why spring is his favorite time to experience the city. For Dutch artist Christiane Smit, a vacation on Paros in 2008 changed the course of her life. Drawn instinctively to the Cycladic island, she stayed and has lived in villages across Paros ever since. Today, she runs a ceramics atelier in Lefkes and owns minimalist clifftop villa Moonhouse, while restoring a century-old stone house in Kostos. Here, Smit shares the shoulder-season pleasures that keep her on the island year-round, and where to eat and stay. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, moving to Santorini from Greece's mainland 11 years ago was an easy choice: “It is the mecca of Greek white wine.” Since then, he has worked across the island’s wineries before launching Orycton, a small-batch Assyrtiko made with grapes from old vines. Now based in quiet Monolithos, Kouloglou has lived throughout Santorini, gaining an intimate understanding of its villages, landscapes, and rhythms. Here, he shares why autumn is his favorite season to explore the island. Greek family recipes are often passed down by instinct rather than instruction—a pinch here, a glug there, learned at the kitchen table. Food writer Anastasia Miari has spent nearly a decade documenting these dishes and the older generations and remote villages that have kept them alive. Her cooking celebrates Greece’s culinary traditions, while her latest book, Mediterranea, expands the journey across the region, from Moroccan tagines and Turkish breakfasts to Sicilian pasta. “Alive. That’s how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. Having lived in the capital since she was 18, Sbokou has watched the city continually evolve, while retaining its irresistible energy. For her, the joy of visiting somewhere lies in understanding its local rhythm. Here, she shares why autumn is so magical in Athens, alongside some of her favorite places to explore in the city. Lead editors: Sarah Allard, Shannon McMahon, Arati Menon, Lisa Riehl Writers: Shannon McMahon, Chadner Navarro, Noo Saro-Wiwa, Olivia Morelli Visuals and social media: Sophie Knight, Mercedes Bleth, Lucy Bruton Syndication editors: Kat Chen, Skyli Alvarez This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: The Best Luxury Cruise Lines Now Rival the Finest Hotels
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.53
The luxury cruising landscape—or seascape, rather—has grown tremendously over the past few years. And it's no longer just traditional ocean cruises. Travelers accustomed to the finer things in life can now have their pick among expedition vessels plying previously inaccessible polar regions, sumptuous river ships sailing from the Amazon to the Mekong, and flashy new superyachts worthy of Page Six. Aboard, passengers can expect all the same perks they'd find at the world's most exclusive hotels, from personal butlers to multi-story penthouses. This year alone has seen a boom in ultra-luxe yachts, built not by established names in the cruising industry but rather by hotel brands. Sailing with far fewer passengers, they give the vibe more of a private charter or a floating hotel than a traditional cruise ship, with thoughtful approaches to dining and design. Scheduling, too, is shifting. Many posh lines are extending Mediterranean itineraries into the shoulder season and even winter, meaning there are more options for luxury voyages than ever before. Not to be left behind, the old guard—Regent Seven Seas Cruises, Seabourn, Crystal—are continuously making adjustments to meet the needs of today's luxury traveler. Regent is reducing the passenger count on Explorer Class ships to expand cabin sizes while readying to unveil the opulent Seven Seas Prestige ship in December. Seabourn will soon announce a fleet-wide makeover of its culinary programs. Crystal, which has dropped “Cruises” from its brand name, is readying the new-build Crystal Grace for June 2028. Luxury is also creeping aboard expedition ships. Silversea extends its all-suite, butler-outfitted, complimentary caviar philosophy to four exploration vessels, including the Galapagos-only 100-passenger Silver Origin. Scenic Luxury Cruises & Tours, now sailing two sleek 270-passenger yachts capable of polar cruising, debuts 270-passenger Scenic Ikon with two helicopters, a submersible, and 15 dining venues in April 2028. Luxe French line Ponant scores with 245-passenger Le Commandant Charcot, the only luxury icebreaker at sea and can sail to the true North Pole. Seabourn sails the 264-passenger Seabourn Venture and twin Seabourn Pursuit, two lavish all-suite polar-class expedition ships cruising remote itineraries, each with two submarines. All of this to say, there’s never been a better time to hop aboard a luxury cruise line. Below, we round up the names to know across all categories. Yacht The 94-passenger Amangati, which is now open for reservations and will set sail in spring 2027, embodies the hotel brand’s space and privacy design, and even offers a two-deck spa with a Japanese serenity garden. It’s so catered to the one-percenter that it offers “host suites” for passengers’ personal service or security staff as well as two helipads. Consider this ship particularly ripe for charter. The 95-suite, residential-leaning Four Seasons I, which debuted in March 2026, has a one-to-one passenger-crew ratio, meaning your needs will never go unmet. The 79-suite Four Seasons II will arrive in May 2028 for further Med sails, showcasing two-to-four-bedroom suites on the upper decks and a whopping 11 culinary concepts. Only breakfast is included in cruise fares, a luxury cruise first. (Passengers should plan for about $250 per day, per person for food and beverage.) Late stays and overnights in ports, deep dives into well-being (including the Lanserhof Reset, a longevity experience on the November inaugural transatlantic crossing courtesy of the renowned medi-spa group), and personalized shore excursions are among the amenities. This line’s stunning bespoke ships feature three fully automated rigs capable of delivering 100% wind-powered propulsion in favorable conditions. Dynamic positioning and LNG propulsion are among its energy-efficient and environmental accomplishments. The 54-suite Orient Express Corinthian features five restaurants under the culinary direction of superstar chef Yannick Alléno, whose restaurants have won multiple Michelin stars, and sails the Med until autumn. Twin Orient Express Olympian sets sail next spring. Some excursions are included in the price, others are not. From the hotel brand known for its luxe amenities, personalized service, and fine dining, find three all-suite, all-inclusive ships—149-suite Evrima, 224-suite Ilma, and 226-suite Luminara. Each offers five restaurants and a marina for watersports. Menus from the brand’s Michelin-star-earning chefs are de rigueur, as are personalized spa therapies, and high-end boutiques such as Cartier. Expedition Le Commandant Charcot, the only luxury icebreaker, can travel to the true North Pole and other ice-bound destinations. This French ship offers Le Nuna, the only Alain Ducasse fine-dining restaurant at sea. Ponant also features six bilingual explorer ships for warmer climes. This elegant ocean-going line sails two twin expedition ships, 264-passenger Seabourn Venture and Seabourn Pursuit. Both possess PC6 Polar Class standards, meaning they are capable of pushing through ice. All-suite accommodations, excellent dining, and crew pampering enhance expedition adventures. Scenic currently possesses two sleek 228-passenger ultra-luxury vessels dubbed “discovery yachts” excelling at polar cruising. Both feature 10 dining venues, a spacious spa, two helicopters, one submersible, Zodiacs, kayaks, and stand-up paddleboards. Beyond its classic ocean liners, Silversea’s four expedition ships include three venturing to Poles, Kimberley, Australia, and other remote locales, and one in the Galapagos. Silversea is also opening The Cormorant at 55 South, the Earth’s southernmost hotel in Puerto Williams, as an easier waystation to Antarctica, in October 2026. Ocean Crystal’s two ultra-luxurious ships, 740-passenger Crystal Serenity and 606-passenger Crystal Symphony, feature butler service for all, pillow menus, a Nobu Matsuhisa-affiliated Asian restaurant, and 24-hour room service. Owned by Abercrombie & Kent Travel Group, Abercrombie & Kent partners with Crystal for special voyages combining land elements. With three 922-passenger ships already sailing, EJ unveils Explora IV in summer 2027 with 461 suites, five heated pools, and seven restaurants. This ship and Explora III feature a private dining chef’s table, beach-club-style Shore Club eatery, wine-tasting cellar, and an expanded kids club with family-oriented destination experiences. Near-twin Explora V sets sail in December 2027 and Explora VI in August 2028. Oceania’s seven ships are devoted to culinary superiority. Beyond Oceania Sonata, discover Oceania Aurelia, with just 238 accommodations, in November 2027, and Oceania Arietta in 2029. Oceania Cruises teams with Condé Nast Traveler editors for insider tips on activities ashore. Bilingual French line Ponant is hailed for intriguing itineraries across 12 intimate ships, from sailing vessels to expedition. English-only cruises sail in partnerships, often with Smithsonian Journeys. The December debut of Seven Seas Prestige heralds the newest of the line's seven-ship fleet. Lavish new suite categories feature accommodations with in-suite elevators, private gyms, and personal butlers. These three ocean liners feel more quiet luxury than over-the-top opulent—just the way devotees like it. The all-suite 600-passenger Seabourn Encore and Seabourn Ovation offer multiple fine-dining venues and a fee-extra Retreat for extra privacy and service. The 458-passenger Seabourn Quest just underwent an extensive refurbishment. With two twin mega-yachts, 112-passenger SeaDream I and SeaDream II sport a relaxed yachting lifestyle. Signature elements include sophisticated cuisine, attentive crew, and a watersports marina platform. SeaDream III promises a somewhat bigger and more elevated sailing experience to more destinations in 2029. Beyond exploration vessels, Silversea sails eight all-suite ultra-luxury ships where butlers pamper passengers and complimentary caviar abounds. Expect multiple other included amenities, too. River The three all-suite ships in this European line arguably deliver the best gastronomic experiences on rivers. Included outings might range from an al fresco candlelit dinner at a French winery to private palace concerts in Vienna. Ever-expanding Uniworld will count some 24 distinctly designed ships by 2028, each reflecting the sailing region. The design-forward riverboats mirror charming boutique hotels, with itineraries in Europe, Vietnam, Cambodia, and Egypt. Not as uber-luxury as some of the other names here, AmaWaterways is a more affordable luxury river cruise option that still offers an incredible sense of intimacy and low-impact cruising thanks to the ships' small sizes. Most notable recently is the line's launch of an itinerary on Colombia's Magdalena River, the first of its kind since the days of the steam ship. With one of the most extensive fleet of river cruises vessels in the world, river cruising is Viking’s bread and butter. While Viking falls on the more accessible end of the luxury cruise spectrum, it’s frequently voted the best river cruise line in the world by CNT readers thanks to its Scandanavian design, exceptional service, Nordic spas, and adults-only atmosphere.

item.title: Off-Season Greece: To Avoid the Crowds on Crete, Hike and Ski in Early Spring
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.25
This is part of Off-Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favorite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to hotel owner Nikos Tsepetis. For 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has run Ammos, one of the most talked-about hotels in Greece. The seaside boutique hotel in Chania, northwest Crete, is a manifestation of the man himself: joyful and design-focused with a commitment to high-quality cuisine (including his Red Jane Bakery) and local roots. Tsepetis’s improvisational approach to hospitality creates a home-away-from-home warmth that keeps many of his guests returning, year after year. Born and raised in Chania, Tsepetis is deeply connected to his hometown, which he believes is different from other towns in Crete, because “we are more international and welcoming to foreigners, and it's a multi-layered city." Yet, 80 percent of his staff are locals, he says. “It adds to the experience, because you always meet people who were born here, who remember the past, so there is this continuity." Here, Tsepetis tells us why spring is his favorite time of year in Chania. What would you say is the sweet spot time of the year to visit? Just before high season. April and early May are my favorite time of year because the climate is amazing. Chania is on the western end of Crete and is the prettiest part of the island because it's greener, and we still normally have snow on the Lefka Ori [White Mountains]—you can see them from the sea while swimming. In spring, everything is very fresh, everything is well painted; you can go to the villages and monasteries, and all the flowers are out. Also, spring often coincides with Easter, which is important in the Greek Orthodox religion. I don't care at all about religion, but it's still very spiritual and beautiful. What do you love most about being there during this season? It's less busy. The rain cleans everything and the snow melts, so we are greener than other parts of the island. Everything's fresh and new; you can feel the rejuvenation, so spring is a very sweet time. Who’s around this time of year? Traditionally, Chania benefited from the presence of foreigners, even before it became touristy. It’s very urban, with more than 100,000 permanent residents, so you have everyone from hipsters and freaks to lefties living here—not the expected Greek island crowd. It's always very lively, and what sets it apart from some other towns in Crete is that the locals are a driving force with a very loud voice. They are not here to serve the foreigners. Where would we find you eating during this time? My all-time favorite local is Evgonia Tavern. Only a very simple tavern, it has fish and meat in a non-fish environment. I love Periplous Restaurant for its unbeatable location at the beautiful Tanneries Hotel. It’s one of the old buildings by the water where they used to process leather. In spring we go to the villages, because it's still very mild and there aren’t too many people. I always go to Ntounias, a very old, well-known rural taverna in the middle of nowhere near Drakona in the mountains. There's a crazy guy there, Stelios Trilyrakis, who has been involved with slow food for 30 years. You don't know what you’ll eat or when you’ll eat it. It's very inexpensive, and he cultivates everything himself. In Greece, we love French fries. And Stelios makes amazing chips by cooking them in olive oil in a ceramic pot. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? We're famous for doing a traditional Tsoureki Easter brioche, a kind of braided bread that's sweet but not too sweet. Once a year we also eat a special soup called magiritsa made from lamb intestines, lungs, and liver. We normally eat it at home—it’s not so much a restaurant dish—but we do a very good one at Ammos. Also, Nyketerida is famous for it. Spring is about beans and greens—we have beautiful asparagus and the best artichokes—and goat roasted in the oven with potatoes, zucchini, and tomatoes. We also have a very famous dish called dakos, a barley rusk with tomato sauce and this amazing goat’s cheese called mizithra. One of the best places to eat it is Costas Cafeneion, a family-run cafe in village Maza, which is between Chania and Rethymnon. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? In January and February, people from around the world come here for the mountains and skiing, including the annual Pierra Creta ski mountaineering race. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Summer is very hot and can be dry, and then we have the winter, which is rainy. But in spring, the weather is cooler and you can hike, ski, and swim. The sea is actually colder in spring than in winter because of the snowmelt. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? I’m biased, but Saturday is a great day to hang out at my Red Jane Bakery early in the day. I think it's very pretty. At around 2:00 p.m., I’ll visit my small wine shop next to Red Jane, and I always have one cigarette per day with one glass of wine. On Saturdays, it gets busy and the crowd is very interesting. They’ll have wine with a sandwich in our beautiful, small yard. I also love hanging out at a small, humble taverna called Kafeneio Fix in the old Turkish neighborhood, or I’ll go to Tamam, an amazing taverna inside a beautiful Turkish hammam dating back to 1645. Spring is also the beginning of the open cinema season. My favorite open-air theater is Attikon. Another one, Kipos, shows mostly old Hitchcock-style films in a public garden created during the Ottoman era. If I want to have a final drink before going home, I’ll go to Fagotto, a jazz bar that has been there for 40 years. Do you have any favorite activities during this time of year? I love hiking all the way down to Chora Sfakion, a small coastal town in the south. From there, you can either take a boat or walk for an hour along a very steep and narrow path—not for the faint-hearted—to Sweetwater Beach, a tiny cove made up of very tiny pebbles. If you dig your hand in it, sweet water from the mountains comes out. This article was originally published in Condé Nast Traveller UK.

item.title: 16 Best Resorts on Private Islands for an Ultra-Exclusive Getaway
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler Score: 2.22
For many, true relaxation looks like dropping off the map—settling down on a secluded, sparsely populated island where no one knows anything about you, save for your favorite tropical cocktail. The very best private island resorts balance downtime and adventure; personal space and hospitality; rugged, natural beauty and state-of-the-art facilities. Scattered across the turquoise waters of Indonesia, the Maldives, and Turks and Caicos, some of these properties are wonderfully far-flung, while others, like Little Palm Island Resort & Spa in Florida and Lovango Resort and Beach Club in the US Virgin Islands, don’t even require a US passport. No matter where you decide to book your bungalow, you can rest assured that exclusivity and quietude take top priority at the properties on this list. Offering everything from fresh meals tailored to your preferences to bespoke spa treatments, these resorts are built on the idea that it’s all for you. Whether you’re seeking an open-air villa that floats above crystal-clear water, a luxury ecolodge powered by wind turbines, or a safari-style escape where jungle hikes are always on the table, these are the world’s best private island resorts—each the very definition of paradise. - Read Full ReviewLocation: Tetiaroa, French Polynesia Actor Marlon Brando’s legacy lives on at his former private getaway in French Polynesia, now a hyper-exclusive, eco-minded retreat where travelers come to escape it all. Relax in one of 35 stylish, palm-thatched villas, each a grand fusion of indoor and outdoor space, the beach just footsteps away (alternatively, go even bigger with the island’s sole over-the-top residence). Enjoy island bike rides, treatments in the stickwork cocoons of the Varua te Ora Polynesian Spa, and French-tinged, Polynesian-influenced dining by French celebrity chef Jean Imbert. Nature tours led by in-house researchers offer a deeper connection to the island, while daily cultural experiences like Polynesian dance classes, ukulele lessons, and traditional weaving sessions introduce guests to local traditions. Make sure to save time to explore the other islands of the Tetiaroa Atoll, which also belong to the Brando family, where untouched beaches, preserved reefs, and thriving seabird colonies are as gorgeous as when Brando first encountered the location in 1960. All meals, libations (including Champagne), in-room dining, and daily spa treatments are bundled into the all-inclusive rate, allowing for carefree indulgence at every turn. And although The Brando immerses guests in barefoot ultra-luxury, it also quietly stands as one of the world’s most sustainable resorts—powered by solar energy and cooled by innovative seawater systems—preserving the paradise Brando so deeply loved for generations to come. —Antonia Quirke - Read Full ReviewLocation: Little Torch Key, Florida This adults-only private island is a study in tropical chic, redefining the castaway fantasy right on American soil. There are a total of 30 thatched-roof bungalow suites (some freestanding, some within larger bungalows) across the four-acre island, many with four-poster beds and outdoor copper bathtubs. Thanks to a smart layout and smarter landscaping, you’ll encounter other people less often than you’d expect (a strict cap at 60 guests helps). All suites have water views, outdoor showers, and furnished decks; most also overlook private slivers of white-sand beach and are kitted out with hammocks, loungers, and firepits. The Dining Room has sweeping sea views, and the spectacular SpaTerre complex is underscored by a breezy two-story atrium. Paddleboard or kayak through mangrove mazes as eagle rays swim by, laze the day away on a beachfront hammock, or simply enjoy the day resting on a poolside lounger.
