item.title: 11 most beautiful autumn train journeys in Europe that encourage slow travel
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 4.02
Summer is a gorgeous time to enjoy train-hopping on France’s Mediterranean coast (the Train de la Côte Bleue is a journey you must add to your summer 2027 bucket list) or southern Italy on a regional train from Naples to Reggio Calabria – but autumn is arguably the best time to visit Europe by train. While summer sees hordes of tourists travelling from around the world, putting pressure on rail networks and often making a train trip feel like a sauna, autumn – as well as spring – allows you to visit even some of the continent’s most popular destinations with a little more ease and comfort. While Switzerland and Italy may be the ultimate destinations for scenic train travel, there are routes across Europe that combine fabulous scenery with interesting sights and activities at both ends of the journey. We have gathered some of the best train rides across Europe to give you some ideas for your next train adventure. Italy Train line: Vigezzina Centovalli Railway Italians love to complain about their railway system, but the truth is Italy has one of the best – if not the best – train travel offerings in Europe. Simple regional trains often offer fabulous views over the Italian countryside and coastlines – my yearly train from Naples to Paola is one of my favourite summer activities – but there are some specific routes that deserve the detour. The Vigezzina-Centovalli Railway connects Domodossola in Italy to Locarno in Switzerland in around two hours, passing through the striking Vigezzo Valley and the Centovalli (Hundred Valleys) and allows travellers to stop and visit charming villages such as Santa Maria Maggiore or impressive sites like the Sanctuary of the Madonna del Sangue in Re. In autumn, the service becomes known as the ‘Foliage Train’. Just note that the special foliage ticket allows one intermediate stop on either the outward or return journey, rather than unlimited hopping on and off, so choose wisely. Switzerland Train line: GoldenPass Belle Époque (from Montreux to Zweisimmen) When it comes to scenic train routes, Switzerland always makes it to the top of the list. Out of the many famous routes, the Bernina Express is probably the most popular, but I think that is a route that can wait for winter. Instead, autumn is the perfect time of year to book a GoldenPass Belle Époque train and admire some truly stunning Swiss foliage while sitting in vintage 1930s-style carriages. This route takes travellers from Montreux to Zweisimmen in around two hours through the Gruyère district and the Pays-d’Enhaut. The carriages have panoramic windows, offering uninterrupted views of lakes, mountain peaks and forests along the way.T Greece Train line: Odontotos Rack Railway (Diakopto to Kalavryta) Greece is more popular for boat-powered island hopping than for train travel, but the country has a few gorgeous routes up its sleeve. If finding an unspoiled Greek island is becoming more and more difficult, the Peloponnese region is still fairly under the radar and has a lot to offer year-round. The Odontotos Rack Railway from Diakopto to Kalavryta takes around one hour and shows you a different side of Greece, following the Vouraikos River through its dramatic gorge. Take this opportunity to enjoy a few days in Diakopto, a lovely seaside town usually still sunny and warm in autumn, before getting a complete change of scenery when arriving in the mountain town of Kalavryta. France Train line: Strasbourg to Sélestat via Molsheim, Obernai and Barr (following the Route des Vins d'Alsace) If there is one event that defines autumn in Europe, it is the wine harvest, and France has a fabulous train route to celebrate this time of year by rail. The Route des Vins d’Alsace winds through eastern France and offers a wonderful introduction to the Alsace wine region. There are a few itineraries that can be created following this route but, if it’s your first time in the region, starting from the beautiful city of Strasbourg seems like a good option. From there, take the Strasbourg-Sélestat line that runs through vineyards and allows you to stop in some charming towns such as Molsheim, Obernai and Barr. From early August to mid-October, wine villages across the region host a packed calendar of harvest festivals and events, so make sure you check the calendar and organise your visit to coincide with an event that catches your eye. Portugal Train line: Douro Valley Line (Linha do Douro) The Linha do Douro is a 160-kilometre historic line that connects the city of Porto to the village of Pocinho, running alongside the Douro River, and crossing 35 bridges along the way. The one-way trip is three hours and twenty minutes, but the full journey can still be tackled as a day trip, returning to Porto the same evening. If you don’t feel like committing to a seven-hour train journey in a day, you could stop in the charming town of Pinhão for a wine tasting at Quinta do Bomfim or Quinta das Carvalhas. It cuts one hour off the journey each way and you can still do it in one day if you take the morning train from Porto and make sure you are back in time to take the last train back to the city from Pinhão station. Serbia and Montenegro Train line: Belgrade to Bar If you thought that the Balkans didn’t have great train routes, the trip from Belgrade to Bar will change your mind. With its eleven hours and 476 kilometres, this is a very long train journey that takes travellers from the green hills of Serbia to the rugged mountains of Montenegro. The journey can be made on an overnight service year-round, while a daytime train operates seasonally. In 2026, it runs until 30 September, although it’s worth checking the operator’s website before travelling as timetables can change. Of course, the morning train is the one to take to be able to fully enjoy the views through the Dinaric Alps. The railway crosses 435 bridges – the most spectacular being the 498-metre-long Mala Rijeka Viaduct, which rises almost 200 metres above the valley floor. This is neither the quickest nor the most comfortable train ride you can take in Europe, but it’s definitely worth it if you are passionate about train travel. Norway Train line: Flåm Railway Not only is this one of the most beautiful train journeys in Europe year-round, but in good Norwegian fashion, the route is extremely well organised for tourists who want to enjoy everything that the area has to offer. You can simply book your train tickets and enjoy the ride, or choose a package that includes excursions and accommodation through Norway in a Nutshell. The train journey is twenty kilometres long and lasts around one hour one way, taking you through peaks, valleys, waterfalls and rivers. From cycling, hiking and swimming to ziplining, there is a lot to do along the way so you can spend one day or a full week exploring. Austria Train line: The Arlberg Railway This train route connects the Austrian cities of Innsbruck and Bludenz and is 136 kilometres long, with direct trains completing the journey in around one hour and 45 minutes. During this time, you will speed through charming Alpine villages, rivers and steep-sided valleys framed by mountain peaks. If you are travelling from Innsbruck, this is only one of the many stunning train routes you can take around Austria, to Switzerland or through South Tyrol all the way to Italy, but it’s an ideal option if you want maximum scenery without committing to a full day on the rails. Germany Train line: West Rhine Railway If you are looking for a train journey that will immerse you in nature but want a less obvious alternative to the Alpine railways of Switzerland and Italy, consider Germany’s West Rhine Railway. The route stretches for 185 km, starting from Cologne and arriving at Mainz via Bonn, Koblenz, and Bingen. Cologne makes an excellent starting point, with its Gothic cathedral and lively riverside neighbourhoods worth exploring before you board. The two-hour journey is stunning from beginning to end, but the highlight is the Rhine Gorge, a UNESCO World Heritage Site visible from the train. Bulgaria Train line: Rhodope Narrow Gauge Railway This train from Septemvri to Dobrinishte runs four times a day year-round, takes about five hours for the one-way trip, and costs only a few euros. This route is the closest thing in the Balkans to an Alpine train ride, winding through the valleys and gorges of the Rila, Pirin and Rhodope mountains and stopping at Avramovo, the highest railway station in the Balkans. If you want to stop anywhere during your trip, make it the town of Velingrad, the country’s most popular thermal spa destination.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Winemaker Michael Kouloglou on Santorini's flavours, viticulture and seaside peace
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.90
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to winemaker Michael Kouloglou. For winemaker Michael Kouloglou, the decision to move from the mainland to Santorini 11 years ago was a simple one. “It is the mecca of Greek white wine,” he says. Since relocating here from the Athenian Riviera town of Piraeus, he’s worked with a number of local wineries before launching Orycton, his small-batch Assyrtiko featuring grapes grown on old vines from all over the island. It was a winner at the 2023 Decanter World Wine Awards. On top of the siren’s song of Santorini’s prized volcanic terroir, however, Kouloglou says he appreciates that the region’s windy conditions allow him to pursue his other passions: surfing and kitesurfing. He’s currently settled in Monolithos, a quiet seaside village in the east – but has historically lived all over Santorini, which has offered him great insight into the rhythm of the island. “Each village has its own unique character,” he says, “far beyond the image [of Santorini] that most visitors see.” Here, the longtime Santorini local shares why autumn is his favourite time of year – and all the treasures of the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit – when the travellers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? If I had to choose the best time to visit, I would choose the entire off-season, from late September until around May. Every part of [offseason] has its own personality: Autumn brings relief after harvest, winter offers complete peace, and spring fills the island with optimism as nature comes back to life, just before the new season begins. What do you love most about being there during the off-season? Santorini has two completely different lives. One is the island that millions of visitors experience during summer. The other begins in October and lasts until spring. That is the Santorini only the people who live here truly get to know. By the end of harvest [in September], both the vineyard and I are exhausted. After weeks of living on adrenaline, my body is desperately asking for rest. Around the end of September, the evenings become cooler; you need a sweater after sunset, the days grow shorter, and the strong summer Meltemi (the Aegean wind) gives way to a gentler, northern wind. Everything feels softer. All the locals are tired after another demanding [tourism] season, but at the same time there is a feeling of optimism. Restaurants and bars begin to close for the season, and that's when the closing parties begin; friends you haven't seen for months suddenly reappear. You don't even need to make plans; you know you'll see them somewhere during a closing party. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travellers at all? During autumn you'll still find some travellers, but they are completely different from the summer crowds. They usually come looking for a quieter side of Santorini; they enjoy walking, hiking, discovering wineries and small villages, instead of rushing from one attraction to the next. By the end of November, even the last seasonal workers have left the island. We have a saying here that "the last boat has sailed." From that moment on, Santorini belongs almost entirely to its locals. Conversations become longer, people have time for each other again, and everyday life feels calmer. I think that's the Santorini most visitors never get the chance to experience. What’s notable about the locals in Santorini: do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? One thing that has always impressed me about the locals is how deeply everyday life is connected to the Orthodox Church and its traditions. Almost every small chapel on the island has its own patron saint, and every saint's feast day is celebrated with a panigyri, a traditional village festival. During the summer, many of these celebrations continue late into the night with traditional music, dancing and plenty of local wine. What I also find fascinating is that many of the locals still organise their year around the feast days of the saints. They won't say, "I'll start pruning in late November." They'll say, "I'll start after Saint Philip's Day and I have to finish before Saint Alexios' Day." That's how they measure time. It's a tradition that has been passed down from generation to generation, and it's still very much alive today. Where would we find you eating during this time? During the off-season, you will most likely find me at Pentozali, a traditional taverna that serves authentic meze from both Santorini and Crete. I absolutely love it for its relaxed atmosphere, its genuine food, and its people. What I appreciate most during this time of year is that it becomes a gathering spot almost exclusively for locals. It is very common for me to run into someone who has just finished a hard day's work in the vineyards. We’ll sit down together for a glass of wine and a little chat, with absolutely no rushing around. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? If you are lucky and the spring timing is right, the dish to order is definitely an omelette with wild asparagus. It’s a rare treat because you can't just find it every day; it completely depends on whether someone woke up early in the morning and gathered the wild asparagus fresh from the countryside. Another staple that is almost always on the table is our traditional Santorini fava topped with sautéed onions. It is incredibly simple, but when cooked properly, you truly don't need anything more. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? As the summer venues close, the life of the island doesn't disappear; it just shifts to the places where people actually live year-round. Areas like Karterados and Messaria become the real hubs. They are central points on the island that stay busy and full of life all year. The the local closing parties of fall range from wild gatherings by the beach bars to more laid-back evenings in traditional cafés and small local hangouts. Later, in the winter, as people begin gathering more at homes, these central areas remain the heart of our social life. But if you want to talk about a completely hidden side of Santorini that comes alive in a very quiet, spiritual way, it’s the Askitaria. These are old stone monk lodgings perched right on the edge of the cliff on the mountain between Perissa and Kamari. In the spring, you will find many locals sitting there for hours, doing nothing in particular but gazing out at the endless blue, the passing ships, and distant islands like Anafi, Ios, and Anydro. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Autumn and winter are much warmer and sunnier than most people expect. They bring a rare, beautiful peace. For us winemakers, even the rain is a blessing, not “bad weather” – it’s a relief to see the vines finally get a drink after months of summer drought. The main disadvantage, if you can call it that, is the unpredictability: March, for instance, is a strange and stubborn month with strong winds, cold snaps, and constant weather shifts. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect off-season Saturday starts slowly, without checking my watch – perhaps walking through the narrow paths of the caldera in Fira or Oia. Later, I would meet up with friends. There is always an excuse for an impromptu barbecue, either with meat or, even better, fresh seafood; almost every group of friends here has at least one good fisherman. We would share a coffee or wine, talk without any rush, and if we are lucky, someone might randomly pick up a lute, a tsampouna, or a violin. No big plans or appointments needed, just letting the night unfold naturally. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? My favourite activities are tied to the water. The Aegean is ideal for kitesurfing due to its consistent winds, and as paradoxical as it may sound, specific weather systems often generate great surf here during the winter. We have a small but tight-knit community of surfers on the island, and when the conditions are right, we all head out into the water. Even though the water is still cold, the feeling is incredible. Sometimes you might even catch people paddleboarding inside the Caldera with absolutely no sea traffic, no cruise ships or catamarans, just you travelling parallel to the old quarries and rusty iron piers that hold the island’s history.

item.title: “I think every place has surprising, inexplicable quirks if you know how to pay attention to them.” RF Kuang takes us to Taipei in her new novel, Taipei Story
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.70
In RF Kuang’s latest book Taipei Story, the genre of the campus novel outgrows its name. The novel follows Chinese-American college freshman Lily Chen, who leaves the pale, male, and Yale environs of New Haven, Connecticut, for an intensive Mandarin-language program in Taipei for the summer. While her own family has never set foot in Taiwan, Lily holds on to the belief that perfecting her Mandarin will finally reconcile the shortcomings of being a diaspora kid. And when it came to choosing a place to study the language, travelling to Taiwan conveniently didn’t require her to apply for a visa. But on this quixotic mission to achieve total fluency, she finds that the gulf between her and her complicated family history won’t simply mend itself through diligent study. Her presumptions quickly unravel as she seeks answers in the gaps between economy seats on the flight from Boston to Taipei; in the uncertain, stilted words of Chinese heritage speakers; and in arthouse cinemas and concert halls she’s drawn to for the promise of blending in. From the seasonally inappropriate hot springs of Beitou to the glossy, souvenir-flogging halls of Taipei Taoyuan International Airport, the plot of this coming-of-age story doesn’t shy away from the uncomfortable realities of travelling abroad. Compounded by the sudden passing of Lily’s grandfather – which renders her initial motivation to study Mandarin moot – these follies only deepen beneath a veil of complicated mourning. And yet, they are also softened and forgiven with a grace that comes uniquely from allowing ourselves to be vulnerable in foreign places. Condé Nast Traveller spoke with Kuang about how home, identity, and the split between two places inspired Taipei Story, which is now available in bookstores. Walk us through your research itinerary for Taipei Story. The first place I looked was personal experience. When I started jotting down notes for what would become this book, I didn't know what it was going to be. I was just trying to make legible a tough time in my life when my Gong Gong passed away and I was in Taiwan. I was also in an intensive language program where I was wandering aimlessly around Taipei, meditating on [concepts of] home and cultural alienation. I wasn't walking around with a research agenda. I was just following crowds into places to see what they were seeing. If a long line of people was swarming, I would just join it. I would end up at screenings of movies I'd never heard of, or bookstores that I didn't know existed because I felt so blank, confused, and empty. I wanted somebody else to show me the answer to, “what is your city?” and if I became a ghost in its wake, was there a way I could totally erase myself? A lot of the descriptions in the novel where Lily ends up going to a place by accident, like the National Concert Hall, are places I also encountered by accident. Then, I started thinking about turning all those notes into an exaggerated, fictionalised version of what this experience would be – like if I were even younger and more dim-witted about how the world works. I read a lot of the major modern Taiwanese authors [like Kaori Li, Bai Xianyong, Chen Yingzhen, Wu Ming-yi, and Yang Shaung-zi – all mentioned in the author’s note and available in English translation] and wondered how they were thinking about home, identity, and being split between their mainland cultural heritage, and what it meant to be Taiwanese. How does this novel interface with – the sometimes impossible – expectations of homecoming? I'm fascinated with fantasies of homecoming and the narratives we buy into about how certain cultural experiences can return you to the fold. A lot of Chinese heritage speakers end up getting these flattened experiences in the US that feel like touch points, but are actually silly ways to reconnect – distilled cultural simulations such as Lunar New Year, red envelope parties, and film screenings. I say this not to mock diasporic kids; it makes total sense. You get so little, so you take whatever you can have, even if it's not region-specific or what your parents experienced. In Lily's case, I'm fascinated by the promises of heritage speaker-study abroad programs (editor’s note: these are linguistic immersion programs designed for students who grew up in households speaking a second language) because they hold so much promise and meaning for many people attending them. With Taiwan in particular, if you think about it just on the logical level, every step of this premise that you could, as a Chinese-American, go to Taiwan, to study Mandarin, to feel closer to your family on the mainland – is crazy. Lily's family has never been to Taiwan. She's the only person who's ever stepped foot there until her mom has a layover. When she finally gets there, she starts learning all the ways in which she is so wrong and how her experiences of Chineseness and the trajectory of her family history has absolutely nothing to do with Taiwan. In the end, she is a little more aware of this complexity and moves towards a more genuine, honest encounter of a strange place. She's like, I'm a foreigner, this is a weird summer, and maybe that's okay. In what ways does foreignness, or a lack of fluency, act as a source of fuel for travel and exploration in this novel? I definitely think [feeling out of place] is generative because I’ve felt like an outsider culturally for most of my life. My family immigrated [to the US from Guangzhou when Kuang was four-years-old], and I never felt like I quite belonged in the world of Dallas, Texas. I was a pretty happy kid, but when you're on the periphery, observing how people behave, I think you just get more perceptive. When I go back to China, that’s also not home, which is not a unique perspective. I think almost every immigrant kid feels this way. When I'm in China, I am looking at my family, and I observe cultural codes that they're following, and I have to figure out how these rules work because I didn't grow up understanding them innately. Being reflective about all of this makes you a good writer. In Lily's case, I don't think she perceives her bumbling and ignorance as virtues. For her, it’s a barrier between her and the rest of the world. Because she's so afraid of getting things wrong, she never asks for help and is never willing to embarrass herself. The ethical argument that the book is making is that embarrassment is really good for you. To admit, “I don't know what's going on,” and also “somebody helped me,” is an attitude I wish we all embraced more, not just when we're travelling, but in our entire lives. I find it a strength, and Lily finds it a weakness, and by the end of the book, she's at least accepted that she's gonna mess up, and she might as well own it. From the Poppy War trilogy to your last novel Katabasis, you often take on the perspective of being a student. Why return to the eyes of an undergraduate for this story? This book was very different because it's the first book of mine where the protagonists weren't growing up with me. When I was working on the Poppy War trilogy, I was a teenager, and they're teenagers, then they're undergrads, grad students, and in their late-20s. I was writing very reflexively to try to understand the world from my vantage point in life, but I had a couple of life changes in the past few years that made me more interested in going back. With the maturity of turning 30, I have more comfort in making fun of the person I used to be. When I was writing Taipei Story, it was like, I could write a memoir of what I experienced, or I could make things even more ridiculous, even more embarrassing, and reach back to the person I was when I was 18 going to Beijing for the first time and overwhelmed with everything I didn't know. The key to writing from the point-of-view of adolescence is not from this position of condescension that the youths are so silly, but to be kind to your younger self and recognise that all of your insecurities, all the things that you were failing at, everything that you got wrong, are deeply hilarious and also a really shared experience. There's a lot of humanity in cringe. By setting a story in modern-day Taipei, the narrative acknowledges Taiwanese-Chinese geopolitics, and beyond that, the country’s past with Japanese colonialism, the Chinese Civil War. How did you want to depict Taipei as a city with those layered histories? I wanted to be really cautious here, because I'm not Taiwanese. I'm not an expert in Taiwanese history or literature. As I pointed out in the author's note, this is not a voice from the inside but the very filtered perception of an American teenager who’s learning about all of this for the first time. I did want to poke gentle fun at the way that people generally take Western ideological frameworks that are very binary and project them onto local histories with no attention to what locals are actually saying. There's the first chapter where her little cohort of friends are running around the city, and there’s a pecking order based on assumptions about race. People would ask her where should we go? What should we eat? And she’d always pretend to know the answers and go Google them in the bathroom. They do the same thing when they're at Chiang Kai-Shek Memorial Hall trying to understand, is he a good guy or a bad guy? Is he like George Washington? Should we be taking selfies with him? I wanted to give the experience of somebody who feels like they ought to be an expert by virtue of the ethnicity that they were born into, but who’s actually totally detached from genuine knowledge of the place or history. How did grief form your characterisation of Taipei? [When Lily’s grandfather passed] it was a snapping moment for her. Up until that point, she is trying to slot all of her experiences into this predetermined narrative that this is getting her closer to the person she could have been if her family had never left China. After her grandfather passes, she is thrown into this weird grief and confusion, and she gives up on that goal altogether. She recognises the futility of trying to go back and becoming a version of herself that never existed. Paradoxically, this frees her up to take in the things she closed her mind off to before. Now, she's okay with being a tourist. She goes on these Klook experiences [to Pinglin Tea Museum and Yehliu Geopark]. She’s on a bus with American families from Philly doing all the canned, predetermined activities just thinking, “oh, this is fun,” and learning a lot. Despite all the complex grief that is in this novel, it’s also very funny. Is Taipei a place that is particularly funny to you or has its own language of humour that you wanted to capture here? I think every place has surprising, inexplicable quirks if you know how to pay attention to them. One in particular I'm obsessed with is Taiwan English. I was inspired by a blog post by Tao Lin, an author who also wrote a novel called Taipei. It was just a series of pictures that he took walking around of ridiculous translations, and some of them are accurate on a very literal, character-by-character level, and some of them, I can't believe you would get this result if you ran it through any translation app. But it's not just in Taiwan either. You see it on the mainland. For instance, my mom was wearing a shirt, that just said, “GO FUCK” in repeating block letters. She bought it at a clothes market with her sister when she was in China, and she was only paying attention to the fabric, and she was like, “Oh, it's so lovely. Does this colour look good on me?” and didn't register the text at all. I said, “Mom, do you know what that says?” She turned it inside out and wore it that way for the rest of the day. This article was originally published on Condé Nast Traveler.

item.title: 9 best hotels in Jaipur, India's beautiful Pink City
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 3.62
As one of the most beautiful corners in India, it's only fitting that the best hotels in Jaipur are among some of the prettiest in the world. With its scope of stunning palaces, formidable forts, and vibrant markets, Jaipur reveals itself to tourists like no other city, and checking in to one of these tried and tested Condé Nast Traveller-approved hotels guarantees a bucket-list stay fulfilled. From palace hotels that offer the royal treatment to bijou retreats full of colour and character, here we list some of our favourite places to stay in the Rajasthan capital. Editor's picks of the best hotels in and near Jaipur - For honeymoons: Samode Palace - For families: The Oberoi Rajvilas - For a boutique stay: Villa Palladio Jaipur What is the best time to visit Jaipur? The best time to visit Goa is from November to February. The heat and humidity give way to more pleasant sunny days by December, and the waves are gentler during this time. December also brings the Christmas spirit to several local homes, and bakeries and decades-old stores stock up on local Christmas sweets like kalkal, dodol and neureos. This is also peak tourist season in Goa, which means hotel and flight prices shoot up at this time. When is the off season in Jaipur? The off-season in Jaipur, from April to October, brings sweltering summer temperatures followed by rains. This period is characterised by lower accommodation rates and fewer tourists, making it a cost-effective time to visit. The heat and humidity can make outdoor activities less enjoyable, but the quieter streets and discounted stays offer a more relaxed travel experience. How many days are enough for a trip to Jaipur? A three to four-day trip to Jaipur is ideal for uncovering the city's rich heritage and culture. Start by exploring the grand Amer Fort and its stunning views of the city. Visit the City Palace to admire its opulent architecture and museum exhibits. Jaipur is also famous for its bustling markets, so a trip to Nehru Bazaar is a must if you are in search of traditional juttis, while Tripolia Bazaar is renowned for its beautiful bangles. How we choose the best hotels in Jaipur Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels. More India recommendations This article was originally published on Cntraveller.in

item.title: This medieval Spanish city is Europe's best-kept secret for active travellers
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.93
In case you haven’t noticed, running, cycling and endurance sports are booming. People are signing up for marathons, Ironman triathlons and ultra-marathons in their droves. This surge has had a huge effect on travel patterns – now, more than ever, athletes are travelling to international races and seamlessly weaving training into their holiday plans. As a member of the Irish triathlon team, and a three-time Ironman finisher, I'm one of these people. In my endeavours to bring together my love of sport and travel, I've planned trips that explore a destination's active side, while still ticking classic travel boxes. In doing so, I've realised how valuable a handy guide is when planning these types of trips. Our collective love affair with suffering to get a finisher’s medal has never been stronger. As a result, classic cycling and running destinations such as Mallorca get three-deep with pelotons come April, Tenerife's Teide Loop now needs booking and Font-Romeu regulars are grumbling about rising costs. This July, I travelled from London to compete for my country at the World Triathlon European Middle Distance Triathlon Championships in Banyoles. It's a small city, 20 minutes up the road from Girona. The race course was epic and intimidating: swim 1.9km in the stunningly blue L’Estany Banyoles lake, ride 85km along the smooth-as-butter roads between Banyoles and Girona with some hills thrown in and run 14km by the lake to cheering crowds. The run was supposed to be a half Marathon, but due to the intense heatwave sweeping across Europe, the officials shortened the course by 7km for safety. For the duration of race week, I stayed in the heart of Girona and quickly discovered it truly is the European capital for travellers seeking an active holiday. Girona has that magical and rare combination of everything an active traveller seeks. The roads are almost free of potholes, and drivers here understand how to respect cyclists and runners. There are varied routes ranging from flat and fast to punchy hills for a challenge, with epic views to boot. And, finally, there are plenty of shops and services within the city’s picturesque walls to cater to any athlete's needs. Hundreds of pro cyclists, runners and triathletes live in Girona not for the scenery alone but because the roads are quieter, the tarmac is fresh, and you can climb Rocacorba or freewheel the Costa Brava within 20 minutes of your front door. Georgia Taylor Brown, a multiple world champion in triathlon and Gold, Silver and Bronze medalist across the 2020 and 2024 Olympics for Team GB in triathlon, sums up why she loves living in Girona: “When I first visited Girona, I instantly fell in love," she says. "Training is simple and peaceful here. There are so many options for road cycling on super-quiet roads or beautiful gravel loops that go on forever. Also so many running options; if you want trails, hills, flat, track, Girona has it all. There’s also now a super cool performance lab (H Lab) for those wanting to gain the extra few per cent.” What keeps pulling me back to this city isn't only the terrain, it's that Girona makes living an active lifestyle very easy. Mornings start with proper coffee, often roasted by fellow athletes, in the shadow of Girona’s Gothic cathedral, to the soundtrack of whirring freehubs of the cyclists rolling past on their carbon-framed bikes. Evenings end in one of the many bars and restaurants lining the old town’s cobbled streets (think Barcelona’s Las Ramblas, but far more relaxed). If you’re looking for a rest day activity, head to the cathedral steps (Game of Thrones fans will recognise them instantly), the Jewish Quarter's tangled lanes, and a walk along the medieval city walls for views over the rooftops to the Pyrenees. Girona is a city where I can train like an athlete and seamlessly transition into holiday mode as soon as a session ends. Here is my ultimate guide to tackling this medieval Spanish city like a pro. The ultimate Girona guide for active travellers The best active routes in Girona Cycling Rocacorba, with 12km at 6.5 per cent, is the climb everyone talks about – and for good reason. The opening half lets you settle in, but don’t get lulled into a false sense of security. Ride it early if you can; it gets hot and exposed later in the day. Els Àngels is the more forgiving classic and a much more social climb. It’s shorter, gentler and more rhythmical, which is why locals use it for everything from recovery spins to threshold work. The road is shaded in parts, the gradients are steadier, and the monastery at the top gives it a proper destination feel. The Empordà loop is where the roads flatten out into long, quiet lanes through villages, farmland and open stretches. It’s ideal for steady endurance riding, especially if you want to add volume without constantly thinking about traffic or junctions. Check the forecast, and if you’re heading toward the coast, expect the return leg to feel very different depending on the wind. Running The Carrilet greenway follows an old railway line out of the city, traffic-free and shaded, while the river paths along the Onyar and Ter make for an easy recovery loop. Swimming Head to Lake Banyoles (L'Estany Banyoles), Europe's finest swimming lake, and the swim venue for this year's European championship. If you prefer a sea swim, go to the coves around Aiguablava on the Costa Brava. The best restaurants in Girona La Comuna For the most important meal of the day, La Comuna is where to head, tucked away from the town centre its the perfect place to spot some of the pro athletes that call Girona home. The team are welcoming and the coffee is incredible. Website: lacomuna.co Brovola When I need quick carbs straight after a ride, Brovola’s handmade Focaccia sandwiches are my go-to. Most of their sandwiches are savoury and full of local ingredients and organic meat, but they even have a Nutella-laden version if you need to get those calories into you ASAP. Website: bravola-focacceria.com Idle Hands The ultimate brunch/ lunch spot in Girona. They are also open on Thursday and Friday nights for a well-earned burger made with grass-fed beef. The garlic miso burger is my favourite. They also offer GF versions of their burgers, as well as veggie and pescatarian options. Website: idlehandsgirona.com The best cafés in Girona Oniria A staple of the city's cafe culture and well worth the visit. They also offer Barista and coffee art courses with the café’s Founder Jannik. You can bring back more than extra fitness from your holiday in Girona; perfecting your latte art is a worthy skill to learn during your rest time. Website: oniriacafe.com Classic Coffee Bar Opened in June 2026 as the first café in Spain pouring Illest Drinks, this is the kind of spot where a flat white turns into a conversation served by baristas who are passionate about cycling and triathlon as much as coffee. Classic also stocks some top-notch gear from Surpas if you’re looking to buy new jerseys and bibs. Website: instagram.com Maison Marcel If there’s one thing cyclists, runners and triathletes can all agree on, it's that a pastry is a non-negotiable after a long session. Refuelling with pastries from Maison Marcel is a pilgrimage for anyone training in Girona. Their Jamon Iberico brioche roll is so simple but so tasty. Website: maisonmarcel.eu Where to go shopping in Girona Velodrome Set in a former classic cinema, this is definitely the world’s most beautiful cycling shop, and that’s before you even consider their bike stock. Though, you're missing a trick if you don't also seek out the smaller independent shops sprinkled around the city. Website: velodrom.cc Tata Bikes A family-run cycling boutique in the old Jewish Quarter. After my handlebars got mangled in transit to Girona, Stelian, the owner, immediately stopped what he was doing and sorted them within 15 minutes. I cannot recommend a visit enough for repairs, rentals and beautifully curated gear from a husband-and-wife team who treat every customer like a regular. Website: tatabikes.com Temple Running Stocks road and trail shoes and apparel from Norda, On, Satisfy and more, alongside organising regular runs and events to support the running community. The owner, Aleix, is a talented ultra runner and knows what he's talking about. I picked up a pair of their socks for my race, and they are now my go-to race sock. Website: temple-running.com Where to stay in Girona Hotel Nord 1901 Based in the old town, this little hotel has thought of everything for travellers with bikes. There’s secure bike storage, a pool for recovery and the team have great connections with mechanics throughout the city. The hotel has eighteen rooms that fill quickly with kit bags all season, so book well in advance. Website: nord1901.com Gran Ultònia Offers a secluded rooftop bar if you want to unwind after a day on the trails. This is the perfect place to stay if you’re travelling with a group, as they offer group cycling info sessions on where to cycle, as well as that important secure bike storage. Website: hotelsultoniagirona.com Off Grid Girona Further out of the city, in La Garrotxa, a rustic-luxury 17th-century masia built around cycling, yoga and communal, locally-sourced dining. Off Grid is really the perfect place to unwind after a day on the trails. If travelling in a group, the entire property can be booked. Also, Off Grid isn’t a cyclist-only destination; they host yoga retreats and easy hiking excursions for those who may want to holiday at a slower pace. Website: offgridgirona.com

item.title: 15 best hotels in Mauritius 2026 for dramatic sunsets and sugar-soft sands
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.52
On this volcanic Indian Ocean isle, the best hotels in Mauritius have been upping their game recently with a series of refreshes and villa reveals. It may not have the private island feel of the Maldives or the Indiana Jones giant fauna and tropical jungle of the Seychelles, but a Mauritius escape offers faultless service, white sand beaches, activities (golf, and then some more golf, hiking and paddle boarding) and farm-to-table gastronomy. With its burgeoning boutique rum industry and host of emerging artisans – from textiles to ceramics – be sure to pack an empty suitcase for your return journey. The Mauritius resorts in our edit feature some of the world's top luxury chains as well as some exceptional homegrown brands who are shaping the country’s industry with a proud, hands-on approach. From charming and affordable boutique boltholes to blow-the-budget villa stays, here we round up the best hotels in Mauritius and what makes each one special Editor's pick of the best hotels in Mauritius - For honeymoons: One&Only Le Saint Geran - For kids: LUX* Belle Mare - For an affordable stay: SALT of Palmar Which part of Mauritius is best to stay in? Much of the best hotels in Mauritius are spread out around the coastline, from One&Only Le Saint Géran in Poste de Flacq on the north eastern side of the island to Heritage Le Telfair in Bel Ombre on the south west coast. If you're excited to snorkel in Mauritius, you'll find the best conditions along the west side of the island, particularly near Flic En Flac beach. For easy swimming, opt for a hotel on the west coast where the seas tend to be calmer and warmer. For complete privacy, Shangri-La Le Touessrok is located on its own private island. What is the best time of year to visit Mauritius? June marks the beginning of the Mauritian dry season, and while it's not the hottest time of year to visit the island, temperatures sit comfortably between 20 and about 28 degrees celsius. It's officially ‘winter’ there at this time, and the season lasts until September. The hottest time of year to visit is typically between December and January, but there is also a higher chance of rainfall and the weather feels humid. Read a more about the best time to visit Mauritius. How we choose the best hotels in Mauritius Every hotel on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has stayed at that property. When choosing hotels, our editors consider both luxury properties and boutique and lesser-known boltholes that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for beautiful design, a great location and warm service – as well as serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new hotels open and existing ones evolve. Find out more about our editorial standards and how we review hotels.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Ceramist Christiane Smit on the joy of Paros at its most pure and peaceful
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.46
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to ceramic artist and owner of Moonhouse, Christiane Smit. For Netherlander and artist Christiane Smit, a holiday on Paros in 2008 rerouted the course of her life. “It wasn’t a carefully planned life decision; it was something I felt instinctively,” she says of her sudden move to the Cycladic island. “I listened to that feeling, stayed, and started building a completely new life on the island.” Having lived all over the island since then, she now operates a ceramics atelier in the village of Lefkes, and owns the stunningly minimalist clifftop villa rental Moonhouse – both of which are open to visitors. She is currently completing the restoration of a nearly 100-year-old stone house in the village of Kostos. Here, the now-local shares the shoulder-season delights that keep her on-island year-round, and her favourite hotel-slash-taverna for a warming meal and stay. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit – when the travellers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? For me, the sweetest time in Paros is late spring or early autumn. The island feels wonderfully balanced: Everything is open, but life is still unhurried. I love walking through the villages in the morning, when the streets are still quiet. The air smells of jasmine, fresh bread from the bakery and the sea. You hear church bells, neighbours greeting each other, and the wind moving through the olive trees. The light is what inspires me most; it changes constantly, making the whitewashed houses glow and bringing out every texture in the stone. As a ceramic artist, I find myself collecting those colours, textures and moments every day. They’re as much a part of my work as the clay itself. What do you love most about being there during this season? The season allows me to slow down and notice everything. The colours of the landscape, the textures of old stone walls, the shifting light on the sea – those details naturally find their way into my ceramics. I don’t have to look for inspiration here; I simply have to pay attention. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travellers at all? It’s mostly locals. The cafés are filled with familiar faces, fishermen are heading out in the morning, and shop owners have time to stop and chat. You also meet a small number of travellers: The people who aren’t looking for the typical summer holiday, but who want to experience the island more slowly and authentically. There are also Greek visitors escaping the city for a long weekend or visiting family. It’s a lovely mix, but the locals set the rhythm, and that’s what gives Paros its real character. What’s notable about the locals in Paros; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What I’ve come to appreciate most about the people of Paros is their warmth and sense of community. Even though it’s a popular island in summer, life outside the season is very local. People know one another, and there’s a genuine willingness to help each other. As someone who lives here year-round, that’s something I’ve really come to value. There’s also a deep respect for craftsmanship – from marble carving, for which the Cyclades are famous, to fishing, farming and handmade work. Where would we find you eating during this time? One of my favourite places is the family-run taverna at Hotel Julia in Drios. I love it because it feels authentic and unchanged – a place where generations have welcomed people with simple, honest food and genuine hospitality. My perfect day always starts with a swim in the crystal-clear waters just below the taverna. Afterwards, I walk up for a long, leisurely lunch. There’s something so special about sitting there, the sound of the waves below and nowhere else to be. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? Winter on Paros is the season for revithada (slow-baked chickpea stew), hearty bean soups, and goat or lamb braised with local wine – dishes that are more like daily specials rather than menu staples. But if there’s one meal that defines the island’s quieter months, it’s whatever is cooking in the pot that day (mageirefta). That’s what locals order, and every taverna has its own depending on the day. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? I wouldn’t say any one area suddenly comes alive in the off-season; it feels more like the island returns to its natural rhythm. While Parikia is the social hub for year-round residents, it’s the villages – Lefkes, Marpissa, Prodromos, Kostos, and Dryos – that reveal the character of Paros through seasonal festivals, religious celebrations, and community events. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? You get cooler temperatures, crisp, sunny days, and the occasional rainstorm, which turns the landscape unexpectedly green. The island feels softer and more vibrant. For me, one of the greatest advantages is the sense of calm. Of course, there are a few trade-offs. Stronger winter weather systems can occasionally disrupt ferry schedules, and many seasonal businesses close until spring. But these are minor inconveniences. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? My perfect Saturday begins slowly with a coffee in my house, catching the first sunlight. From there, I’ll often wander through Lefkes, Marpissa, or Prodromos before a long lunch at a traditional taverna. In the afternoon, I usually head back to my ceramic studio. The quieter months are when I’m most creative. Without the intensity of the summer season, there’s space to observe, reflect, and create. At sunset, I love taking a walk along one of the beaches or coastal paths. Even in winter, there are many clear, sunny days, and the light over the Aegean is extraordinary. I usually end the day with friends over a simple meal and a glass of wine. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? I love walking the ancient Byzantine paths that weave between villages. With few people on the trails, the silence becomes part of the journey. This winter is especially meaningful, as I’ll be putting the finishing touches on a small renovation project in the village of Kostos, a space I’ve been shaping with the same care and intention that I bring to my ceramics. Creating a home is, in many ways, another form of making, and I find great joy in both!

item.title: 14 best walking shoes that have saved our feet, from city breaks to hikes
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.44
Sourcing the best walking shoes for travel is no easy feat. You need a pair that delivers all-day support as you clock up thousands of steps, without looking so functional that you stick out clearly as a tourist. And because nobody wants a carry-on weighed down by extra footwear, whatever makes the cut needs to be versatile enough to pair effortlessly with your entire holiday wardrobe. To save you from the misery of travel-day blisters, the editors and writers at Condé Nast Traveller have rounded up their tried-and-tested favourites – eliminating the guesswork so you can step out in complete comfort. Read on for our full edit, or skip straight to your preferred style below. item.title: We’re calling it: this autumn is the witchiest yet. Here’s why
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.44
Witches are stepping out of the shadows. They’re lighting up the big screen and casting their spells all over your social media feed. They’re frolicking in Welsh woodland at witchy retreats. They’re buying medicinal herbs at quaint boutiques. They're getting tarot readings and manifesting under the full moon. So come closer, my pretties, because the mystical has officially gone mainstream, just in time for autumn’s spooky season. Perhaps there’s something in the stars. In the wake of the solar eclipse, we’re looking to the universe and opening ourselves up to its infinite possibilities, magic included. Hollywood is giving witchcraft its moment in the moonlight, too. September sees the release of Practical Magic 2, the long-awaited sequel starring Nicole Kidman and Sandra Bullock, reprising their roles as the Owens sisters. Then in November, Hexed hits our cinema screens, Disney’s animated tale of a teenage girl who discovers she has secret magical abilities. That same month, the first UK flagship Harry Potter store will open in central London, a vast two-floor emporium for budding witches and wizards. TikTok is also bringing this once hush-hush world to a new audience, with 9 million posts using the hashtag #WitchTok. The online community showcases everything from tarot readings and spell tutorials to crystals and manifestation, making the occult more accessible to curious newcomers than ever before. For those ready to swap scrolling for something more immersive, Britain’s witches are gathering in person. On 24 October, Witch Festival arrives in Cornwall with more workshops and ceremonies than you can shake a wand at. Visitors can make oracle cards and herbal blends for yoni steams, delve into Cornish and Celtic folklore and, as darkness falls, gather for a collective fire ritual. Then on 14 November, Witchfest Market makes its debut in Lewes, with stalls piled high with cosmic wares and spell supplies, alongside a programme of esoteric talks. Offering a deeper dive, The Dreaming is an arts and crafts country house, once owned by interior designer Laura Ashley. Set within the leafy, ancient landscape of the Elan Valley in mid-Wales, it’s since been transformed into an enchanting healing centre by singer and activist Charlotte Church. Dust off your broomstick as The Dreaming’s witch retreats, held a handful of times a year, have proved so popular they sell out at lightning speed. “The response has been pretty extraordinary,” says Church, who created the course with High Priestess Tree Carr. “We’re adding as many dates as we realistically can, because the appetite for it is clearly there.” For Church, this surge of interest in her witchcraft retreats taps into a larger collective shift. “We live in a culture that has become incredibly disconnected, from the natural world, from community, from our bodies and, in many ways, from a sense of ritual and meaning,” she says. “There’s something very beautiful about returning to practices that remind us of the power incarnate in life.” That sense of reconnection is cultivated over five days, as guests use releasing rituals to banish negative thought patterns, dip into herbal baths, cast spells and listen to stories around the flickering campfire. Dream weaving, a practice involving dream incubation, takes place nightly, before participants retire to rooms decked out in flowing white fabrics, tatami flooring and lunar imagery. The archetype of the cackling wicked witch, once feared and mocked in equal measure, is being reconsidered, says Church. “The figure of the witch has historically been associated with people, especially women, whose knowledge, independence or power sat outside accepted structures. I think reclaiming the witch now can be about reclaiming intuition, creativity, community, our relationship with the earth and our own agency.” Nowhere understands this reckoning quite like Salem, the coastal Massachusetts city across the pond. It was here that the notorious witch trials took place in 1692, when 20 innocent people accused of witchcraft met a particularly gruesome end. In a curious twist, today Salem is a glorious witchy wonderland, filled with female-owned metaphysical businesses. More than a million tourists swoop into Salem for Halloween, and 2026 looks set to be a bumper year as the city also celebrates its 400th anniversary. The trick-or-treat season kicks off in early October with the Haunted Happenings parade through the cobbled streets. A month of celebrations and events follows, including a Ghostbusters gathering, gothic horror storytelling at the atmospheric House of the Seven Gables and a comedy night in Salem’s Witch Village. New for this year, The Witchery, a creative studio where practising witches teach their craft, has expanded to a second location in Salem’s wharf area. Alongside their beloved broom-making classes, The Witchery has added spell jar workshops, recreating the vessels that people once hid beneath their homes to ward off malevolent forces. Yours will be filled with twinkling crystal chips and good intentions, ready to take home and manifest positive change. The coven is growing in Los Angeles too, with the recent opening of the Witch’s Cottage. The two-floor café, restaurant, bar and event space harnesses its Hollywood location, with interiors that wouldn’t look out of place on a movie set. The fantasyland was created by Danielle Ozymandias and Celina Lee Surniak, two queer witches, as an ultra-inclusive space. “You do not need to be a practising witch to visit us,” says Lee Surniak. “When we built this place, we had the intention for people to come in from the urban, hyper-industrialised world to seek solace and comfort in our little forest.” Witch’s brew coffee is served beneath lights shaped like pointy black hats in the bakery, while the bar resembles an enchanted woodland. A highlight of the devilishly good cocktail list is the protection spell cocktail, made with agave and smoked black foam to ward off negative vibes. There’s also a calendar of regular metaphysical happenings, such as bewitched burlesque, magic mic nights, sound baths and sessions exploring the shadow self. Ozymandias says it’s not surprising that witchcraft is moving into the mainstream. “We’re seeking ways to belong, to feel safe, to feel cared for, because the current systems of capitalism, consumerism and patriarchy aren’t helping people.” “We are not meant to live and work ourselves to death,” Ozymandias adds. “Matriarchy, the turning of the seasonal wheel and witchcraft are much more rewarding.” Perhaps, amid the breakneck pace of modern life, there’s a certain allure in slowing down, following the moon rather than the clock and finding a coven of kindred spirits.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Hotelier Agapi Sbokou says Athens comes alive in the autumn
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.40
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of Greek hotel brand Phāea. “Alive. That's how Athens feels to me,” says Agapi Sbokou, co-owner and CEO of the Greek hotel brand Phāea. Sbokou grew up in Crete but has lived in Athens since she was 18. “There was never really a debate about where to live. We go back and forth between Athens and Crete, but the city just feels so buzzy. It’s a place that is constantly transforming.” Sbokou knows a thing or two about why people are drawn to a particular destination. “When you go to a place, it should be about understanding the local rhythm,” she tells me. “I'm in love with Athens. It’s a place that you can continue exploring your whole life.” Here, Agapi explains why autumn is so magical in the Greek capital, and lets us in on some of her favourite places to visit at this time of year. Tell me what you love most about Athens. Walking around and exploring. The city transforms with the seasons, and it feels completely connected with nature. For example, my neighbourhood is full of these beautiful trees called jacarandas, which have very small, lilac flowers. It completely transforms the whole neighbourhood when they bloom. Elsewhere in the city, some areas are filled with bitter orange trees, which smell strongly when they bloom. There are a lot of young people here, and recently a lot of young travellers are coming to stay and live in Athens. They all come with a very open heart and the desire to explore as we, the locals, do. Athens is not about what’s cool and what’s not – it’s about discovering new things, revisiting old places, and watching the city transform over time. That’s what I love. When is the best time to come to Athens? When it’s not too busy, but local life is buzzing? I would say April and October or November. I've always been a summer person, but to be honest in Athens spring and autumn are the most beautiful seasons. In April, the blooms are starting to appear. There are beautiful smells around the city. But autumn is great because the weather is very mellow. There's still the warmth from the summer, and there is very little rain, so it's very pleasant and you can walk around all day. What makes autumn so special in Athens? There's a different light about the city, which is not that classic Greek light that you see during summer. It's more yellow and soft. The city starts preparing for winter, so there is a kind of excitement with the locals – people are returning from the islands, they still go swimming in the sea and still it's quite warm. It's the perfect season because it combines it all. Who’s around this time of year? There are travellers year-round. But in autumn, it's a different kind of traveller. People who come during this season have a slower appreciation of the city, which I love. I think that's what tourism should be. We should spend more time exploring a place and really getting a sense of it to understand its rhythm, rather than going in and out, just ticking off things. Do as the locals do. Maybe spend two hours in a coffee shop. Get to know the person sitting at the next table and start a conversation. Spend three hours in a museum, not one. There are so many museums here, and not just the big ones. The Benizelos Mansion is the oldest house in Athens, or, of course, the Benaki Museum with the Nema Collection. There are so many things to discover, and it shouldn't all be packed into one trip. The kind of travellers who appreciate this tend to come off-season. What’s notable about the locals in Athens; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? An appreciation for a slower way of life, I guess. Athens is very much about its neighbourhoods, which is characteristic of the city and its people. You start your day at your local coffee shop, then visit your local barber, grocery store and dry cleaner. You stop for a few minutes, you exchange a few words. That's very typical of people here. You have a sense of community. Sometimes you buy things and you don't need to pay – they know you, and write it in a notebook and you pay at the end of the month. Athens feels like a village, even though it's a city of four million. Where would we find you eating in autumn? I love exploring new places, but I also love going to the same places again and again, because then you begin to know the people. There is a new generation of fantastic restaurants that embrace Greek cuisine, but I’d rather visit the ones that have been around for 20, 30 or even 50 years. I go to Manári Taverna a lot, which is in the city centre. It's right by a Byzantine church, and it has very traditional cuisine with strong Cretan influence. There is Pharaoh, a very cool restaurant where everything is slow-cooked over a wood-fired grill. It has the best music and the coolest bar, so it's really fun to visit. Plus, it belongs to a friend, so it's always fun to see him and to catch up. There’s a place called Dourambeis where I've been going with my dad since I was a kid. It's very traditional, and it has the most delicious fish. In autumn, these places are perfect because they are traditional and laid back, but really good food. They all use excellent, seasonal ingredients. Speaking of seasonal ingredients, what is the most traditional dish that people should eat when they come in autumn? That's a good question. It's hard to say, because the weather in Greece stays warm into autumn, so we tend to drag summer dishes into the year. For example, one very traditional dish we continue to eat in autumn is gemista. It’s often made with very ripe tomatoes – you empty them, and fill them with rice, mince meat, and other ingredients like herbs and nuts. You could replace tomatoes with courgettes, or aubergines, or peppers. It is very, very Greek and very traditional. And then, of course, in autumn, we eat a lot of pastries and pies. The most typical one is spanakopita, a cheese-and-spinach pie. Those are more home-cooked recipes, though. Athens is like the melting pot of the whole of Greece, so a lot of wider Greek traditions are incorporated in the restaurants. Skioufichta is a specific thick pasta dish, made by hand. You boil it in a broth, and then it's sprinkled with cheese. And it's the most delicious dish, very soothing, very appropriate for autumn – perfect with a glass of red wine. Order this at Manári; it's one of my favourite dishes there. Are there any areas of Athens that really come alive in autumn? I've always lived in and around Kolonaki. It's an area that's quite buzzing and quite well known, but I love the streets that are purely residential. There are a couple that are quite high, with amazing views, because Kolonaki is at the bottom of Lycabettus Hill. From those streets, you can see straight down to the Acropolis, in between buildings. In the autumn, when the light is right, it just feels amazing and very Athenian. It's almost like a secret – you know that if you turn down a specific street, you’ll suddenly get this view. That feeling always makes me feel very lucky to be there. In autumn, it’s easier to be more spontaneous in Athens, because it’s not as busy. It feels like normal life is back, so you can access museums, galleries, exhibitions and restaurants more easily. We Greeks are very welcoming. We want to share the best of what we have. It’s the perfect time to do that.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Hotelier Nikos Tsepetis on how to explore Crete's green heart during spring, without the crowds
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.35
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to hotel owner Nikos Tsepetis. For 30 years, Nikos Tsepetis has run Ammos, one of the most talked-about hotels in Greece. The seaside boutique hotel in Chania, northwest Crete, is a manifestation of the man himself: joyful and design-focused with a commitment to high-quality cuisine (including his Red Jane Bakery) and local roots. Tsepetis’ improvisational approach to hospitality creates a home-away-from-home warmth that keeps many of his guests returning year after year. Born and raised in Chania, Tsepetis is deeply connected to his hometown, which he believes is different from other towns in Crete, because “we are more international and welcoming to foreigners, and it's a multi-layered city”. Yet 80 per cent of his staff are locals, he says. “It adds to the experience because you always meet people who were born here, who remember the past, so there is this continuity”. Here, Tsepetis tells us why spring is his favourite time of year in Chania. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit? Just before high season. April and early May are my favourite time of year because the climate is amazing. Chania is on the western end of Crete and is the prettiest part of the island because it's greener, and we still normally have snow on the Lefka Ori [White Mountains] – you can see them from the sea while swimming. In spring, everything is very fresh, everything is well painted; you can go to the villages and monasteries, and all the flowers are out. Also, spring often coincides with Easter, which is important in the Greek Orthodox religion. I don't care at all about religion, but it's still very spiritual and beautiful. What do you love most about being there during this season? It's less busy. The rain cleans everything and the snow melts, so we are greener than other parts of the island. Everything's fresh and new; you can feel the rejuvenation. So spring is a very sweet time. Who’s around this time of year? Traditionally, Chania benefited from the presence of foreigners, even before it became touristy. It’s very urban, with more than 100,000 permanent residents, so you have everyone from hipsters and freaks to lefties living here – not the expected Greek island crowd. It's always very lively, and what sets it apart from some other towns in Crete is that the locals are a driving force with a very loud voice. They are not here to serve the foreigners. Where would we find you eating during this time? My all-time favourite local is Evgonia Tavern. Only a very simple tavern; it has fish and meat in a non-fish environment. I love Periplous restaurant for its unbeatable location at the beautiful Tanneries Hotel. It’s one of the old buildings by the water where they used to process leather. In spring we go to the villages because it's still very mild and there aren’t too many people. I always go to Ntounias, a very old, well-known rural taverna in the middle of nowhere near Drakona in the mountains. There's a crazy guy there, Stelios Trilyrakis, who has been involved with slow food for 30 years. You don't know what you’ll eat or when you’ll eat it. It's very inexpensive, and he cultivates everything himself. In Greece, we love French fries. And Stelios makes amazing chips by cooking them in olive oil in a ceramic pot. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? We're famous for doing a traditional Tsoureki Easter brioche, a kind of braided bread that's sweet but not too sweet. Once a year we also eat a special soup called magiritsa made from lamb intestines, lungs and liver. We normally eat it at home – it’s not so much a restaurant dish – but we do a very good one at Ammos. Also, Nyketerida is famous for it. Spring is about beans and greens – we have beautiful asparagus and the best artichokes – and goat roasted in the oven with potatoes, zucchini and tomatoes. We also have a very famous dish called ‘dakos’, a barley rusk, with tomato sauce and this amazing goat’s cheese called mizithra. One of the best places to eat it is Costas Cafeneion, a family-run cafe in Maza village, which is between Chania and Rethymnon. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off-season? In January and February, people from around the world come here for the mountains and skiing, including the annual Pierra Creta ski mountaineering race. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Summer is very hot and can be dry, and then we have the winter, which is rainy. But in spring the weather is cooler and you can hike, ski and swim. The sea is actually colder in spring than in winter because of the snowmelt. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? I’m biased but Saturday is a great day to hang out at my Red Jane Bakery early in the day. I think it's very pretty. At around 2pm I’ll visit my small wine shop next to Red Jane and I always have one cigarette per day with one glass of wine. On Saturdays it gets busy and the crowd is very interesting. They’ll have wine with a sandwich in our beautiful, small yard. I also love hanging out at a small, humble taverna called Kafeneio Fix in the old Turkish neighbourhood, or I’ll go to Tamam, an amazing taverna inside a beautiful Turkish hammam dating back to 1645. Spring is also the beginning of the open cinema season. My favourite open-air theatre is Attikon. Another one, Kipos, shows mostly old Hitchcock-style films in a public garden created during the Ottoman era. If I want to have a final drink before going home, I’ll go to Fagotto, a jazz bar that has been there for 40 years. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? I love hiking all the way down to Chora Sfakion, a small coastal town in the south. From there you can either take a boat or walk for an hour along a very steep and narrow path – not for the faint-hearted – to Sweetwater Beach, a tiny cove made up of very tiny pebbles. If you dig your hand in it, sweet water from the mountains comes out.

item.title: Off Season Greece: Author Anastasia Miari on Corfu's thriving food scene and why spring is the best time to savour the isle
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.30
This is part of Off Season Greece, a collection of guides highlighting the year-round appeal of Greece's most popular destinations, courtesy of our favourite local tastemakers. In this edition, we speak to food writer and author Anastasia Miari. Whenever I’m feeling disconnected from myself or from Greece – the place my mother’s family is from, and whose traditions I grew up with – I muster up the energy to make a comforting Greek meal. But whether it’s my yia yia’s old-school-style avgolemono soup, my mom’s traditional pastitsio, or my thea’s Americanised spanakopita, the recipe is rarely ever already written down. As with so many other cultures’ time-tested family dishes, they’re usually passed on by doing; surmising how many box grater’s-worth of tomatoes you'll need, or eyeballing the number of glugs of olive oil to add. Enter Anastasia Miari, a food writer and author who has spent the better part of a decade travelling all over the Mediterranean to document not only Greek recipes, but create an extensive, photographic encyclopedia of the many octo- and septuagenarians (and their often-remote villages) who passed those very dishes – and their way of life – to younger generations. Nowadays, when I want to try a new or lighter Greek dish than the handful of rib-sticking ones I know, I crack open my stained copy of ‘Yia Yia,’ Miari’s first cookbook. Better yet, when I want to explore the cuisine of the broader region – Moroccan tajin, Turkish breakfast, Sicilian pasta – there’s now also her newer iteration, ‘Mediterranea.’ To say Anastasia is an expert in all things Greek would be an understatement – she was born and raised on the Ionian island of Corfu in Greece’s northwest, and is currently renovating a historic cottage on the Cycladic island of Tinos to enjoy with her family in the summers (and filming a web series about it all). Here, the British-Greek Corfiot shares her guide to the Italian-leaning island’s Venetian traditions, natural splendour, and seasonal dishes – all of which are best experienced in the off-season. What would you say is the sweet-spot time of the year to visit – when the travellers have not yet arrived, but local life is buzzing? I would say May, springtime. Because of all this rain that we get then, the island is fully in bloom in May – it's stunning. It's like being in a Disney movie here. What do you love most about being there during this season? If you have in mind to do the Corfu Trail, which is a hiking trail that runs all the way from the south of the island to the north of the island, the month of May is a particularly incredible month to come in because you tend to have the best weather, but it's also not incredibly hot. You're still able to hike, especially in the morning and evening hours. Who’s around this time of year? Is it all locals? Greek domestic visitors? Are there any travellers at all? Corfu is really interesting because it doesn't have this sort of off-season, on-season vibe as much as the Cycladic islands do. What I mean by that is the island doesn't shut down when it isn't summertime. We have a university and we have a music school on the island, and because it is very cosmopolitan and because it's so big, we tend to retain our residents. People don't tend to move to Athens or to Saloniki as much as they might in more remote Cycladic islands. So of course, there are a few travellers, but it's not as many as you'll find in July and August. And I think it's usually people who love to hike and people who like to be in nature, so it's a different kind of traveller. What’s notable about the locals; do they have any of their own unique traditions or a reputation amongst Greeks for anything in particular? What's notable about the locals in Corfu is that, supposedly, we're the craziest in all of Greece? [Laughs] Other Greeks tend to say that Cretans and the Corfiots are the crazies of the nation. But I do think we are quite distinct in Corfu because we have this incredible heritage that comes from Italy, and we love to align ourselves with the Italians. The Venetians came and colonised 500 years ago, and many vestiges of our Venetian past are still visible, not just in the architecture and in our food. Where would we find you eating? The places that eat in the summer tend to also be open in the winter, and I think that's great because you are always able to rub shoulders with local clientele. One of my favourite places to eat is Marina's Tavern in Corfu Town because they do all of the classic yia yia home-cooked dishes in a really great home-cooked style – eating a pastitsada or a stifado at my léas table. So I love Marina's Tavern for all of the traditional home-cooked dishes that they serve. What’s the seasonal dish to order at this time of year? The dish to order is tsigarelia, which are like wild greens that you find at that time of year. And here in Greece, we sauté them with lots of spices. Again, this is a sort of vestige of the Venetians, and [a result of] our being put on the spice trail by the Venetians. So it includes lots of spices like cinnamon, cloves, and cayenne pepper. So cigarella, that's a great dish to have. Are there any areas of the island that really come alive during the off season? In the off-season, I think Corfu Town is the place to be because even everyone else from the rest of the [surrounding] island tends to sort of congregate in Corfu Town.
