It’s really popping off, especially because of the universities there: there's a high concentration of people hanging out in town; it's very much alive. Any coffee shop you go into will be full of people. Again, Corfu isn't one of those sort of Disneyland islands that shuts down in the winter and opens up this sort of like fake display of life in the summer. It's very much alive all year round. How does the weather change the destination during this time of year, and what are the (dis)advantages of that? Corfu is one of the wettest islands in Greece, so if you try and come in May you’ll have the occasional rain shower. But generally, it's just a very pleasant temperature and really great to experience the best of the island, which is its nature. September or October can be the trickiest months. What does a perfect Saturday in the off-season look like to you? It's fantastic to go into the mountains and visit mountain villages on weekends because I think much of the coastline has been marred by mass tourism. The real secret and beauty of this island is actually inland, in the mountains. Do you have any favourite activities during this time of year? It absolutely has to be hiking. And I think the most incredible way to live and experience this island is by doing the 112-mile Corfu trail. You don't have to do the whole of it, of course. You could just pick one part of the whole trail because it takes like seven days to hike it in full. It took me a bit longer, but you can pick a section of the trail and do just that. It's unmissable, really. Where to stay: Snugly in a pine-studded cleft beneath Mount Pantokrator, the island's tallest mountain, The Merchant's House has six guestrooms carved out of the stunningly renovated stone-walled shell of a 14th-century Venetian building. High ceiling rooms with chunky stone walls are far from mediaeval, however: there are Coco-Mat mattresses and large balconies with spectacular views over to the Albanian coast opposite.

item.title: I spent a night in Kenya’s remote bush, and it changed how I think about safaris
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.21
It’s the night of the blood moon in northern Kenya. We sit in a loose semicircle around a crackling bushfire, our canvas chairs settled into the sand of a long-dried riverbed. The flames warm our faces as embers drift up into the starry sky. Gin and tonics sweat in our hands while the bush comes alive at night. Somewhere nearby, hyenas giggle and whoop in the darkness, and a silent group of giraffes glides across the riverbed ahead, their tall silhouettes graceful in the half-light. As the moon slips into the earth’s shadow, soft rhythmic chanting rises from the surrounding manyattas. Samburu women sing, their melodic voices carrying across the plains as part of a ritual to mark the eclipse and guide the moon back to life. We sit quietly, listening as it glows crimson and is slowly reborn. In that moment, caught between moonlight, wildlife, and Samburu tradition, it’s impossible not to feel the captivating pull of Sarara. Sarara sits within the vast Namunyak Conservancy in northern Kenya. It’s more than just a safari destination; it’s a community-led conservation project run with the Samburu people, who have lived here for generations. The project protects over 850,000 acres of wilderness and creates sustainable livelihoods for the local community through tourism, conservation, and cultural programs. The people are at the heart of the experience. Many guides, hosts, and team members come from nearby villages, bringing a deep knowledge of the land, wildlife, and traditions that no guidebook can match. Life beyond the game drive Head out on guided walks and game drives with Samburu trackers, swim in natural rock pools tucked into the hills, or ride on horseback across the open plains. But time here offers a window into life beyond the safari, too. Sarara opens the door to the community behind it, with opportunities to visit the nearby Reteti Elephant Sanctuary — Africa’s first community-owned elephant orphanage — where rescued calves are raised by local keepers before eventually returning to the wild. I fell in love with Long’uro, a baby elephant found trapped in a well, his trunk badly injured after a hyena attack. Seeing him now, with a shortened trunk, gently cared for by the keepers who rescued him, says everything about the sanctuary’s work. There’s also the chance to meet the women behind the Milk Mamas programme, one of the first initiatives in the conservancy to provide women with their own independent income by selling goat milk used to feed the orphaned elephants. One afternoon, I joined a circle of beading mamas, sitting cross-legged together with a translator as we stitched bright beads into ankle bracelets and shared stories about our lives. The conversation was relaxed, curious and open — one of the most memorable experiences of the trip. Spending time in a traditional Samburu manyatta offers a glimpse into daily life within these small homestead communities. Visits to local schools and healthcare projects supported by the conservancy give a deeper understanding of life in this remote region and the work being done to support the community. A handful of hideaways Sarara is a small collection of places to stay scattered across the conservancy. Each offers a slightly different way to experience the landscape, from the privacy of Reteti House to the treetop hideaways of Sarara Treehouses and the remote simplicity of Sarara Wilderness, alongside the original Sarara Camp that first put this remarkable corner of northern Kenya on the safari map. Across them all runs the same design philosophy – open, earthy spaces built from natural materials that blend delicately into the surrounding landscape. Sarara Camp Set on the slopes of the Mathews Mountains, Sarara Camp is the original lodge at the heart of the conservancy, comprising six spacious canvas tents with solar-heated outdoor showers and wide terraces overlooking the valley. At the centre sits a beautiful natural infinity pool overlooking a permanent waterhole. One afternoon, we counted nearly twenty elephants from two different herds gathered there, alongside zebras, giraffes and warthogs, like something out of the opening scene of The Lion King. Wildlife moves easily through camp too; one evening, a zebra grazed quietly outside my window, and most mornings I woke to a giraffe browsing just beyond my tent. Reteti House A short drive from Sarara Camp, Reteti House feels altogether more private, bookable by a single group, meaning the space is entirely your own. It’s a secluded hillside retreat with just four tents and sweeping views across the plains below. The main house is a beautiful gathering space filled with African artefacts and rustic details. A small infinity pool is tucked into the rocks beside it, shaded by trees and looking out across the plains. Down below, a waterhole draws wildlife through the night; more than once, I woke to the unmistakable sound of elephants slurping away in the darkness. Reteti is also known for its resident leopard. My first night alone in the tent was slightly nerve-wracking, but the nerves soon turned to excitement as the distant rasp of the leopard echoed through the cliffs and baboons wailed their alarm calls. Sarara Treehouses Sleeping high in the canopy, Sarara Treehouses is one of the most unique stays in the conservancy. Eight tented suites sit among the branches, linked by wooden walkways that wind through the trees while wildlife moves quietly along the forest floor below. Spending the night in the treetops felt completely magical, something I’d never experienced before, and it brought a surprising sense of luxury to the wilderness. Monkeys chatter constantly overhead, while elephants often wander beneath the decks. The main house is the largest of the camps, its heavy timber beams and striking bar creating a beautiful space for long evenings. Amarula on ice quickly became the drink of choice, best enjoyed while listening for another resident leopard, said to nap in a branch within view from my bed. Sarara Wilderness Sarara Wilderness is the most remote of the camps, reached by a short hop in a small plane with Scenic Air Safaris - an experience in itself. The pilots fly low over the plains, pointing out wildlife and Samburu manyattas below, giving a completely different perspective on the landscape as wildlife moves across the savannah beneath the wings. Landing on the remote airstrip, the sense of isolation becomes immediate. The spacious tents are intentionally temporary, designed to move with the landscape over time, which adds to the feeling of being somewhere truly wild. Days are spent exploring the conservancy with Samburu guides whose knowledge of the land is extraordinary. The wildlife encounters were some of the most memorable of the trip - watching a line of lionesses stride past our vehicle, sitting quietly among an unbothered herd of elephants with a week-old calf and spotting cheetah, leopard and even the rarely seen serval cat. Out here, the wilderness feels closer, wilder, and totally unfiltered. In the end, what defines Sarara is not just the wildlife or the landscapes, but the people. Days quickly turn into friendships with the Samburu guides, hosts and staff who share their knowledge, humour and stories so generously. There’s a genuine sense of connection here, and plenty of opportunities to give back - whether through community projects or simply supporting the people who make this place what it is. It’s that spirit of shared stewardship that makes Sarara feel less like a destination and more like something you become part of, even if only for a little while. Return domestic flights from Nairobi to Namunyak airstrip with Scenic Wilderness start from $600 per person, or alternatively, you can opt for a private air charter with Scenic Air Safaris for up to 9 people at a cost of $3,470 for the aircraft.

item.title: Condé Nast Traveller invites you to A Taste of the Cayman Islands at Wild by Tart this month
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.17
September has long been synonymous with back to school. But in the world of Condé Nast Traveller, it also means making exciting plans for the year ahead – and these typically revolve around the hottest restaurants on the horizon and travel. In the spirit of prolonging the summer sun that is suddenly setting earlier in London, there might be no time more perfect than the turn of the month to join Condé Nast Traveller for an evening celebrating the Cayman Islands at Wild by Tart, Belgravia's chicest coal station-turned-eatery. Set to be hosted by acclaimed Caymanian street food chef Diego Smith, who will be bringing the island's vibrant culinary Caribbean culture to life through an array of cocktails, canapés, and a dinner with wine pairings, we already expect this to be the kind of event where guests will leave happily debating their favourite dish. Not to mention, we'll take any excuse for an evening with a compelling culinary voice from an equally covetable location. Over the course of the evening, Chef Diego Smith will bring the islands to the table via an expertly-curated menu inspired by Cayman’s exceptionally fresh and flavourful produce, all steeped in local traditions and deep sense of place. You can expect anything from mahi ceviche in fresh orange marinade, jerk pork belly on cassava charcoal, grilled chicken papaya salad and traditional Cayman snapper, coconut and breadfruit run-down stew. And if dessert (we won't spoil it) isn't enough to convince you to book a one-way ticket to George Town in your cab home, we don't know what will. From stories behind the kitchen door to the zingy flavours you'd expect straight of a grill on a turquoise water-hemmed beach, we're already counting down the days to this evening that'll be the perfect way to settle back into the bustle of London, all while dreaming for what's ahead. When: Wednesday 30 September from 6.30pm Where: Wild by Tart, 3-4 Eccleston Yards, Belgravia, London, SW1W 9AZ Tickets: From £100 per person, including a cocktail-and-canapé reception and dinner with exceptional wine pairings. Book here.

item.title: My favourite farm stay in the UK: Tewinbury Farm, Hertfordshire
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.13
It’s a rare treat to be able to take my two small children away for the weekend without having to strategically pack and mentally prepare for the journey. On a particularly sunny weekend in July, we hopped on the tube and wound our way to Finsbury Park station before boarding a Great Northern train for 25 minutes to Welwyn Garden City. From there, we strolled up to the taxi rank outside the shopping centre and a 7-minute drive later, we arrived at Tewinbury Farm. Suddenly the air was fresher, time slowed down, and the only sound was the trickling of the chalk stream. What originally started as a dairy farm of just 50 cows in 1931 has grown and evolved into a 700 acre estate with a hotel, restaurants, a cookery school, a wedding venue, farm shop and a shiny new fitness centre. The impressive set-up is still owned and operated by the William family who originally owned it, now three generations later. The hotel itself is expansive with an array of rooms scattered about from cosy woodland huts to lakeside lodges and generous rooms in the main building. My brood and I checked into the spacious King Edward room in the main building – in a previous life the building operated as the farm's potato shed, and thus all the rooms are named after potatoes. While I eyed the plump primary bed and countrified details, my son dashed up the stairs to discover a delightful mezzanine kid’s bedroom, all kitted out with toys, a rocking horse, tent and farm books. All the details are beautifully considered and elevated, right down to the old-fashioned Polaroid camera on offer to capture family memories during our stay. Elsewhere, the lakeside, woodland and shepherd’s huts are equally slick and all impressively built and renovated by an in-house team. If I was returning sans-children, I'd be booking into one of the lakeside huts, all pine-green wooden slats, petite kitchenette and private hot tubs. Just outside are fire pits for roasting marshmallows and mini pontoons with seating overlooking the lake. The latest coup for Tewinbury is the freshly opened (2026) Farm Club, a sprawling fitness and wellness space. Hotel guests and club members can use the show-stopping open-gym, book into a group class including reformer pilates, and relax in the recovery yard featuring ice baths and saunas. With children in tow, there was no sadly time for a sauna. Instead we skipped off to explore the estate – there’s the central courtyard with a snooker and foosball table, plus a nearby vintage tractor to climb and play on. Further exploring will lead you to plenty of lawn to run around on and an ample wooden playground that will keep wee ones entertained. But of course the starring attraction is the animals – there’s a herd of friendly cows that will plod over to say hello, some pedigree pigs and three quirky alpacas. For grown ups, the real drawcard for the farm though is the fresh produce. This is the kind of place where a steak and simple garden salad will knock your socks off; the distance from farm-to-fork is mere steps. Fittingly, Tewinbury has a cookery school headed up by chef Lee Maycock. Or you can leave it to the pros at Cowshed, where everything is seasonal, homemade and feel good, from farm-reared pork chops to chargrilled trout caught from the local chalk stream, and sourdough bread ingeniously served with chorizo butter. For more casual bites, there’s the Granary Kitchen, while on the weekends the pizza oven is fired up in the courtyard, making it the ultimate hangout for all ages. Before checking out, pop into the farm shop where you can take some of the farm’s current seasonal hits home with you.

item.title: New London restaurants to try in September 2026: our editors' honest opinions on the openings everyone's talking about
item.description:
Source: Condé Nast Traveler UK Score: 2.13
We've always got one eye on any new restaurants opening on the London food scene. Our editors are on the ball for the latest openings in each London neighbourhood, from Covent Garden restaurants to Shoreditch hotspots. For the ultimate list of places to eat in the city, check out our definitive guide to London's best restaurants. These are the places that we consider the crème de la crème, from generations-old spots that have stood the test of time and Michelin-starred dining rooms that get better each year to mind-blowing new openings from this list that we decided deserved a spot on the ultimate round-up of the best restaurants in London. For new restaurants opening in London recently, we've seen follow-ups from some of the city's biggest-name chefs and a handful of restaurant openings that have stopped us in our tracks: from London's newfound love for BBQ to a Turkish restaurant that's turning heads. These are our favourite openings of the past six months. How we choose the tastiest new restaurant openings in London The best new restaurants in London are the most exciting places to eat that have just opened in the capital city. Ranging from small affairs with daily changing menus from up-and-coming chefs to Michelin-starred spots with fresh new menus, these are London's new restaurants we've got our eye on right now. Every restaurant on this list has been selected independently by our editors and written by a Condé Nast Traveller journalist who knows the destination and has eaten at that restaurant. When choosing new restaurants, our editors consider both high-end and affordable eateries that offer an authentic and insider experience of a destination. We’re always looking for stand-out dishes, a great location, warm service, and serious sustainability credentials. We update this list regularly as new restaurants open in London. Best new London restaurants in September 2026 Waterhouse Project, Bethnal Green At the start of September, husband-and-wife team Gabriel Waterhouse and Patricia Wakaimba opened the doors to Waterhouse, a much-anticipated restaurant, wine bar and garden set inside a Victorian warehouse on buzzing cobbled Ezra Street, just off Columbia Road Flower Market. Following the closure of The Water House Project in June, their new home is an impeccably designed space, flowing from raised beds outside, where the chefs pick fresh herbs, into a bar area with stainless steel countertops and handcrafted oak furniture, and through to the dining room, which serves 24 covers in an intimate nightly sitting. The food measures up to the space. Chef Gabriel draws on his Northumberland upbringing and the region’s traditional cooking techniques, while adding a playful touch with in-house ingredients such as miso, koji and garums. Start with a punchy, syrupy fig leaf martini at the bar before embarking on the 11-course tasting menu. The ensemble hits a high note immediately with a rich, comforting cep and Madeira tea, before moving into bites that challenge the palate while remaining comforting and, ultimately, delicious. The courses balance refreshing zing, like the oyster with cucumber and sorrel, with familiar but elevated mouthfuls, like the moreish onion crumpet. Larger plates, including a smoked haddock porridge (oyster mushroom for vegetarians), hit a hearty note. The meal ended on singing hinnies, a traditional griddle cake, with boozy-forward lavender and Laphroaig cream. If you manage to have some room left, the seasonal cheese selection isn’t to be missed. This is a savoury, umami-rich tasting menu that has immediately risen to the top of my list for celebratory meals. The team have nailed the difficult task of creating fine-dining plates without a stuffy atmosphere. Gabriel and Patricia’s history of supper clubs, where their journey began, can still be felt in the environment they’ve curated at Waterhouse. Chloe Laws Address: 7A Ezra Street, London, E2 7RH Website: waterhouse.com Bar Blondie, Queen's Park Queen's Park is having a little moment in the limelight of late, preening and showing off as curious eyes turn its way thanks to a slate of clever openings (Don't Tell Dad, where a queue forms for glossy cinnamon buns and plump pains au chocolat every morning; The Salusbury, a smart pub with a dining room that punches above its weight; Naples-inspired joint Casa Felicia) joining some long-standing favourites like Harry and Meghan's favourite Italian Ida and brewery Wolf Pack. Now, everyone's talking about a wine bar that's taking interiors inspiration from Spaghetti Westerns and looking to four imaginary muses – the writer, the actor, the architect and the director – to pull together its cellar book. The Bar Blondie site used to be Milk Beach, an Antipodean all-day restaurant which kickstarted the Queen's Park foodie revolution eight or so years ago. The space is still owned by Aussie Elliot Milne, who's given it a tip-to-toe renovation. Interiors, designed by Macaulay Sinclair (also behind Dishoom's Permit Room and Hawksmoor, among others), are now mid-century sexy with a masculine edge: nutty woods, dark greens, art curated by The Other Art Fair founder Ryan Stanier. The menu looks to France and Italy: delicate grilled artichokes with pecorino di fossa and honey and silky Cantabrian anchovies in puddles of Provençal olive oil are perfect to share, while heartier pastas (we especially liked the paccheri alla vodka with nduja) are the smart choice if you're settling in for the evening. Award-winning sommelier Alexandra Price has curated a wine list that celebrates everything from well-known, beloved estates to emerging producers. I visited earlier in the summer, on opening night, but live close enough to confirm that the buzz has sustained into autumn, too – this is a smart Act II for a cosy neighbourhood joint. Sarah James Address: 19-21 Lonsdale Road, NW6 6RA Website: barblondie.co.uk Best new London restaurants in August 2026 Oudh 1772, Borough Chef Aktar Islam is something of a Brummie legend. He was the first British-born Bangladeshi chef to be awarded a Michelin star in 2019, just one year after opening his debut restaurant, Opheem, in Birmingham's Jewellery Quarter. A few years later, Opheem became the joint-first Indian restaurant to receive two stars, alongside London's Gymkhana, in the 2024 ceremony. Opheem's status as the city's go-to Special Occasion table to book is firmly cemented. So when news of Islam opening in London reached me, a native Brummie, I was naturally a) very proud (how often do chefs find success outside of London and then transplant to Zone 1?) and b) desperate to get through the door. And it is quite the door. Oudh 1772, Islam's Borough restaurant, is set across a Grade-II listed Victorian townhouse, where each storey sits sort of wonkily on top of the next. That's not to say it's not beautiful: designer Polina Sychova collaborated with Islam on the soft, sumptuously layered spaces – all curvy arches and thick drapes, peppered with antiques from Lucknow and even a bespoke hand-painted ceiling in the attic bar. Rather than bouncing across the Indian subcontinent, Islam's menu focuses on the flavours of Awadh, a historic region in the northern state of Uttar Pradesh. Regional street food is a playful place to start: chaat with white peas and potato or gol guppa (better known here, perhaps, as pani puri) are crispy and best eaten with your hands, a perfect way to start any evening. We boldly take on the mutanjan dum biryani with oxtail, a king prawn kebab and the Awadhi monkfish curry – be warned that while this might certainly be a white tablecloth sort of establishment, the portions are hearty. They're also, luckily, all perfectly pitched – perfumed biryani, garlicky prawns, creamy curry. Like Opheem before it, this is undoubtedly somewhere for a properly nice supper – prevented from ever becoming too proper by the friendly team and Islam's plucky menu. Add it to the list for your own next Special Occasion. Sarah James Address: 66 Union Street, London SE1 1TD Website: oudh1722.com Kismet, Borough Somewhat unexpectedly located above The Globe Tavern, a buzzy pub on the corner of Borough Market, is Kismet. After passing a throng of pint drinkers, visitors climb a winding staircase and enter a Turkish meyhane – a traditional tavern known for live music and family-style meals. Kismet has captured that atmosphere perfectly: dark, glittering mahogany benches, delicate lace curtains and vintage photographs make the restaurant feel wonderfully homely. Turkish music bubbles away in the background, with live performances on the qanun, a traditional string instrument, even hosted every Thursday evening. The menu follows Turkish meyhane cooking, so come prepared to share. Start with Atom, a thick buffalo milk yoghurt topped with chilli butter; cool and tangy against the gentle heat, it is particularly good scooped up with bread or piled onto Sigara Böreği, a crisp pastry filled with salty white cheese. From the charcoal grill comes Tavuk Şiş, smoky chicken thigh with red pepper, alongside Patates Kizartmasi, fried Cyprus potatoes. Wash it all down with Basketcase, a bottled lager brewed in partnership with Coalition Brewery, or, my personal favourite, a glass of raki. The Turkish anise-flavoured spirit is made for sipping alongside food, its clean, herbal finish acting as a refreshing palate cleanser between bites. The final flourish comes with dessert, when waiters glide between tables carrying silver trays above their heads. Lowered on request, they reveal rows of Turkish tea in delicate tulip-shaped glasses and slices of pistachio baklava drowned in syrup. Kismet is only a year-long residency in the space, so visit while you can. Amelia Dhuga Address: Upstairs at The Globe Tavern, 8 Bedale Street, London, SE1 9AL Website: kismet.london Cue Point, Latimer Road Cue Point is determinedly not a newcomer to the London restaurant scene. For a decade, the hybrid Afghan-Texas BBQ of Kabul-born chef Mursal Saiq and head chef Joshua Moroney has been making a name for itself through pop-ups, residencies and stints at breweries. This summer, they've finally found a permanent home for their low-n-slow, fired-up cooking. Cue Point at The Garden Bar is set inside an unchic West London boozer with, as the name hints, a truly enormous garden out back. Here, meat – Wagyu brisket, oak-smoked lamb shank, black lime pepper chicken bites – is smoked to meltiness, or else cooked over licking flames. Saiq's immaculate Afghan flavours are anything but shy and retiring, and a perfect match for Moroney's expert BBQ techniques. Those chicken bites' gnarly exteriors give way to soft meat – we boldly paired ours with the smoked pimento garlic chilli cheese flatbread to start. Wagyu brisket steak served with fluffy Texas naan and cowboy butter is a non-negotiable, although we'd also recommend ordering the flaky chilli-citrus seabass for something a little (emphasis on the word) lighter. The sticky toffee pudding with Bertotti kulfi was a surprise standout: moreish and sweet, Saiq works with West London gelataria Bertotti to perfect the kulfi. The team serve a special menu on Sundays, when Saiq tells me that people try to sneak in the door; advance reservations are so hard to get. This is West London's opening of the summer, and a must-book for anyone seeking serious flavour. Sarah James Address: Garden Bar Grill & Smokehouse at 41 Bramley Road, Notting Hill, London, W10 6SZ Website: cue-point.co.uk Rosina, Wandsworth It's been 20 years since chef Adam Byatt opened Trinity, which in restaurant years is practically ancient. In that time, the Clapham Old Town spot has not only survived but thrived, earning a Michelin star and cementing itself as a south London favourite – its signature beef tartare is still one of the best dishes I’ve ever had, and I don’t even like beef tartare. So when Byatt opened his latest table, Italian-inspired Rosina, in Wandsworth Common, it was busy from day dot. Busy but effortlessly breezy, with smart couples seated at white linen tables adorned with plates of bread, lemons and olives, and single white candlesticks. Antipasti comes to the table with a vibrant flurry – crimson tuna crudo, smoked sardines on toast, and a heavenly bowl of rainbow Datterini tomatoes with basil, nectarine and buffalo mozzarella. This is the kind of place where everything is confidently simple, and the bread basket is put to good use mopping up every sauce and vinaigrette. For mains, a pillowy turbot is roasted on the bone and swimming in lemon, capers, parsley and wilted spinach. The intriguingly named ‘post-service pasta’ was my favourite; an understated yet masterful bowl of spaghetti with anchovy, chilli, garlic and parsley, essentially the dish Byatt likes to make for himself after a shift in the kitchen. Wonderfully oily and crunchy in equal measure, I ate every tiny crumb and noodle. Pudding is served from the marble trolley that holds court in the centre of the restaurant, with tiramisu rustically served with a generous dollop tableside. If there’s room to try two, the not-too-sweet but cheese-heavy Rosina's torte is a worthy option; the torte and the restaurant are named after Byatt’s daughter Rosie, who also works in the kitchen. Lauren Burvill Address: Rosina, 35 Bellevue Road, London SW17 7EF Website: rosinarestaurant.co.uk All Roads, Brixton I visited All Roads during one of London's many 2026 heatwaves, so it says something about how delicious the food is that I wasn't remotely overwhelmed by the plates of mac and cheese, lamb from the house pot or fried wings that were placed in front of me on one of the hottest days of the year. While the rest of London was digging into light salads, or maybe a barbecue, I was more than happy to get stuck into the hearty dishes from chefs and partners Malika Green and Paschelle Brown, who have finally put down roots in Brixton following three years of sold-out supper clubs. The menu blends Caribbean cuisine with British, European and Southern American influences, resulting in a list of dishes that are hearty, moreish and full of flavour. Split into snacks, smalls, grill and plates (with just two or three dishes to each), it's tempting to order the whole menu – take three friends, and you probably could. Unfortunately for me, I was with just one friend, so we had to be discerning (albeit still rather greedy). Having tried over half of the menu, I truly think it would be difficult to order badly here, but my favourites were undoubtedly the chilli parm clams, served in a sweet and salty tomatoey-soy sauce, with crispy pancetta and topped with parmesan, or the impossibly cheesy baked mac and cheese. We ordered a fresh tomato salad to break up the dishes, and ended with homemade sorrel cheesecake ice cream. In the end, despite the heat, there's nowhere I'd rather have been on a Wednesday evening than here in Brixton Village, soaking up the vibe, flavours and fun of this memorable new spot. Abigail Malbon Address: 44 Atlantic Road, London SW9 8JN Website: allroadsldn.com Hon’s BBQ, Hackney Wick After earning a fiercely loyal following during his two-year residency at All My Friends, chef Man Hon Luk's first bricks-and-mortar restaurant – in the spot formerly occupied by Silo above Crate Brewery – was a natural next step. I never made it to the pop-up, but just knowing that Hon perfected his craft at world-renowned, Michelin-starred Interstellar BBQ was reason enough to clear the diary, hotfoot it over to Hackney Wick and see what all the fuss was about. The space is cool, casual and buzzing – high ceilings, whitewashed walls and simple red wooden tables and chairs let the food do the talking. Hon’s cooking is clearly shaped by his time in Texas, but what lands in front of us is something entirely his own: smoky, low-and-slow meats elevated with Chinese flavours and techniques. Every bite melts in your mouth, with just the right hit of spice and sweetness and the kind of deep caramelised crispy bits you’d fight your fellow diner for. The beef short ribs with Sichuan peppercorn sauce are the star of the show (tender, peppery and sticky) but don’t sleep on the sides; perfectly crunchy green beans with an umami-rich glaze, and a silky mac and cheese with a tangy mustard-laced sauce. Our only regret? Opting to share a bowl of the creamy mango coconut pudding – one each is a must. Sarah Allard Address: First floor, Unit 7, The White Building, Queen's Yard, London E9 5EN Website: honsbbq.com Best new London restaurants in July 2026 Vesper, Exmouth Market When Jackson Boxer opens a new London restaurant, it’s safe to assume it’ll be a smash hit. The chef and restaurateur behind buzzy Brunswick House, Dove and Henri has just opened a new neighbourhood spot on Exmouth Market. Interiors are industrial, with bare brick walls, a metal bar in the centre and curtains hiding candle-lit tables in intimate corners. There’s also plenty of tables that spill onto the sun-drenched street. We dined at Vesper a full month after opening, as tables really are that hard to come by. We made sure to book an early 6pm reservation, as the infamous burger you may have seen plastered all over your Instagram, often quoted as one of the best burgers in London, is ordered off-menu to 10 lucky customers on a first-come, first-served basis. We secured the fourth burger of the evening. The bun is covered in sweet glaze, hugging a hefty slab of seared and torched beef with a rare centre, layered with caramelised onions and oozing gorgonzola sauce. We’d recommend sharing, or you’ll be rolling home without a chance to try any of the other delicious plates. Our favourite dish of the night was the fried potato pizzette: a little circular pizza bread topped with pineapple, stringy stracciatella cheese and mortadella. Other highlights include the green bean salad coated in goat's cheese and gooseberry tahini, the chicken agnolotti – al dente pasta pockets bursting with fragrant chicken liver in a madeira jus. For pudding, order the punchy poached apricot flavoured with ginger and amaretto. Plates were scraped clean, as were our little gimlets, previously filled with the Vesper martini finished with a little squirt of citrus oil. Sophie Knight Address: 8-10 Exmouth Market, London EC1R 4QA Website: vesper.restaurant Langosteria, Whitehall Italian seafood restaurant group Langosteria has a knack for attaching itself to smart addresses in glamorous European locations, from Milan's Design District to St Moritz and the waves at Paraggi near Portofino. So it’s no surprise that the Milanese group’s first UK outpost has made a beeline for Raffles London at The OWO. Whitehall's neoclassical Portland stone grandeur doesn't quite evoke the summery spirit of the Ligurian Riviera, but once you pass through its doors, you're transported to that familiar Langosteria world, with its signature animated wallpaper and matching ambience. Here, everything is bold and impactful with a touch of experimentation – including the bar cocktails. From the concise list, the Pomodoro Mezcal, a smoky take on a Bloody Mary, confused my vodka receptors, but the Spicy Margarita with jalapeño was the unequivocal star. Food-wise, Langosteria casts a wide net in pursuit of freshness and quality, hauling its catch from Italy, Spain, France and Scotland. Locavore advocates will scream, but the quality is undeniable. My Sicilian red prawn starter – butter-soft and topped with wafer-thin slices of pecorino – was beautiful. The mains included Langosteria classics like the King Crab Special Edition 2007 and the Brittany Lobster "Spicy Blue”; I plumped for the crispy-skinned black grouper Chateaubriand, its saltiness offset by tangy-sweet caponata (Sicilian aubergine, olive and caper relish). My langoustine with lobster in a puddle of zingy lemon butter was perfectly al dente, but the Milanese turbot with asparagus and saffron proved somewhat immemorable. I chased it all with a glass of Ferrari Brut from a wine list that features most of the Champagne heavy hitters alongside an impressive, Italian-dominant selection of reds and whites. Portions are generous throughout, and for guests of the Raffles hotel, it's just a short stagger to their rooms upstairs. Noo Saro-Wiwa Address: Langosteria, Whitehall Place at The OWO, London, SW1A 2BD Website: langosteria.com Willet's, Chelsea At the back of The Cadogan, A Belmond Hotel, is an elegant wooden staircase that King Edward VII (when he was the Prince of Wales) ascended to visit his lover, the Victorian actress and socialite Lillie Langtry. It still stands as a testament to the history (and discretion) of this particular 1880s Chelsea townhouse, and today, though less steeped in scandal, it is as regal and luxurious as ever. The Cadogan is also home to Willett’s, a new British bistro that seems set to become a hotspot in its own right, even amongst those not staying upstairs. Studio Shayne Brady, the interiors team behind the renovation, has modernised while remaining true to the hotel's history – bathing the space in calming blues and greens. Executive chef Michael Turner (a Gordon Ramsay alum) is producing à la carte dishes that showcase the very best of British produce in unfussy, delicious dishes. The sourdough crumpets with gentleman’s relish and dressed Dorset crab were the definite showstoppers and are destined to become signature dishes. Mini but mighty, I’d have been more than happy with plates of those alone. Seasonality and locality are buzzwords thrown around quite loosely these days, but Willett’s really does do credit to everything that is brilliant about the produce of the British Isles. I'd also recommend the succulent Beef Wellington and the Colchester oysters. We’ve no doubt that this restaurant will become as legendary as some of the hotel’s historic residents. Cass Farrar Address: 75 Sloane Street, London, SW1X 9SG Website: belmond.com Dante, Mayfair Devotees of all things Stateside were intrigued when one of America's best cocktail bars, New York City's Dante, jumped across the pond in 2025 to pop up at grand dame Claridge’s. Rather than tire and bloat at yet another cross-Atlantic collab, the gourmands kept coming. And so, a year later, the hotel restaurant closed its doors for a facelift any Mayfair resident of a certain age would approve of, led by Bryan O’Sullivan Studio, with a fresh palette of green-and-blue tones and fantastical, botanical murals by Beth Rodway, to welcome Dante as a permanent resident of the neighbourhood's slickest hotel. We follow Billecart-Salmon Champagne with a taster of the Negroni Rosa, a watermelon concoction that tastes like a swig of the summer to come. A host of NYC favourites are now on the menu – we sample delicate caviar tarts and champagne pearls and are taken aback by the gargantuan grilled king prawns, their smoky, chilli-butter scent enveloping our booth. If a dish is preceded by the restaurant’s name, you know it’s one the chef’s hedging their bets on. And so the Dante smash burger arrives: a juicy patty coated in provolone cheese and topped with sweet caramelised onion, beside perfectly crispy chips awaiting their saucy demise. Burger devoured and Parmigiano Reggiano-doused veal Milanese inhaled between us, we call on our second stomachs for pudding with a side of spectacle. An espresso martini arrives, my face staring back at me in cocoa dusting courtesy of the bar’s cocktail-printing sorcery, alongside an uber-indulgent sticky toffee doughnut that illuminates our woozy cheeks with a whiskey flambé. It's a fiery finish to a meal I’ll be dining out on for a long time to come. Connor Sturges Address: Dante Mayfair, Claridge's, Brook Street, London W1K 4HR Website: maybourne.com Best new London restaurants in June 2026 The Sea, The Sea, Chelsea When we walk into Pavilion Road’s The Sea, The Sea – already a familiar name in Chelsea, but now a restaurant serving far more than just drinks and oysters – we don’t know what to expect. Above the ground-floor raw bar, tables are bathed in light, and the design is minimalist, but we quickly learn that all attention is poured into the fare. The menu spotlights lesser-known fish, plus whatever catch is locally abundant from the seafood suppliers they've built trusted relationships with. We start with cold sake and a tin of Imperial (as a caviar enthusiast, I love that the sour cream comes pre-topped with chives), followed by butter-soft Isle of Skye scallops with flowering currant. Often, the raw bar usually outshines everything else to me, but three warm dishes – cuttlefish ragu with green almond, smoked Chalkstream trout on a Jersey royal mash, and a rice vinegar-steeped John Dory with maitake – are impossible to top. The ragu is nothing like we imagine: no pasta, just clean-cut cuttlefish with an unbelievably flavourful squid ink salsify that results in an immediate repeat order. Come dessert, don’t look beyond the potato ice cream with smoked eel. It sounds hard to wrap your head around, and for that reason, you must order it. Tamara Southward Address: 243 Pavilion Road, London SW1X 0AW Website: https://theseathesea.net MA/NA Mayfair A new opening in Mayfair comes with glitzy high expectations, which we immediately felt as we were swept through the doors of MA/NA by a suave-suited doorman. He guided us through the long, winding bar space with a house DJ and down to our table under huge bonsais and gold statement lighting. A martini is poured table-side as we browse the extensive menu divided into small plates, robata (meats from the Japanese grill), sushi, steak cuts and large plates. We ordered to share: rock shrimp tempura in a glazed sticky sauce, juicy chicken thigh skewers from the robata grill, a 12-piece sushi platter with fresh cuts as selected by the chef (which could also pass as a piece of art) and the crunchy duck salad with sweet pomegranate. But, our favourite dish, which – fair warning – comes with a big price tag, was the Japanese A5 Wagyu slices served on a hot Himalayan salt stone, which not only flavours, but sears the meat from its heat. Melt-in-the-mouth slices of the finest beef, packed with flavour. MA/NA is on par, if not tastier than some of London's favourite high-end Japanese spots, with equally flashy guests and interiors. Sophie Knight Address: 30 Upper Grosvenor Street, London, W1K 7PH Website: manarestaurants.com Buvette London, Neal's Yard 14 years since its New York debut, chef Jody Williams has brought Buvette (and with it, the spirit of the West Village) to the cobbled streets of Covent Garden – slap bang in the middle of Neal's Yard. This charmingly chic bistro – complete with curated antiques and a black bicycle parked out front – somehow manages to strike just the right balance between familiar and fancy, with a day-to-night menu focusing on locally-sourced produce. We start with a crisp glass of bubbles as we make our selection, following the house suggestion of sharing three to five dishes between two. Plates are indulgent yet remarkably delicate; a vibrant ratatouille, fresh steak tartare, garlicky escargot, and decadent dauphinois. The standout is, unsurprisingly, Buvette's signature croques; we opted for the forestier, a vegetarian riff on the original, paired with a generous pour of white wine (French, naturally). To end, tarte tatin and a mousse au chocolat, followed by a perfectly chilled martini made just the way you like – a highlight among the well-executed classic cocktails on offer. I can’t wait to visit again, whether for a flaky morning croissant and espresso or another evening encounter with that croque... Drew Burns Address: Buvette London, 2 Neal's Yard, London WC2H 9DP Website: buvette-london.com Ornella, London Fields Foodies and film fanatics flocked to Lupa when it opened its doors in Highbury – an Italian feeding frenzy from restaurateur Ed Templeton and chef Naz Hassan, fuelled by The Gentleman star Theo James’ involvement. The reviews were promising, and bookings soon became hard to come by, so it came as no surprise when the trio announced a follow-up – Ornella. On the corner of a leafy suburban street in London Fields, this new arrival is an edible love letter to Milanese fare that the capital’s food scene has long been crying out for, named in honour of the late singer Ornella Vanoni. Inside, it’s simultaneously cosy and sexy, diners tucked into banquettes and huddled around circular tables illuminated by flickering candlelight. Proceedings start over punchy sbagliato and caffè amaro cocktails – easy on those, mind – before the fluffiest focaccia in town arrives, warm and doused in glittering olive oil, alongside wafer-thin slivers of salty mortadella and coppa. There’s a choice of four starters – shoutout to the sea bream tartare, I hear, from my companion – followed by five ‘primi’ dishes. We slurp on salty onion broth and twirl our forks to catch shavings of cheese in the simple yet moreish butter and Parmesan tagliatelle, all washed down with generous pours of Venetian Manzoni Bianco. Naturally, onto secondi, a satisfyingly crisp chicken Milanese, used mostly to mop up heaps of silky mashed potatoes that likely contain more butter than potatoes (no complaints from us). We saunter into the night, hands in circular motions on our stomachs, remarking on how beige and calorific our spread became. No regrets at all, mind, as we plot our return to get snug in one of Ornella’s corners when the mercury drops, if not before. Connor Sturges Address: Ornella, 51 Wilton Way, London E8 1BG Website: ornella.restaurant Mezzogiorno by Francesco Mazzei It’s no small feat bringing Italian summers to London, so it comes as no surprise to any Italophile that Francesco Mazzei is the one leading this charge for the foodie moment that’s taken root within the grand dame walls of London’s Corinthia Hotel. Designed to transport, its namesake and menu are inspired by the southern regions of Italy, where the sun is the most intense at midday, translated as ‘Mezzogiorno’. Personally more accustomed to London’s shades of grey, I was surprised to enter the opulent Northall bar and find myself in a nonna-esque open kitchen that doubles as a walk-through to the main restaurant. Here, a communal oval table sits opposite the kitchen, where an intimate group sit watching folds of dough being expertly handcrafted into pasta and breadsticks by the chefs in their whites. Inspired by the Baroque palazzos of Southern Italy, the restaurant is adorned with custom-made Murano chandeliers hanging from tall ceilings, held up by dramatic pillars adjoined to a waffled terracotta ceiling, which makes me think of a gelato cone. The scene here on a Tuesday evening is mostly out-of-town pals sharing plates, business comrades and on this occasion, a Hollywood A-lister, but the winning majority here were couples holding hands across tables and huddled in booths. We start by nibbling on the longest breadsticks I’ve ever seen - simple and all unique, the only concern is filling up on them, but they are surprisingly light. Next comes an injection of colour with the Pipi Cruski Limone Di Rocca Mayo, a traditional dish of fire-red peppers that are fried and best enjoyed slovenly dipped into lemon butter. Despite the colour, these aren’t spicy and have the most excellent crunch. Among the tables, we tuck into an antipasti of Orkney scallops, which are tender but fragrant alongside Batutta Di Manzo Inglese, a refreshing mix of chopped beef, salad leaves, pomegranate seeds and large shavings of black truffle. Mouths still full but contentedly chatting, it’s easy to see the inspiration behind this place. With excellent company and ambience, come and come again, but definitely share the hand-made pasta with native blue lobster sauce and T-bone among the table, while you snack on humble traditional Sicilian vegetables and of course, an entire bowl of zucchini sticks. To finish, the showstopping Tiramisu is necessary - presented to the table in a family-style bowl, the friendly server affectionately spoons the dessert onto our plates, like they are welcoming us to the family. Megan Wilkes Address: Whitehall Place, London, SW1A 2BD, United Kingdom Website: corinthia.com/en-gb/london/mezzogiorno/ Kumori, Soho Slap-bang in the heart of Soho, Kumori is a 30-seat handroll bar where most of the action happens at the counter, creating an intimate, immersive feel. Inside, the space feels a little like stepping into a spaceship – all brushed-metal surfaces and iridescent pink and purple lighting. From the plump made-to-order handrolls to the carefully curated soundtrack, everything about Kumori feels cool, fresh and considered. Knees brush as we pore over the tick-box menu, leaving me spiralling as I weigh up how many of the handrolls I can reasonably fit in; there are simply too many good options. The cocktail list is an equally delicious debate, eventually landing on a yuzu mezcal margarita and sitting back to settle in for the show. Behind the counter, chefs move with speed and precision through a menu curated by head chef John Randy De Guzman (formerly Nobu, Tobi Masa and Katsuya). Each roll is served from chef to patron the moment it’s made, turning dinner into a kind of live theatre. Lucy Bruton Address: Kumori, 26 Denman Street, London W1D 7HX Website: kumorirestaurant.com Best new London restaurants in May 2026 Tavern, Shoreditch I’m still thinking about those little melted cheese-filled choux buns that kicked off dinner (the chunion puff), and the dense brown butter muffin that we finished on. But also every course we inhaled in between, which was cooked on open flames from the team behind Michelin-starred Restaurant St Barts in Farringdon. Nest, the high-end tasting-menu restaurant that once sat on this site, is no longer open. The trio behind it, Johnnie Crowe (Co-founder), Brendan Appleby (executive chef), and Kirsty Easterbrook (head chef), have moved away from fine dining, rebranding and reopening as Tavern, a much more casual affair with a nose-to-tail concept using seasonal British produce. I loved the new bistro-style interiors mixed with oldy-worldy pub furnishings. Dark, mismatched wooden chairs, scattered with shaggy sheepskins, are tucked beneath linen-topped tables with flickering candles. Kick things off with a Tavern Pickleback cocktail – a dirty martini infused with pickle juice, served with a cocktail stick of cured meat inside. Small plates (actually on the larger size) are flung out of the kitchen quickly; order the fire bread coated in wild garlic and, obviously, the chunion puff to start. For mains, we loved the asparagus with a dollop of buttery hollandaise and cured egg yolk, the pork and cuttlefish sausage with squid-ink mustard and the huge joint of smoky sirloin with a side of charred leaves, beetroot and horseradish. For dessert, have the black koji custard tart, bitter and sweet at the same time. Sophie Knight Address: Tavern, 374-378 Old Street, London, EC1V 9LT Website: tavernlondon.co.uk The Latimer, North Kensington The Latimer is a true family effort. It's been recently brought to life by Rochelle Canteen co-founder Melanie Arnold, St John and Sessions Arts Club partner Jon Spiteri, and their three children, Lorcan, Fin, and Molly, who have brought their own prowess to London hotspots Caravel and Koya, respectively. Given this resume, I already knew I’d be in good hands when it came to the food, but the clan have also captured a remarkably warm neighbourhood feel. Though it’s been open for just over a week, when we visit, guests here walk around comfortably with a sense of knowing the place. We ordered grilled asparagus in a herb sauce we’d drink by the bowl if we could, confit trout with green beans and new potatoes, and our must-have: unbelievably tender pork belly skewers braised in cider, served with a dollop of applesauce. Grilled-to-perfection sea bream with tiny green and yellow tomatoes in a delectable aioli, and a courgette linguine tossed in stracciatella followed. There are two desserts – an amaretti crumble and a chocolate mousse. Plus, I’m impressed by the drinks here – at £12, they’re decently priced for West London and the chicest thing about the pub. I opt for the Westway, a tequila-and-blood-orange shrub short drink, but mentally bookmark South of the Border, a black coffee-and-reposado tequila drink, for when I’m next here on a weekend. Tamara Southward Address: 274 Latimer Road, London W10 6QW Website: thelatimer.co.uk Bar Etna, Newington Green Does London really need another hype-y pizza joint? Having been left as cold as a next-day margarita by a couple of recent openings, I was sceptical – but having spent the evening being charmed and carbloaded by the team at Bar Etna, I can attest that it absolutely does. Perhaps I shouldn’t have been surprised – this is the dream-team project from Four Legs’ Ed McIlroy (Finsbury Park’s Tollington and The Plimsoll) and Joe Beddia (owner of Philadelphia-based, Bib Gourmand-garlanded Pizzeria Beddia). Their special relationship has resulted in an East Coast pizza bar with mid-century Milanese design and top-notch seasonal British ingredients. The downstairs bar is reserved for walk-ins, while upstairs is (slightly) more formal tables, where we huddle knee-to-knee with strangers in front of an open kitchen from which servers twirl out piping pizzas. The menu is no-fuss: three spritzes plus a special (a tomatini-inspired affair on our visit); negronis or vermouth on tap; an Italian-focused wine list; a couple of snacks; and four thin-crust, Italian-American style pizzas to choose from. Creamy “judion” (butter) beans arrive floating in silky olive oil and liberally doused with salt and lemon zest – perfectly simple and perfectly done, a hint of what’s to come. The must-order tomato pie is a Philly staple of salty, herby tomatoes spread on springy focaccia. My fellow diner deems it “the best, most upscale version of primary school traybake pizza you’ve ever had”. For pizza, we go for a simple Number One (tomato, mozzarella and Neal’s Yard coolea), which elegantly manages the dance between a thin, crispy base and a satisfying amount of flop. The Number Two (cream, cantabrian chillis, greens, coolea) is our favourite, with just the right amount of chilli heat, but the appropriately volcanic Etna Curry Pizza blows my socks off with one bite; it’s not for me, but those made of stronger stuff might enjoy this playful tribute to a curry house saag paneer. A stainless steel coupe of espresso soft serve is tiny and chic and just right to cut through all the carbs. One night after opening, Bar Etna was heaving, with a real house party feel. With plans for late-night pizzas by the slice on Fridays and Saturdays, I can already tell that the pavement outside will be spilling over this summer – and with the recently opened The Gold Tooth (from the pair behind London Fields’ Papi) and existing favourites Cadet and Yield nearby, Newington Green is fast becoming one of the buzziest food spots in this part of town. Olivia Squire Address: 47 Newington Green, London N16 9PX Website: instagram.com/bar.etna.london Idalia at Pillar Hall, Olympia There’s something sparkly happening in West London. Last month saw the opening of Pillar Hall – a landmark new live music venue, 30,000ft restaurant and speakeasy set within a truly magnificent Grade II-listed space, as part of Olympia’s tidy £1.3 billion regeneration. Originally designed in 1886 by architect Henry Edward Coe, it was built for exhibitions, concerts and even the circus. Vivienne Westwood staged her first catwalk show here; Britain hosted one of its earliest film screenings; and now, 140 years on, it’s back with a new outfit for a fresh dose of razzle-dazzle. At its heart sits the sweeping restaurant, Idalia. The name is an alternative moniker for Aphrodite that was rather more in vogue in the 1880s. The vast, gleaming dining room is all verdant glamour, inspired by the nearby gardens of Kensington and Olympia, with space for 300 – so not your quiet Tuesday supper spot. The sparkling wine list is all English and excellent, but do start with one of the cocktails, which are playful, theatrical things served in everything from pink-crusted globes to glass handbags as an homage to Dolce & Gabbana. Of course, it’s a fine dining experience. In the kitchen, Samantha Williams – formerly Angela Hartnett’s executive chef – delivers a modern British menu with the odd Asian interlude. Reasons why, unsure, but why not, I say – and to be fair, the Asian stuff is really good. A bowl of Gochujang chicken thighs are juicy, crispy and drizzled in zesty sriracha mayo, while the whole roasted Turbot, which arrives theatrically and is deboned tableside, comes with a heaping scoop of shichimi togarashi butter oozing atop the skin and some fresh pickled daikon. It’s melty-soft and perfect for sharing, best served with a side of the beef tallow chips – the swankiest fish and chips you’ll eat all year bar none. Finish with the pistachio cheesecake, which is truly humongous and has famously racked up quite a reputation in only the first week of opening. This is a thoroughly grand affair perfect for your next big do – and such a glitzy night deserves a little flourish. Charley Ward Address: Pillar Hall, Olympia Way, London W14 0EY Website: pillarhall.co.uk Fenix, Mayfair I’ll never say no to a Greek salad, but a salad plus endless dips, pittas and charcoal-fired meats and seafood? Count me in. Fenix is a smart Greek-Mediterranean restaurant in the heart of Mayfair (right next to Green Park station), serving sharing plates with a slightly modern twist. The menu is split into spreads, salad, cold dishes, meze, open fire, pasta and rice and sides, and the choice is overwhelming – in the best way. At first glance, I knew I'd have trouble choosing from the vast menu, and there were multiple extra dishes I’d have chosen if I had endless stomach space, but in the end, we went for a little bit of everything. Start with the dips – the spicy feta is creamy with a bit of a kick, but the smoked taramasalata was the real star of the show; full of flavour, a perfect smooth texture and just gorgeous spread across pillowy pita. We saved a little bit of our dips for the meze (the halloumi tempura and caramelised aubergine with tahini miso are must-orders) and added spicy sea bass carpaccio, spicy sweetcorn and orzo with langoustine and feta to finish things off. There wasn’t a dish I regretted, although in hindsight I was probably too stuffed for the crème brûlée – but who can say no to a sweet treat? The space is massive, but it still feels intimate. During our Thursday night dinner, we were catered to by multiple members of staff (all of them friendly and knowledgeable) and our reservation was stretched out for nearly three hours, without ever feeling rushed. The decor is clearly slightly themed towards a taverna (think raffia and wood, plenty of greenery and paved flooring) but avoids being gimmicky thanks to the chic combination of textures and light colour palette. I’d come back here with friends visiting London to show them a cool spot in the city, and for a menu with an endless list of crowd-pleasers. Address: Fenix, Stratton House, 80 Piccadilly, London W1J 8HX Website: fenixrestaurants.com Café Jikoni, Stratford It’s rare for a toastie to be anything more than a rushed, forgettable meal, but at Café Jikoni, that all changed. The Goan aubergine achaar and Mony’s cheddar toastie was one of the best bites I’ve had this year, and without question the finest toastie I’ve ever eaten. The staff insisted we try it, and despite my initial scepticism at choosing a sandwich over something more elaborate, I was quickly proved wrong. It was spicy, oozing, and bright with freshness. To me, the mark of an exceptional chef lies in their ability to elevate the humble. Ravinder Bhogal is a clear master of this, able to refine even the most staple of dishes. Born in Kenya to Indian parents, she is an award-winning food writer, TV presenter, journalist, cook, and restaurateur, and her breadth of experience is evident in every dish. Jikoni Marylebone has long been an essential part of London's dining scene, and now Bhogal has expanded the concept with an all-day café and restaurant housed on the lower ground floor of the new V&A East Museum in Stratford. The striking building feels like a natural home for her food: elevated yet relaxed, inclusive, and creative. Standouts ranged from the nibbles – such as the Shambaa pickles and umami-rich oregano fries – to larger plates like butter beans aglio e olio, topped with irresistibly crunchy pangrattato, and a deeply comforting massaman curry. As someone who eats predominantly plant-based, I found Jikoni sets a high bar for vegetarian cooking, proving it can be just as inventive, flavourful, and satisfying as any meat-based dish. The tofu massaman and butter beans were particularly vibrant and memorable. From the drinks list, the sweet, smoky strawberry margarita and a satisfyingly dry martini are both worth your time. To finish, I watched the sun set over the canal while indulging in an intensely rich Vietnamese coffee brownie, alongside a picture-perfect yuzu, pandan, and strawberry iced bun. Address: Café Jikoni at the V&A East Museum, 107 Carpenters Rd, Queen Elizabeth Olympic Park, Stratford, E20 2AR Website: jikonilondon.com Best new London restaurants in April 2026 Teal by Sally Abé, Hackney Tucked along a leafy Hackney street, Teal by Sally Abé feels immediately at home among neighbourhood pubs, cafés and delis, just a short stroll from London Fields. With its soft green interiors, potted plants and light-filled dining room, the space strikes a balance between relaxed local charm and quietly confident fine dining. This is the latest opening from Sally Abé, whose résumé spans some of London’s most respected kitchens, including Restaurant Gordon Ramsay, The Ledbury and The Harwood Arms. Here, her cooking leans into British produce with a sense of nostalgia, revisiting historic touches such as the £1 “penny lick”, a playful nod to Victorian-era street treats. The menu opens with thoughtful bites, including a standout Locket’s savoury: a salty-sweet mouthful of Stilton on toast, with a fruity finish. Starters showcase the kitchen’s finesse, particularly a delicately balanced asparagus tartlet with Old Winchester, and a Dorset crab royale lifted by peas and lovage. Mains are richer and more robust, from an artichoke and hazelnut vol-au-vent to beef sirloin with wild garlic, Cornish mussels, and a deeply flavoured haunch of deer. Desserts are a highlight. A marmalade ice cream sandwich walks the line between bitter and sweet, while a marshmallow teacake paired with Earl Grey custard offers a playful finish. While traditional British menus can lean heavily towards meat, Teal makes a strong case for its vegetable dishes, which stand confidently alongside their counterparts. The wine list is thoughtfully curated yet accessible, with English options such as Sussex sparkling wines appealing to the local crowd. Service is warm and assured, completing a restaurant that already feels like a natural fixture in the area. Address: Teal by Sally Abé, 52 Wilton Way, London Fields, E8 1BS Website: tealbysallyabe.com Taverna Ermou, Marylebone Taverna Ermou is the closest you’ll feel to being in a Greek taverna in London. Tiled chequered floor, marble tables topped with a little candle, traditional chairs made of wood and straw and lots of framed hand crochet doilies often seen in old-school Greek homes. Staff dressed in white shirts and black aprons run around serving a packed out and very loud restaurant off the already busy James Street in central London. This is the second branch of Ermou, following the original in Athens. It’s warm, welcoming and slightly chaotic – a recipe for a fun evening with friends. The menu is like the interiors: extremely traditional. Expect classics like tzatziki, Greek salad, and super succulent chicken souvlaki. Plates are meant to be shared, served on stainless steel platters and thrown in the middle of the table – we were happy to find there's no skimping on portion sizes either. Every dish was big enough for at least three or four people to share happily. You’ll want to order a bunch of dips, we can’t recommend the deconstructed spanakopita dip enough – a warm spinach and feta paste served with crispy bread. Then order mezze plates, including the Saganaki, which we have seen pop up all over our Instagram: a runny graviera cheese coated in a flaky kataifi phyllo sprinkled with pistachios and spicy honey. A fresh salad and a few bigger plates from the grill and pasta section, such as spiced beef and lamb kebabs, charred octopus and rich creamy crab orzo. We’ve also heard great things about the brunch menu. This all-day dining spot might have just taken the lead as the best Greek restaurant in London. Sophie Knight Address: Taverna Ermou, 38-40 James Street, London W1U 1EU Website: ergonfoods.com Burro, Covent Garden Burro – or butter, in Italian – certainly lives up to its name. Simple ingredients reign supreme here, but in our three-course dinner, we had anchovies with butter and crostini, sole with a butter-and-prosecco sauce, and garlicky Jersey royal potatoes swimming in the good stuff. Personally, I had no complaints (the more butter, the better), but diners should be warned that it’s easy to lean towards heavy dishes… although, isn’t that what lovely Italian dining should be about? It’s very easy to over-order when the menu starts with a selection of antipasti so tempting you could ask for one of each, but I’d certainly recommend the aforementioned anchovies, plus pillowy-fresh foccacia and melty Salumi. When it came to Primi, we misjudged; the fettuccine with duck and porcini ragù was heavy and a little salty; in all honesty, I had hoped for a little more flavour or fun. The sole lifted my spirits a little, but it was dessert – rhubarb granita with vanilla cream – that really left me wanting more. It’s rare for me to skip a tiramisu, but in this case, I was ready for something a little bit lighter, and thank god, because I stumbled upon one of my favourite puddings in a long time. The restaurant is undoubtedly set for big things: its location in Floral Court in Covent Garden is pretty perfect, and comes from a known name in the industry, Conor Gadd, co-owner of much-loved Highbury restaurant Trullo. This is a more suave, grown-up version, where theatre-goers mingle with after-work diners, and the vibe inside is relaxed and fun – helped along by a great team of staff who happily share suggestions. High ceilings, fancy tablecloths, and art dotted across the walls add to the opulence. I'll certainly return to try the constantly changing menu, but I'll be hoping the granita remains. Abigail Malbon Address: Burro, 2, Floral Court, Floral Street, London WC2E 9FB Website: trattoriaburro.com

item.title: The 12 New Cookbooks We Can’t Wait to Cook From This Fall
item.description:
Source: Eater Score: 2.01
We have reached that time of year again. Every good tomato suddenly prompts the pondering: Will this be the last one for the season? The heat begins to give way to crisper breezes, and we start to crave the comfort of windows fogged up from bubbling pots of soup instead of thinking about how to minimize our time in front of a hot stove. The 12 New Cookbooks We Can’t Wait to Cook From This Fall The season’s exciting new releases include Asian American croissants, divorce cooking, Indian street food, foraged treats, and more Luckily, this season’s cookbooks offer many exciting ways to joyously warm ourselves in the kitchen, whether by baking border-traversing croissants and comforting counter cakes, or keeping the stove simmering with Dutch ovens of borscht, beef noodle soup, or budae jjigae. There are diversions from the standard cookbook on this list, too, like a divorce-inspired reflection (in which the essays are just as essential as the recipes) and a treasure trove of a garden almanac that feels like an escape into another world. I’ve compiled 12 selections from the fall cookbook season that have me especially excited to cook and read this fall and winter. Joyce Tang with Soleil Ho Hardie Grant, out now If you feel like everything is an Asian American bakery now, you’re right. In the Bay Area, Bake Sum — with its Spam-musubi-esque croissants and ube pineapple buns — was an early adopter of the current trend, starting as a pandemic pop-up in 2020 before opening its Oakland location the following year. In her colorful and playful new cookbook, chief baking officer Joyce Tang pulls back the curtain on her cuisine-bending treats, like quiche inspired by chawanmushi, the Japanese savory egg custard, and danishes in the style of okonomiyaki and aloo matar, the Indian dish of spiced potatoes and peas. The bakes involving laminated dough are ambitious, weekend-worthy projects, but the book takes a welcomingly progressive approach, easing in novice bakers via puddings and jellies (its first recipe is a simple, anyone-can-do-it microwave mochi) before exploring more advanced techniques in its chapter on cakes, and then making its way to croissants. This is a book for the person who counts big baking projects among their favorite ways to spend the colder months. Carla Lalli Clarkson Potter, out now Lalli, who won audiences over as Carla Lalli Music during her time at Bon Appétit, has catalogued the dissolution of her 24-year marriage in a cookbook. With its reflections on motherhood, identity, and where a background in restaurants fits into those things, Lalli continues the narrative thread of releases like Tanya Bush’s Will This Make Me Happy and Rebecca May Johnson’s Small Fires. That’s to say that you’re here as much for the essays as for the recipes. The latter, including dishes such as “weeknight lamb chop special, for any number” and “quick beans and rice for when the avocado is ripe,” are delightfully loose and flexible. These are realistic suggestions for weeknights when you’re burnt-out, but also for those glorious instances in which you care more about getting yourself on the sand than fussing about what to make for your beach trip (for those instances: peaches with lime and salt).Many of these ideas were birthed during “separation summer,” when Lalli often found herself eating alone after years of cooking for four. These recipes (and the words that accompany them, like a list of things that “made [Lalli] feel free”) will feel useful on bad days, sick days, and anytime you need to give yourself grace, but also whenever you need to be reminded of how much pleasure life offers. Richard Christiansen Chronicle, September 15 Pleasure Principles is the newest book from Richard Christiansen of Flamingo Estate, the Los Angeles-based lifestyle brand so luxurious and sprawling in its ambitions that even Martha Stewart has described it as “over the top.” Pleasure Principles is predictably maximalist; not specifically a cookbook, it feels like picking up a paper trail while exploring the lush thicket of Christiansen’s secret (if oft-Instagrammed) garden. Stories about the building of Christiansen’s property veer into detours about the history of camellia plants and Coco Chanel, interspersed with archival imagery and photos of flora shot in the style of high-fashion editorial. A primer about the vast range of sage plants gives way to a checklist of garden tasks for January, seasonal project ideas (“help build a bird’s nest” or “make a sage tincture”), and recipes for pasta with sage leaves embedded in the dough and vegetable broth featuring lotus petals and dried skullcap. Pleasure Principles feels like an immersive fantasy world: Open up any random page for a little hit of magic, or an escape into Christiansen’s sparkly, greenery-filled universe. It’s a book that’ll make even winter feel vibrant and full of possibility. Meherwan Irani with Jamie Feldmar Ten Speed Press, September 22 This is a book that will make you want to have a party. That’s partially because recipes like the deep-fried, carb-on-carb vada pav and crisp, thin dosa with coconut chutney will feed six or more (and benefit, process-wise, from the economy of scale). It’s also because it feels raucous and alive, full of bright colors, bold typography, and big proclamations, ready for joyful debate. Is vada pav, as Meherwan Irani writes, “without question, the greatest sandwich of all time”? Is this, indeed, as the title suggests, the best Indian cookbook in the world? This is food that makes you want to crowd around a table, tearing off pieces of seekh kebab with fluffy, still-steaming naan and crushing cold beers. Whether Indian street food is, as Irani audaciously claims, the “best food on the planet” remains up for discussion, but for those of us who can’t get to India or to Irani’s lauded North Carolina restaurants Chai Pani and Botiwalla anytime soon, this book is a good way to test that argument. Alexis Nikole Nelson with Jeanelle Hayner Olson S&S/Simon Element, September 22 Alexis Nikole Nelson, also known as Black Forager, is a bright spot in the doom spiral that social media can often be. Nelson is known (and widely loved, picking up nearly 5 million followers on TikTok alone) for her bubbly disposition, whimsical vibe, and clever creations such as syrup infused with pine cones and color-changing pine-needle cookies. She demystifies the vast array of food that you can forage without even having to go deep into the woods, like acorns and the fruit of the linden trees that are abundant in many parts of the United States, and balances practicality, safety, and play in the process. Her long-awaited cookbook gets its name from the catchphrase that ends her videos: “Happy snacking. Don’t die.” With recipes like pickled magnolia flowers, Japanese knotweed granita, and maitake mushroom “steaks,” this book promises to be a guide to seeing even your suburban neighborhood through new eyes. Dona Murad Quadrille, September 22 New York City’s Librae Bakery draws on its owner Dona Murad’s upbringing in Bahrain with an Indian and Portuguese mother and a Bahraini Persian father; her time spent working in Copenhagen with her husband Andre, who is French Moroccan; and her new life in NYC, where Andre grew up. Naturally, the bakery has embraced the language and perspective of “third-culture” cuisine from the start, serving croissants with pistachio frangipane, scented with rose water; morning buns spread with labneh and za’atar; babka with both lemon curd and loomi (black lime); and more. Much of this book requires getting comfortable with Murad’s “mother dough” recipes — like ones for croissant dough, morning buns, and enriched dough — or working with sourdough starter. For those new to these more involved bakes, Murad provides thorough, nicely documented steps and imagery. If you need something easier than croissants, Murad’s cookies and breads, including cleverly topped sheets of focaccia, provide a more approachable entry point. Another book for bakers who don’t turn down a challenge, Librae is also for anyone who respects traditional pastry techniques but wants to push flavors further. Clara Lee and Eddo Kim Workman, October 6 If it can’t still be summer, at least it’s almost soup season. Here, Clara Lee and Eddo Kim break Korean soups into fundamentals — a chart compares the qualities of guk versus tang versus jjigae versus jeongol; the first section of the book is about making broth, then categorizing those soups into applications. There are quick-cooking soups, soups for slower nights, soups for each season, soups that are especially restorative, and soups for sharing; you could spend the entirety of the coming colder months cooking exclusively through this repertoire. If Lee and Kim’s names are familiar, that’s because they ran the cherished San Francisco superette Queens, which closed in 2023 to transition into a line of pantry staples. The shop has been described as “iconoclastic,” representing the new wave of Korean American cuisine. Consider Korean Soups essential for anyone who loves to be cozy, anyone who’s looking to deepen their understanding of Korean home cooking, or anyone who simply needs more ways to use the gochujang they bought for cookies a while ago. Kay Chun Knopf, October 6 Recipe developers I know cite NYT Cooking contributor Kay Chun among their favorite recipe developers, and it’s easy to see why. Her book starts off with snacks and pickles, Chun adding low-lift but flavor-packed flourishes: She quickly marinates sardines to top toast; her calamari gets a gilda-esque zhuzh, skewered with fried peppers and olives. Gather Around My Table delivers on its promise of simple, weeknight-friendly food that doesn’t feel boring, with dishes such as grilled tofu simmered in soy sauce with aromatics, and then given the ssam and taco treatment with both a perilla leaf and a tortilla. Wakame and a shallot vinaigrette featuring grated tomatoes make her green salad livelier and less run-of-the-mill (her mustard vinaigrette, meanwhile, gets amped up by doenjang). I appreciate that Chun gives tofu an entire chapter, too, coaxing even omnivores to employ it more, as in her pork breakfast sausages with crumbled tofu for added moisture and protein. With Gather Around My Table, Chun consistently offers low-effort ways to make familiar dishes more interesting and rewarding. Eric Sze and Elyse Inamine Hardie Grant, October 13 We’ve come full circle: Fusion is good again, or at least so proclaims chef Eric Sze, known for his New York City restaurant Wenwen and the recently closed 886. His debut cookbook Taiwanese?, emphasis on that question mark, is an ode to letting Taiwanese food be fun, free, and a little freaky: His lu rou fan, also known as lo ba beng, the dish of braised pork over rice, includes the “strange addition of peanut butter,” for example. Why the hell not? Especially when Sze has, as documented in the book (with vivid imagery from star photographer Alex Lau), gone on a bonkers crawl of 60-plus bowls of lu rou fan in a single week; he’s earned the right to experiment. Taiwanese? is not the traditionalist’s guide to the cuisine, but anyone who likes seeing the commonalities between disparate cuisines and playing with the boundaries between them will get a kick out of this book, which includes recipes such as seared zhajiang lasagna with pork and octopus, and beef noodle soup burgers. Suffused throughout is an impish irreverence: Sze calls a soup made with yellow-fat chicken, regular chicken, and goth Silkie chicken “diversity chicken soup”; he’s known, at Wenwen, for the “BDSM chicken” (that incredibly involved recipe’s in here, too). Taiwanese? is a good pick for anyone who’s serious about food but also sees some of the self-imposed rules around it as really not that serious, or for anyone who’s got a great relationship with their local butcher. Caroline Schiff Abrams, October 13 This is, as the name would suggest, a book for the daily-3-p.m.-sweet-treat kind of people. But it’s also a book about making baking less annoying and more chill, a boon for anyone who would love baked goods more often but hates the thought of all the fuss. In her debut cookbook, beloved New York City pastry chef Caroline Schiff, formerly of Gage & Tollner, assures you that sifting is generally unnecessary, and that your baked goods will probably be fine even if you forgot to bring the eggs to room temperature.
