Her ideas will appeal to the baker without a dishwasher — her giant chocolate chip cookie dirties one bowl and requires no mixer nor hand beater. It’s also for the snacker who wants to reap as many rewards as possible out of a single burst of effort (see: the black and white coconut macaroons and the cardamom counter cake with chocolate ganache, both of which keep for a week). Schiff describes her lifestyle as one in which “there’s always something sweet in [the] kitchen — no special occasion required,” allowing friends to stop by anytime for cake and tea (and that’s both definitions of the latter). Daily Dessert is a call to be less fussy and to enjoy ourselves more, and who isn’t enticed by that? Alissa Timoshkina Quadrille, October 20 The cozy hits continue, and as someone who prefers to eat most food out of the comforting confines of a bowl, I appreciate Alissa Timoshkina’s commitment to a highly specific pursuit: spoonable food. In Lozhka, you’ll find a tour of Eastern Europe through all things slurpable and scoopable. Much of this is soup or stew, as to be expected, but oh, the variety! Here is Slovak and Belarusian mačanka, a mushroom stew infused with sauerkraut brine (and which Timoshkina serves with lokše, crepes made with mashed potato dough); Armenian lentil soup with the tannic touch of both prunes and walnuts; and so many ways to use millet, barley, and beans (on that note, this is a great book for anyone who is trying to eat more fiber). There are filled dumplings and drop dumplings and steamed bread dumplings! I don’t want to hope for a long winter, but with this book to work through, I also wouldn’t mind it quite as much. Lucas Sin Artisan, October 27 Lucas Sin, the chef formerly of New York City’s Junzi, has always been very good at explaining how to cook; his cooking tutorials via Instagram Stories buoyed me through the early pandemic and taught me techniques I still use today. As a cookbook author, he’s a natural. His first cookbook combines his conversational yet helpfully specific instruction style with his clear passion for Hong Kong’s cha chaan tengs, diners where you’ll find set meals of macaroni in soup, luscious scrambled eggs, and toast. The photography here is gorgeous, indulgent, and transportive, each page a rich text: Sin offers a trove of highly readable little insights, like the backstory as to why roast pork belly and tofu skin over rice became known as “A Man’s Romance” (the answer: a viral, anonymous Hong Kong blog post), cast-iron sizzling pan etiquette, his favorite places in Hong Kong to get the dishes mentioned, and more. Sin is in the process of opening his own cha chaan teng in NYC and is testing out his repertoire of dishes in an extremely popular pop-up; especially for those of us who still haven’t gotten a seat, Cha Chaan Teng is the next best thing.

item.title: Affordable Alternatives to Japan's Most Crowded Destinations
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.91
Japan welcomed more visitors in 2025 than ever before, and most walked the same ten streets. The crowding is real but concentrated: a few temples, villages, and viewpoints absorb most of it, while places offering the same experience sit half empty a valley away. Budget travelers hear a tempting promise: quieter must mean cheaper. Sometimes it does. Sometimes the quiet option adds a shinkansen leg or a rural bus that erases every yen saved on admission. The only way to know is to do the math, so this article does it for four popular swaps using prices checked in August 2026 from official sources. That timing matters: JR East raised fares on March 14, 2026, and Kyoto doubled its accommodation tax two weeks earlier, so numbers from older guides are quietly wrong. The pairings come from the Crowd-Free Japan Index, which matches 40 of Japan's most-visited places with curated quieter alternatives. Kanazawa Instead of Kyoto: The Savings Are on the Ground, Not the Rails Kanazawa is often called "little Kyoto," which annoys both cities, but the comparison holds where it counts. The Higashi Chaya geisha district is a smaller, calmer Gion where the teahouses actually let you in: Ochaya Shima charges ¥500 to walk through a working 1820s interior. In contrast, most Gion teahouses remain entirely closed to casual visitors. Omicho Market delivers the seafood-breakfast experience of Tokyo's Tsukiji Outer Market, with locals still doing their shopping there, and entry to Kenroku-en, one of Japan's three great gardens, costs ¥320, compared with ¥500 for Kinkaku-ji or ¥500 for Kiyomizu-dera, each ticketed separately. The biggest savings come from where you sleep. Kyoto's average hotel rate hit a record ¥20,195 per night in 2024. Since March 1, 2026, the city has charged a ¥1,000 per-person-per-night accommodation tax on rooms priced at ¥20,000-49,999, double the previous rate. Kanazawa's tax on the same room is ¥500. | Cost item (August 2026) | Kyoto | Kanazawa | | Shinkansen from Tokyo, one way | ¥14,170 | ¥14,600 | | City bus, single ride | ¥230 | ¥220 | | Transit day pass | ¥1,100 | ¥800 | | Headline garden or temple | ¥500 | ¥320 | | Accommodation tax, per person | ¥1,000 p.p. per night | ¥500 p.p. per night | Note the first row: The train from Tokyo to Kanazawa costs slightly more than the train to Kyoto. The swap pays off in everything after you arrive and compounds with every night you stay. Shima Onsen Instead of Ginzan Onsen: The Clearest Budget Win in Japan Ginzan Onsen's gaslit street has become so popular that the town now meters its own visitors. In winter, day visitors park two kilometers out and ride a shuttle; evening entry requires a paid reservation (¥1,150 in the first season, capped at 100 people per hour), and after 8 pm the street closes to everyone but overnight guests. Those overnight stays start at roughly ¥25,000 per person with meals, and reaching the town from Tokyo costs about ¥13,000 by the Yamagata Shinkansen, plus a ¥1,000 bus that takes cash only. Shima Onsen, tucked in a Gunma river gorge, offers the same Taisho-era wooden-ryokan romance with none of the metering. Sekizenkan's main building dates to 1691, making it Japan's oldest hot-spring inn building, and it is often said to have inspired the bathhouse in Spirited Away; its budget rooms start at ¥10,450 per person. The riverside cave bath Kawara-no-yu is open to day visitors from 9:00 to 15:00 without charge. Best of all, a direct highway bus runs from Tokyo Station for ¥3,500 one way and ¥6,300 round trip, about three and a half hours. | Cost item (August 2026) | Ginzan Onsen | Shima Onsen | | Transport from Tokyo, one way | ~¥14,000 (shinkansen + bus) | ¥3,500 (direct bus) | | Night in a heritage ryokan | From ~¥25,000 p.p. with meals | From ¥10,450 p.p. at Sekizenkan | | Soaking without staying | Winter evenings ticketed | Free cave bath, 9:00–15:00 | One honest caveat: the bus runs once daily each way and must be reserved by 4 pm the day before. If you miss it, the rail route via Nakanojo costs more and takes longer. Book the seat, then relax. Ainokura Instead of Shirakawa-go: Let Your Routing Decide Shirakawa-go itself is not the budget problem; walking the village is free, the Wada House costs ¥400, and the viewpoint shuttle costs ¥300. The problem is that everyone arrives on the same reservation-only buses (¥2,800 one way from either Kanazawa or Takayama) and shares the lanes with them. Ainokura, a village of twenty thatched gassho-zukuri farmhouses on a mountainside in neighboring Gokayama, is listed as a World Heritage site with a fraction of the foot traffic. It is also free to enter on foot, and the World Heritage Bus from Takaoka or Shin-Takaoka costs ¥1,100, less than half the Shirakawa-go fare. Whether that saves you money depends entirely on your routing. Traveling the Hokuriku Shinkansen anyway? Step off at Shin-Takaoka and Ainokura is the cheaper, quieter choice. Based in Kanazawa or Takayama with no plans northward? The extra rail leg to Takaoka eats the difference, so the direct ¥2,800 bus to Shirakawa-go wins. The best-value option for seeing both: the ¥4,000 two-day unlimited pass covers Ainokura, Suganuma, and Shirakawa-go on one ticket, and costs less than buying a single round trip separately. Related: Travelers looking beyond Tokyo and Kyoto can find more ideas in Go Backpacking's guide to Japan's Chubu region. Naoshima and Teshima Instead of teamLab: When Quieter Costs More Honesty requires one counterexample, because quiet does not automatically mean cheap. Tokyo's teamLab Planets charges from ¥3,600, with date-based pricing. The contemplative alternatives are Naoshima and Teshima, neighboring art islands in the Seto Inland Sea: the Chichu Art Museum costs ¥2,500-3,000 with timed reservations that cap visitors. The Teshima Art Museum costs ¥1,800-2,000. The direct ferry from Uno Port to Naoshima costs ¥370, while the ferry to Teshima costs ¥780. Per ticket, the islands undercut teamLab. Per trip, they usually don't: Uno Port is a Shinkansen ride and two local connections from Tokyo, and that transport dwarfs the admission savings. The swap only makes financial sense when Setouchi is already on your route, say between Osaka and Hiroshima. If it is, take it without hesitation; if not, this is the case where the crowded option is genuinely the affordable one. The Cheapest Alternative: Don't Leave the City You're In The most expensive way to escape a crowd is to cross half of Honshu. A same-day dash from Tokyo to Kyoto for Fushimi Inari's torii gates costs over ¥28,000 in return shinkansen fares before you have eaten anything. Meanwhile, Nezu Shrine, one of Tokyo's oldest, has its own tunnel of vermilion torii at the Otome Inari sub-shrine, costs nothing to enter, and sits a ¥180 metro ride from central Tokyo. The same logic covers bamboo. Kamakura's Hokoku-ji temple has a grove where you can sit with matcha for ¥400 admission plus ¥600 for the tea. The Great Buddha at Kotoku-in across town charges ¥300, and the train from Tokyo costs ¥1,040. That makes a full bamboo-and-Buddha day out possible for under ¥5,000, compared with visiting Arashiyama's grove at the far end of a ¥28,000 round trip. Even garden-hopping scales down: Kiyosumi Garden charges ¥150 for stone-hopping across carp ponds that Shinjuku Gyoen crowds pay ¥500 for. Altitude works the same way. Shibuya Sky's rooftop charges ¥2,700 online for daytime entry and ¥3,400 for sunset slots, and shares the deck with everyone else who booked the same golden hour. Sunshine 60's Tenbou-Park observatory in Ikebukuro shows a comparable skyline for ¥700 on weekdays, and the free 26th-floor observation lobby of Carrot Tower in Sangenjaya, a few minutes from Shibuya on the Den-en-toshi line, faces Mount Fuji at sunset and charges nothing at all. Four Rules Before You Swap - Price the final leg first. Rural alternatives live or die by the last bus or ferry: its fare and, above all, its schedule. One missed daily departure can force a taxi that costs more than the whole day. - Admission is rarely the problem. Japanese entry fees are modest: ¥150-800 covers most of the attractions in this article. Accommodation and intercity trains decide your budget, so compare hotel rates and lodging taxes before temple tickets. For a broader breakdown of travel costs, read Go Backpacking's guide to backpacking Japan on a budget. - Some crowded icons are free. Fushimi Inari charges nothing; Shirakawa-go's lanes charge nothing. Swapping away from them buys you a better experience, not a cheaper one. Know which reward you're paying for. - Recheck prices from 2026 onward. The March 2026 JR East fare rise and Kyoto's doubled accommodation tax made many older budget guides inaccurate. The official links above reflect August 2026 prices. Quiet and cheap usually travel together in Japan, but not always, and never automatically. Run the numbers for your own route, and you'll often find the lesser-known option costs less and gives more. When it doesn't, at least you'll know before the bus timetable tells you.

item.title: Kilimanjaro Routes Compared: Which Should You Choose?
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 6.05
Seven official routes lead up Kilimanjaro, and most people narrow their choice to two or three within an hour of reading about them. Machame is the popular one, Lemosho the scenic one, Marangu the one where you sleep in huts instead of tents. Those labels are accurate but don't affect whether you reach the summit. Kilimanjaro is 5,895 m (19,341 ft) high. Its standard trekking routes do not require technical climbing equipment (ropes, an ice axe), but the extreme altitude makes acclimatization essential. The number of days on the mountain matters. Five-day itineraries leave less time for acclimatization, while some operators report summit success rates around 95% on eight-day climbs. These are operator-reported figures, not mountain-wide averages. The takeaway is simple: allow your body more time to adapt before summit night. How the Routes Actually Work Seven official ascent routes exist, but they don't stay separate all the way up. Every climb has three phases, and the route you choose changes each of them differently. The approach (the first four to six days) is where the routes differ. Lemosho starts in quiet rainforest on the western flank. Rongai comes from the dry northern side near the Kenyan border. Machame and Marangu climb from the busy south. For four to six days, you circle toward Kibo, the main volcanic cone, gaining altitude through rainforest, moorland, and alpine desert. This is where you acclimatize, so the number of days here matters most. Summit night. The approaches converge toward Kibo, with most standard itineraries using one of two main summit routes. If you came via Machame, Lemosho, Shira, or Umbwe, you leave Barafu Camp around midnight, climb to Stella Point, then walk the crater rim to Uhuru Peak. Marangu and Rongai climbers leave Kibo Hut, and their route to Gilman's Point takes longer because much of it runs over loose volcanic scree. Either way, you gain about 1,200 meters in the dark. The Western Breach is another summit route, but rockfall and unstable ice make it risky. For that reason, careful operators avoid it. The descent. The park separates uphill and downhill traffic. Routes that summit from Barafu come down the Mweka corridor, a trail used only for going down. Marangu and Rongai climbers walk back down the Marangu trail, sharing it with groups heading up. The Routes, Side by Side | Route | Days | Start from | Sleeping | Traffic | Pick it if | | Machame ("Whiskey") | 7 (or 6) | South | Tents | High | You want the classic climb-high-sleep-low profile and the Barranco Wall, and crowds don't bother you. | | Lemosho | 8 (or 7) | West | Tents | Low early, medium later | It's your first high-altitude climb, and you can spare the extra day. | | Marangu ("Coca-Cola") | 6 (or 5) | Southeast | Wooden huts | High | Sleeping in a tent is not an option for you. | | Rongai | 6 | North | Tents | Low | You want quiet, or you're climbing during the short rains. | | Northern Circuit | 8–9 | West, then north | Tents | Very low | You prioritize extra acclimatization time and a quieter approach. | | Umbwe | 6 | South | Tents | Very low | You're already acclimatized and want a steep, direct route. | | Londorossi (Shira) | 6–8 | West, by vehicle to the plateau | Tents | Very low | You want open views from day one and understand the altitude trade-off. | Route by Route Machame: the "Whiskey Route" (7 days) Machame is the most popular route on the mountain, and the nickname compares it to Marangu, the "Coca-Cola Route." The key differences are that Machame is tougher and steeper, and you sleep in tents. In seven days, you pass through every climate zone Kilimanjaro has, from wet rainforest at 1,800 meters to the frozen crater rim. The third day takes you up to Lava Tower at 4,600 meters and then down to Barranco Camp at 3,900 meters to sleep. That is the "climb high, sleep low" principle built into the route, which is why Machame acclimatizes people so well despite its pace. The next morning you scramble the Barranco Wall, a near-vertical face that needs hands for balance but no rope. The downside is traffic. Machame and Marangu take the lion's share of expeditions, and you will share camps with hundreds of other climbers. The Barranco Wall gives the climb real mountaineering character, and the scenery earns the route its reputation. Still, anyone choosing Machame has to be willing to move in a stream of other groups and share the intermediate camps. The other decision on Machame is between six and seven days. The difference is a single night at Karanga Camp after the Barranco Wall. Drop it, and you go straight from the wall to Barafu and into summit night on the same push, when accumulated fatigue shows up. For example, ALPO runs the Machame Route on the seven-day schedule and keeps that Karanga night for this reason; the company reports 95-97% of its climbers reaching the summit on that version. Its guidance on the six-day option is that the success rate is lower. Lemosho (8 days) Lemosho starts on the remote western flank at Londorossi Gate, about three hours' drive from Moshi. The first two days run through rainforest that the southern routes never touch, and you may not see another group. This is where you are most likely to see colobus monkeys. The route then crosses the Shira Plateau from west to east, one of the highest plateaus on Earth, and on the eight-day version you spend two nights up there, at Shira 1 (3,500 m) and Shira 2 (3,840 m). That slow gain is the whole point. From the plateau, Lemosho joins the Machame trail, so the Lava Tower day, the Barranco Wall, and the summit night are the same. The main decision on Lemosho is whether to do seven or eight days. Dropping to seven means crossing Shira in one long stage and losing a night of adaptation, which helps most. Lemosho also costs more than Machame, partly because of the long drive to a remote trailhead and partly because the extra day adds food and crew wages. For someone whose first real altitude climb is this one, the eight-day Lemosho remains the most balanced option; the gain comes slowly enough that your body has time to catch up. Marangu: the "Coca-Cola Route" (6 days) Marangu is the only route where you sleep in permanent wooden huts instead of tents. The huts are dorm-style, with anywhere from 4 to 20 people per room and shared bathrooms. It is also the historic original route and the one with the gentlest approach gradient, which is how it got its reputation as the easy one. That reputation can be misleading: a gentler trail does not remove altitude challenges. If you prefer hut accommodation, compare daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities carefully, and favor the six-day itinerary over the five-day version. Summit night climbs from Kibo Hut toward Gilman's Point, and the route uses the same trail for ascent and descent, so you meet descending groups on your way up. The sensible rule is to choose Marangu in exactly one case, when a tent is physically or psychologically not an option for you, and then to take six days, never five. Rongai (6 days) Rongai approaches from the north, close to the Kenyan border, after a long drive to the trailhead. The northern flank is drier, making Rongai the sensible pick if climbing during the short rains in November. It is also the quietest standard route, with a real chance of larger wildlife on the lower section. The early terrain is less dramatic than on the western routes, and summit night from Kibo Hut is long and monotonous. It is probably the most undervalued route on the mountain: introverted, wild, and worth the trade for silence. Editor's note: For a firsthand perspective, read this account of climbing Kilimanjaro via the Rongai Route, from life at camp to the midnight summit push. Northern Circuit (8-9 days) The Northern Circuit is one of the longest itinerary options, giving you more time to acclimatize. As a result, it has one of the higher summit rates. It starts on the western side, like Lemosho, then swings around the northern face of Kibo on a nearly empty traverse before rejoining the main trails for the summit push. The extra days provide more time to adapt, although individual responses to altitude vary. It is generally among the more expensive options because you are paying for a longer expedition, and it requires solid multi-day trekking endurance. If reliably reaching Uhuru Peak is the goal and time is not the constraint, this is the route. Umbwe and Londorossi (Shira) Umbwe is the steepest line on the mountain and the most direct, climbing a narrow forest ridge that almost no one else uses. Its rapid ascent leaves little time to acclimatize, making it a better option for trekkers who are already acclimatized. Previous altitude experience alone is not a substitute. Londorossi, sometimes called the Shira Route, approaches from the west but begins with a vehicle transfer straight onto the Shira Plateau at 3,400 meters. The views open from day one. You give up the gradual gain that every other route builds in, which is worth considering before you book. What To Weigh Before You Book Days on the mountain. When comparing itineraries, prioritize acclimatization time. Look beyond total trip length to daily sleeping altitudes and acclimatization opportunities. Extra time helps, but fitness and previous altitude experience do not guarantee protection from altitude illness. Follow your guide's safety advice and be prepared to turn around. That is not a guidebook opinion. Yevgen Staroselskiy, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions, is a Master of Sport in Mountaineering and holder of the "Snow Leopard" title (#376), with more than 130 major climbs behind him, including Everest (8,848 m, 29,029 ft) and K2 (8,611 m, 28,251 ft), and 25+ groups guided to the top of Kilimanjaro. His view of the time question is blunt: I've climbed Everest and K2, and I can tell you that no route on Kilimanjaro needs that kind of preparation. What it does need is that you take the altitude seriously. Give your body the days, walk slowly, and almost any physically active person will reach Uhuru Peak. Where I see people fail is when they try to save a day. - Yevgen Staroselskiy, Master of Sport in Mountaineering, co-founder of ALPO Guided Expeditions Everything else on this list is secondary to that number. Tent or hut. A binary question, and it settles Marangu yes-or-no before anything else. Crowds. Machame and Marangu are busy. Rongai and the Northern Circuit are not. Lemosho is quiet for two days and then joins the Machame stream. Summit night profile. From Barafu, the climb to Stella Point is steeper, but you are mostly on firm ground. From Kibo Hut, you spend more hours on scree before you reach Gilman's Point. Season. Compare expected rainfall and trail conditions for your travel dates with your operator. Wetter periods mean muddy trails and reduced visibility; the northern approach is generally drier. Conditions vary, so avoid treating any seasonal window as a guarantee of dry weather. The dry windows are June to early October and mid-December to early April. During the short rains in November, the northern side stays drier, which is a point in Rongai's favor. In April and May, the trails wash out, and clouds hide the views, so no route is worth doing then. A Quick Decision Guide - First high-altitude climb and you can spare eight days: Lemosho. - Seven days, and sharing camp with other groups does not bother you: Machame, on the seven-day schedule rather than six. - You will not sleep in a tent: Marangu, six days, no shorter. - Climbing in November, or you want the mountain mostly to yourself: Rongai. - More time for acclimatization and a quieter approach: Northern Circuit. Whichever route you choose, prioritize an itinerary that allows time to acclimatize rather than booking the shortest option. This article was published in partnership with ALPO Guided Expeditions.

item.title: How To Turn a Long Flight Into Useful Personal Time
item.description:
Source: GoBackpacking Score: 5.81
A long flight can feel like dead time because it sits between two places and belongs to neither. Yet it is also one of the few stretches in modern-day travel when everyday demands temporarily lose their grip. The trick is not to fill every minute but to offer a small menu of activities that fit different energy levels. A downloaded book, a notebook, a favorite album, and a short game of PlaySolitaire each offer a different way to experience the journey. That compact game loop matters because it creates a clear beginning and ending when the hours ahead feel shapeless. Stop Planning the Flight Like a Workday Travelers often board with an ambitious list. They plan to finish a novel, clear a laptop folder, watch three films, and arrive with a new language skill. This turns a quiet journey into a performance test. Cabin conditions rarely cooperate. Sleep may be broken, concentration can fade, and the person beside you may need to move just as you settle into something demanding. A better plan is flexible. Choose several low-effort options and let your attention decide which fits the moment. Build a Menu Instead of a Timetable A useful flight menu has contrast. Bring something to read, something to listen to, something to write, and something to play. Download what you need before leaving home because a plan that depends on perfect onboard internet is not much of a plan. Keep choices easy to reach. If every activity requires unpacking half your backpack, you will likely return to scrolling through the entertainment screen without choosing anything. Choose Activities With Natural Endings Open-ended entertainment can cause time to feel longer. Endless feeds and large game worlds provide no clear stopping point, so an hour disappears without feeling complete. A chapter, a crossword, a journal page, or a single hand of solitaire has a finish line. PlaySolitaire works well in this role because its rules are familiar and each round stands on its own. You can put it away when the meal arrives without feeling as though you have abandoned a larger mission. Load the game before departure so the cached version can be reopened if your flight lacks reliable Wi-Fi. Alternate Attention With Real Rest Not all quiet moments need an activity. After reading or watching something, close your eyes for a while. Look out the window when the view allows. Stretch when it is safe to move around the cabin and drink water regularly. The aim is not to defeat boredom at all costs. It is to move gently between focus and rest so neither becomes exhausting. A good activity should support that rhythm rather than call for constant attention. Leave Part of the Journey Unclaimed The most memorable travel days are rarely controlled minute by minute, and the journey can follow the same principle. Leave space for a conversation, an unexpected film, or simply doing nothing. Long flights become easier when they stop being a problem to solve. With a few carefully chosen options and permission to change your mind, the cabin becomes a temporary room of your own. You may not use every hour productively, but you can arrive feeling that the time was yours. This article was published in partnership with PlaySolitaire.io.

item.title: The Quick Sauce That Changed How I Cook Fish
item.description:
Source: NYT > Dining & Wine Score: 2.23
Advertisement Friends often ask me how to cook more fish at home — not salmon, they’ve figured that one out — but the white fish their doctors recommend for its lean protein. They know it cooks quickly and like how it tastes, but worry about preparing it. Recipe: Caramelized Garlic Fish That’s how I felt when I first started cooking professionally, and for myself. It was one thing to learn how to sear flaky white fish on the line in a restaurant, another to make it at home. I was on a tight budget, but even if I hadn’t been, I wouldn’t have been able to find fish as fresh as the kind available at restaurants or the Asian markets of my childhood. Then I made a fish recipe that changed my kitchen life. In her 2001 cookbook, “Pleasures of the Vietnamese Table,” the chef Mai Pham shared her recipe for cá kho tộ and described it as the “one dish that best represents Vietnamese home cooking.” Originally from the south of the country, freshwater snakehead fish (cá lóc) is braised (kho) in a clay pot (tộ) until it becomes deeply savory and a little sticky. Bright with cilantro and black pepper, it begs to be spooned over rice and shoveled. It’s all comfort and still light, punchy but delicate with nuance. And the whole dish comes together in less than 20 minutes. The first time I tried it, I couldn’t believe how easy it was for how good it tasted. I didn’t have a clay pot, but it was, as Ms. Pham promised, “also delicious cooked in a regular pot.” It starts with melting sugar past golden, and then stirring in oil and garlic. As the garlic sizzles and softens, it releases its fragrance into the dark amber caramel. Adding fish sauce and water stops the sugar from going over its bittersweet cliff to burned and turns it into a funky sauce to soak into the fish, and then glaze it with a mahogany shine. This sauce is unbelievable with fish and just as good with tofu, chicken, beef, pork, duck and all kinds of vegetables and seafood. Sometimes known as nước sốt (or kho sauce in English), there are countless variations in Vietnam and its diaspora. Some melt the sugar with oil or vinegar; others add shallots, coconut water or both. As the dish became part of my rotation, I stopped flipping open Ms. Pham’s book and started adjusting it to my taste. I throw in a lot more garlic, splash in less water and skip the scallions in favor of more cilantro. She called for catfish fillets, which are earthy like snakehead fish, but cod, fresh and frozen, is always at my market and its mildness benefits from the big flavors. (Using crosscut fish steaks hews more closely to the dish’s origins, and the bones give the sauce even more body.) It takes only one go to get the rhythm of this sauce. Once you have its pantry ingredients (and stock your freezer with frozen fish fillets), you’ll be able to pull together this one-pot meal any night. Follow New York Times Cooking on Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, TikTok and Pinterest. Get regular updates from New York Times Cooking, with recipe suggestions, cooking tips and shopping advice.

item.title: Arc’teryx Wants the Sperro SV to Be the Last Jacket You Ever Buy—Seriously
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 5.01
Engineered for versatility across high-stakes mountain environments, the Sperro SV underwent rigorous testing during ski tours and ice climbing ascents. (Photo: Courtesy of Arc'teryx) Tucked alongside the interior chest pocket of a two-toned magenta Arc’teryx jacket is a laser-etched QR code—but instead of pulling up the menu at your local pub, it prompts you to register your new purchase, immediately kicking off a record of the jacket’s materials, origin, and, eventually, repair history. A QR code seems simple enough—after all, you encounter dozens of them weekly—but a QR code on a mountain-grade hardshell requires a different level of engineering than the laminated square on your bartop. The internal placement makes it near-impossible to destroy or remove; the laser etching, adapted from the electronics industry, underwent multiple trials to ensure it left a permanent mark without degrading the fabric. So why spend so much time, money, and engineering on a single square inch of jacket? For Arc’teryx, that QR code is the entry point into System 0™, a new framework that reimagines how products can be designed, manufactured, used, repaired, and ultimately regenerated. In fact, the QR code is just one of many updates and innovations Arc’teryx built into its first System 0 jacket, the Sperro SV. Among the others: an easily repairable zipper, a nylon face fabric and backer engineered for chemical recyclability, and reinforcement at common failure points. System 0 started as a “what if” conversation between Arc’teryx CEO Stuart Haselden and VP of Advanced Concepts, Alex Plante, brainstorming what circularity would look like for the company. At that point, Arc’teryx’s ReBIRD program already existed, with a solid infrastructure for product repairs, resale, trade-in, and upcycling, but the team knew they were still missing an actual process—a viable, repeatable way to create products that can be used for longer and ultimately regenerated into something new. “We landed on what product we wanted to develop within that [circularity] concept, and then, while we were developing the product, realized that we didn’t have all the pieces of the system,” says Andrew Yip, Senior Director of Materials Innovation at Arc’teryx. That meant building capability as they went, bringing in people like Kyle Wood, Vice President of Strategy, to focus on circularity. They also recruited for other supporting roles, like sourcing manager for raw materials. Throughout the circularity initiative, Yip and his colleagues used one principle as their North Star: Sustainability alone isn’t a reason for a product to exist. Anything they created had to live up to Arc’teryx’s sky-high standards for technical excellence and durability. “Most sustainable materials and products are just less bad than their incumbent,” argues Yip. “If you’re just going to make something less bad from a sustainability perspective but make it worse in terms of performance, then there really isn’t a justification for it to exist.” To that end, Arc’teryx prioritized abrasion resistance on both face fabric and backer, while refusing to compromise on tear and tensile strength, waterproofing, and breathability—all the things that determine whether a jacket becomes a one-season purchase or a mainstay in your gear closet. They also intentionally aligned on nylon 6 as the key material instead of polyester; even though polyester has more recycling opportunities, the team knew that nylon 6 fabric would perform best. To find the exact nylon content ratio—the perfect number that would make the fabric functionally and financially recyclable—Arc’teryx worked closely with Aquafil, the manufacturer of ECONYL® regenerated nylon. According to Aquafil, the textile is known for high wear resistance and impact strength (aka extreme durability). Finding the perfect jacket material was one thing. But that wasn’t the hardest problem the Arc’teryx team had to solve, says Yip. You already know Arc’teryx for its insanely technical, single-purpose shells like the Alpha SV—a scalpel, according to Yip. “It’s really a precision tool, and it was designed for ice climbing,” he explains. “It doesn’t have hand pockets for a reason—you don’t need hand pockets when you’re ice climbing.” On the contrary, the Sperro SV had to be a jacket-of-all-trades, working in a variety of environments and use cases. “With the Sperro SV, we wanted to make something that was multi-environment, multifunctional, and multi-activity,” details Yip. They needed a Swiss Army Knife, not a scalpel—but that Swiss Army Knife couldn’t compromise on durability. To ensure the Sperro SV was worth its mettle, Arc’teryx tested the jacket on ski tours, hiking trips, snowshoeing expeditions, and even ice climbing. They also partnered with the North Shore Search and Rescue, a volunteer-led organization and one of Canada’s oldest search-and-rescue teams, to make sure the jacket performed in high-stakes scenarios. All that engineering ultimately serves one purpose: creating a jacket worthy of what Yip refers to as custodianship, rather than ownership. “Hopefully, the person who’s purchasing this jacket is somebody who cares about their stuff and is going to take care of the garment, bring it in for repair, and extend its lifetime as much as possible,” says Yip. “And only after many, many years and many, many repairs, when something is no longer repairable, only then is when we take it back.” Hence, the QR code. Arc’teryx hopes that by making it as seamless as possible for customers to track the Sperro SV’s lifespan, materials, and repair history, customers will view themselves as custodians with a responsibility to their gear—instead of temporary owners of a disposable item. If all goes according to plan, the Sperro SV might be the last jacket Arc’teryx ever sells you. At a gulp-worthy $1,200 retail price, most customers are probably praying that they never have to buy another jacket again, but it’s not exactly a sound business strategy in an industry that counts on customers to replace old gear. Yip is strangely okay with that. “When we’re developing new products and prototypes, we know we have something when our athletes and field testers don’t want to give it back,” he explains. “Similarly, I think we’re onto something if we have a commercial product that people can buy and they don’t want to replace it. So personally, I would have no problem with that.” When asked to comment on the price, Arc’teryx reps note that the Sperro SV is priced in line with their most advanced hard shells, and the price reflects the design effort and materials that went into this sustainable jacket. “Circularity at this level of performance requires significant investment across materials, manufacturing, certification, and end-of-life infrastructure,” Arc’teryx acknowledges. They believe that the price reflects the value of three years of unlimited repairs, a product they’re backing to last for years, and eventually, an end-of-life offramp. “When you factor in the total life of the jacket, the value calculation looks different than a traditional purchase,” reasons the brand. Whether consumers will find the price a fair trade-off for the total package remains to be seen. The Sperro SV is just the first “statement of intent,” as Yip puts it, for what System 0 can do within the Arc’teryx playbook. With the streamlined processes and internal philosophies Arc’teryx has now aligned on, they’re free to explore further iterations of circular gear. “We started with a hardshell because it’s what we know, what we make, and what we’re known for—so you can imagine that the other things we’re known for and make well are coming down the pipeline,” hints Yip. And for the Arc’teryx loyalists who worry this new iteration of a hardshell won’t live up to their high standards—you’ve got nothing to worry about. “If anyone were to put on the jacket and close their eyes, it really shouldn’t be different at all compared to anything that we’ve made before. And I think that’s the point,” says Yip. “It’s everything else around it that we’re trying to change.”

item.title: How Skin Tone Affects Wearable Accuracy—and How Tech Giants Are Responding
item.description:
Source: Outside Magazine Score: 3.87
(Photo: Hill background: Fond, Magnus; Fitness Watch: simplehappyart/Getty; Design: Ayana Underwood/Canva) Wearables have become a near-constant companion for many Americans. According to a 2026 study, nearly 107 million people in the United States own one. People track their steps, workouts, and recovery, and increasingly look to those numbers to tell them how their bodies are doing. But for some—particularly people with darker skin tones—there’s a nagging question: Can I trust what my device is telling me? There’s a good reason to ask. A 2025 review of smartwatch accuracy studies found significant variability in how wearable devices performed across skin tones. According to one study included in the review, a major smartwatch brand measured heart rates within five beats per minute (bpm) across a full spectrum of skin tones. Other devices, however, underestimated heart rate by ten to 15 bpm in darker-skinned users during moderate to vigorous exercise. Researchers also found large discrepancies in heart rate readings during cycling and resistance training in people with dark skin. While heart rate metrics help people gauge workout intensity and how quickly their heart recovers after exercise, heart rate readings can also be lifesaving. An irregular heartbeat may indicate serious cardiovascular issues that can lead to blood clots, stroke, and heart failure, and should be flagged to a doctor. An inaccurate reading could miss these red flags. This issue is not news to wearable companies as getting accurate data from darker skin is a known challenge—one that requires extra effort from wearable makers to ensure the data is reliable. Outside contacted eight major wearable tech companies, including Oura, Apple, WHOOP, Google, and Polar, to find out how they’ve worked to address the wearable skin-tone problem. Here’s why wearables can struggle to get accurate readings on dark skin, and how these companies say they’ve improved their tech to ensure better accuracy across skin tones. Most smartwatches and rings rely on a type of technology called photoplethysmography (PPG), which uses optical sensors. Those sensors detect light to measure blood flow. A typical PPG device shines green light into your skin. (If you take a peek at the underside of your fitness watch, you can probably spot those green flashing lights.) Hemoglobin—a small protein in your blood that carries oxygen from the lungs to the rest of the body—absorbs some of that light, and the rest is reflected back onto the sensor. As blood moves through your vessels, the device measures changes in the reflected light to estimate your heart rate. The catch is that melanin, the pigment that gives skin its color, also absorbs and scatters some of the device’s light. The more melanin in the skin, the more light is absorbed. This makes darker skin tones more vulnerable to data loss compared to lighter skin tones, according to that 2025 review. Categorizing skin tone can be tricky because it’s subjective. But dermatologists often rely on the Fitzpatrick Scale. This scale is the dermatology industry standard classification for skin tone groups, according to a study published in the HCA Healthcare Journal of Medicine in February 2026. The scale is based on people’s self-reported observations of how likely they are to sunburn and tan. That data helped classify skin tone into six categories, from Type I to Type VI. Type I skin is the lightest and burns easily and doesn’t tan; Type VI is the darkest and tans easily and almost never burns. Despite the scale’s widespread use, it’s considered flawed, as that same 2026 study noted that its reliance on self-perception and cultural and societal influences complicates categorization. Even though skin tone can affect watch accuracy, it’s not the only factor that can lead to an inaccurate reading. “Noise is the biggest issue,” Michael Rosenberg, MD, a cardiac electrophysiologist who studies wearables in the division of cardiology at the University of Colorado Anschutz Medical Campus, told Outside. Noise, Rosenberg said, includes tattoos, body hair, hydration levels, sweat, and residue from lotions or sunscreens. He said that wrist size, skin temperature, and even freckles can impact readings. Improving wearable tech accuracy takes real intention; however, Apple, Oura, WHOOP, Polar, Google, and other wearable companies have made it a priority. Emily Capodilupo, senior vice president of research, algorithms, and data at WHOOP, said they’re intentional about ensuring their studies include people across all six Fitzpatrick values. WHOOP is a wearable company that sells a tiered membership, where customers pay an annual fee that includes their screenless device and access to their app’s metrics and analysis. “When we notice a population—skin tone, gender, age—where we think we’re struggling performance-wise, we overrepresent that group in the data collection efforts, and that’s a very effective technique for improving algorithms,” Capodilupo told Outside. Capodilupo also said WHOOP has specifically designed an algorithm to compensate for how melanin absorbs light. She said that algorithm is constantly validated and updated. The device monitors how much signal it gets back and adjusts the LED brightness accordingly. If the signal is weaker, the LED intensity increases. This approach comes with a trade-off, she explained. More powerful LEDs use more battery. “That’s a trade that we’re willing to make because we want to make sure that we can stand by the data that we provide,” Capodilupo said. Apple’s strategy is similar. The company says that it addresses the issue at the software and hardware level, including by adjusting how much light is transmitted into the skin and how strongly the return signal is amplified. They also said that in every generation of Apple Watch, software and hardware design factors are driven by ensuring users with the darkest skin tones get a strong signal and equivalent performance. At Oura, the company’s smart ring uses the same PPG technology. Senior vice president of science Shyamal Patel, PhD, said the product’s advantage is that the palm side of the finger tends to have more consistent pigmentation than the wrist. The finger, he said, also provides access to larger arteries, which can produce a stronger signal than what you can measure on the wrist with the same kind of hardware setup. That doesn’t solve for everything, though. Patel said the ring’s “smart sensing” capability means there are a number of paths the light can travel through the skin. The device continuously evaluates which path is producing the strongest signal and adjusts accordingly. In a statement via email, Raija Laukkanen, PhD, said that optical heart measurements have improved over the years largely due to better sensor technology, ergonomics and algorithms. Laukkanen is the director of science collaborations at Polar, a wearable tech company that offers watches based on activity types and other products like chest straps. “Optical measurement remains a practical and effective option for continuous heart rate tracking and everyday training. For situations where precision is the priority, electrocardiogram (ECG) remains our recommended approach,” she wrote. Unlike PPG tech, which relies on light sensors to collect heart rate data, ECG or EKG measures electrical heart signals directly through the skin, so it isn’t affected by pigmentation and is considered the gold standard in heart rate testing. The Polar H10 chest strap uses ECG to monitor heart rate during physical activity where real-time data is necessary. (Some Apple Watch, Polar watches, and WHOOP models offer on-demand ECG readings.) Patel said Oura is exploring new ways to characterize skin tones, such as the Monk skin tone scale (MST), which is a ten-tone visual scale that captures a fuller spectrum of darker skin. Patel’s team focuses on improving algorithms to better translate sensor data into useful metrics that can tell users about their overall health and well-being. Patel also said they intentionally collect data in a broad range of locations worldwide to support diversity. “We need to continue expanding the standards and then continue innovating on how we measure and validate the data,” Patel said. Apple also incorporates a spectrophotometer, which helps measure color more objectively. In addition to the standard Fitzpatrick assessment, researchers can use this lab instrument to measure the exact amount of light reflected at different wavelengths. In a statement via email, a Google spokesperson said, “Google Health takes accuracy very seriously and continuously conducts studies to rigorously test the accuracy of our products among diverse groups of users. We also focus on recruiting a diverse testing population from around the globe for wear testing during our development cycles for Google wearables including Fitbit and Pixel Watch devices.” Though wearables provide a wealth of data on users’ health and wellness, Rosenberg said it’s important to remember that wearable devices are still commercial products, not medical ones. So, it’s reasonable to expect occasional inaccuracies, but he said they do detect overall trends pretty well. To get the most accurate readings, the experts contacted for this story said there are a few things that are within your control: keep a snug fit so that the sensor is in contact with the skin, make sure the sensor isn’t sitting directly on a bone, wipe the sensor regularly so it remains free of sweat and residue from lotions, try to keep the sensor away from any tattoos, and install recent device and app updates. If your device isn’t working properly or starts producing strange results, it’s probably best to ditch it for a new one. Wearables aren’t one-size-fits-all. As the technology evolves, continued research and more representative data will be key to ensuring everyone can trust the numbers on their devices. Want more Outside health stories? Sign up for the Bodywork newsletter. And for tips on how to train, fuel, and recover better, sign up for the Sweat Science 101 newsletter.

item.title: Review: Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.80
The Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket is a lightweight windbreaker for hiking, trail running, and outdoor activities where you don't need full waterproof protection. Its main strength is its breathability and simplicity: it blocks wind effectively while retaining body heat without the bulk or restriction of a heavier shell jacket. - Gender: Men's (Women's – only available in UK) - Weight: 4.0 oz - Fit: Easy to layer with - Material: Nylon - CFM 1.2 (very windproof) - Fit: true to size The jacket has a clean, understated appearance that works well both on the trail and around town. Its lightweight construction makes it easy to pack into its zippered chest pocket, while the fit leaves enough room for layering. It works especially well over a Polartec Alpha fleece, for example. This creates a warm, highly adaptable system for cool, changeable conditions. The fleece insulates while staying breathable, and the Pendower helps block wind without adding much weight. The Pendower hood is pre-cinched behind the head to keep it snug and has a brim to keep the sun out of your eyes. I have a small hat size, so it's a bit slack on me, but it fills out when worn with a fleece beanie (or if you have a larger head). Fully adjustable windbreaker hoods are pretty rare, especially these days in the race to make the lightest weight gear and clothing. The chest pocket is large enough to hold a Smartphone and has a fabric key fob inside, while the stretch cuffs are wide enough to roll up your arm. The exterior fabric is thin and very quiet, even in gusty wind. These details make the jacket easy to wear and use as a windbreaker. As a windproof outer layer, the Pendower performs well in windy and exposed conditions. It is particularly useful when conditions are too cold and breezy for a fleece alone but not wet enough to justify a heavier waterproof shell, which would retain too much body heat. Breathability is reasonable during gentle to moderate activity. When walking quickly or climbing steep hills, heat can build up, especially when worn over a warm midlayer. This combination is best managed by adjusting layers as activity levels change. Unzipping the central zipper, removing the hood, or rolling up the sleeves all let you dump excess body heat without stopping to remove garments. The low weight is one of the jacket’s biggest advantages. It is easy to carry until needed and takes up little space in a pack. The simple construction also makes it practical for regular use, whether walking, traveling, or wearing around town. Rather than a standalone warm jacket, it works best as part of a layering system. Comparable Wind Jackets | Item | Weight | Price | |---|---|---| | Patagonia Airshed Pro Hoodie | 3.7 oz /105g | $139 | | Patagonia Houdini Jacket | 3.7 oz /105g | $119 | | Enlightened Equipment Copperfield Wind Shirt | 2.05 oz / 58g | $120 | | Mammut Aenergy WB Hooded Jacket | 4.7 oz / 132g | $149 | | Katabatic Gear Crest Windshell | 1.8 oz / 51g | $129 | | Rab Vital Windshell Hoody | 4.6 oz /160g | $100 | | Montbell Hooded Tachyon Jacket | 2.5 oz / 71 g | $130 | | Mountain Hardwear Kor Airshell Hoody | 4.7 oz /133g | $165 | | Arc'teryx Squamish Hoody | 5.3 oz /150g | $200 | | Black Diamond Distance Wind Shell | 3.2 oz/91g | $199 | Recommendation Overall, the Berghaus Pendower Wind Jacket is a dependable and versatile wind layer. It works best over a breathable insulating midlayer such as a fleece or wool pullover in cooler conditions, where it helps turn a lightweight midlayer into a more weather-resistant system.
