item.title: Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound Backpack Review
item.description:
Source: Sectionhiker.com Score: 4.61
The Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound 55 Backpack is an ultralight backpack weighing 29.8 oz (819 g) made with Woven Dyneema fabric and Dyneema mesh. This new version is a substantial upgrade from the previous model, with more durable fabrics, a better frame system, and female-friendly (S-shaped) shoulder straps. Together, they make the pack much more comfortable and functional, enough so that existing Unbound owners should consider upgrading to the new model. - Color: Grey - Spec Weight: 29.8 oz (819 g) - Actual Weight: 29.8 oz (819 g) in a size large - Gender: Unisex - Volume: 55L internal storage, 9L external storage - Sizing: Multiple torso and hipbelt lengths - Frame: Contoured aluminum stay, foam back panel - Load lifters: None - Pockets: 6 (2 side, 1 front, 1 bottom, 2 hip belt) - Hydration Compatible: No - Material: Dyneema Woven Composite, 100D Dyneema Gridstop, Dyneema Stretch Mesh - Seam-taped: Yes - Pros: Tougher fabrics and mesh, effectively waterproof, good pockets, multiple torso lengths, excellent attachment points Backpack Pockets and Storage The Unbound 55 is a rolltop backpack that can be buckled together on top or along the sides using webbing straps, which are girth-hitched to the daisy chains along the sides so you can remove them if you don't need them. I prefer securing a roll top with them because I find that they provide better compression than just rolling the extension collar (the top of the pack) and buckling it on top. The top of the extension collar has a stiffener, making it easy to roll shut and helping it stay shut. The Unbound comes with huge side pockets that are great for storing multiple bottles, securing a tent along the side, and holding the bottom of a snowshoe if you hike in winter. The top of the side pockets has an elastic cinch cord for securing the contents. The Unbound does not have an internal hydration pocket or hydration ports, so you'll need to carry water in these pockets or in accessory sleeves attached to the shoulder straps. The hipbelt pockets are similarly large and can easily fit a Smartphone and snack bars or gloves. HMG expanded its hipbelt pocket size a few years ago, so this isn't a net new change. The pack also comes with two open stretch mesh pockets, one on the front and one on the bottom of the pack, which is a feature that's become popular with thru-hikers. The front mesh pocket is pretty unique: it has a top opening and a lower one about halfway down, held shut with elastic. It lets you access items at the base of the front pocket without unloading everything. For example, I keep my tent stakes at the base of the front stretch pocket, and this lets me access them easily. Both the front mesh pocket and the pocket at the base of the pack are made with highly durable Dyneema stretch mesh, since these zones experience considerable contact with the ground. The bottom pocket is a convenient place to store small snacks and trash, or hats and gloves, as long as you don't mind crushing the contents or getting them wet when you take the pack off and set it on wet ground. It has two openings: one on the right when facing forward and a small hole on the left, called a trash port, so you can stuff used wrappers into it. Backpack Frame and Suspension The Unbound 55 has dual contoured aluminum frame stays augmented with foam padding behind the shoulder straps for increased comfort. They terminate behind the lumbar pad at the base of the pack, providing much better load transfer to the hips. This is a major upgrade from the previous version, which had only one internal stay and is more comparable, in terms of load transfer and stability, to the HMG Southwest and Windrider backpacks, making the Unbound comparable to those mainstays of the Hyperlite product line in functionality and comfort. Take, for example, the UnBound hipbelt, which you tension by pushing the straps forward using what's called a Scherer cinch, named after Michael Scherer, who first designed it at Kelty. I get a much better hipwrap with the Unbound than the Southwest, which has been my backpack of choice for many years. The Unbound's shoulder straps, like HMG's other packs, are now S-shaped, making them more female-friendly. They are covered in front with daisy chains so you can easily attach accessory best-of-breed pockets, like the HMG shoulder strap pocket shown, bottle sleeves, or electronics to your shoulder straps. Hyperlite sells a full range of pack accessories. External Attachment Points and Compression The Unbound 55 has low-profile daisy chains sewn along the main compartment's side seams that you can use to secure bulky gear like fishing rods or packraft paddles to the sides of the pack. The pack comes with elastic cords for this purpose, but you can use your own instead. This is more difficult on Hyperlite's other packs, which offer less flexibility in strap placement. If you've ever lost a fishing rod because it's popped out of a backpack's side pocket, you'll really appreciate the intricate webs you can design to keep from losing precious cargo. Comparable Ultralight Backpacks w/Frames | Make / Model | Weight | Fabric | Price | |---|---|---|---| | Hyperlite Mtn Gear Southwest 55L | 29.8 / 845g | Dyneema Woven Composite | $395 | | Durston Kakwa 55L | 31.5 oz / 880g | Ultra 200X, UltraGrid | $279 | | Gossamer Gear Gorilla 50L | 31.9 oz / 904g | Robic Nylon | $275 | | Zpacks Arc Haul 60L | 20.9 oz / 593g | Ultra 100X | $399 | | Granite Gear Crown 3 60L | 32.6 oz / 1040g | Robic Nylon | $260 | | Osprey Exos Pro 55 | 34.6 oz / 981g | Robic Nylon | $330 | | ULA Ultra Circuit SV 48L | 35.8 oz / 1015g | Ultra 200X, Ultra400X | $380 | | REI Flash 55L | 45 oz / 1276g | Robic Nylon | $229 | | Atom Packs Notch EP40 | 29.6 oz / 840g | Ecopack EPX200, EPX400 | $303 | | SWD UL Long Haul 50 | 30.2 oz / 856g | Ultra 200X | $379 | Recommendation The Hyperlite Mountain Gear Unbound 55 is an excellent ultralight backpack for multi-day backpacking trips, excelling across a wide range of trail conditions and gear needs. It differs from Hyperlite's other backpacks in pocket size and placement, offers a more adjustable hip belt, and provides more flexible external attachments. This new version also represents a major upgrade in two key components: a switch from a single aluminum stay to dual stays and the use of woven Dyneema as the pack fabric, making it significantly tougher and abrasion-resistant. The new grey-silver color is also pretty cool. The upgraded Unbound 55 is so impressive that owners of the previous version should consider upgrading if their existing pack is nearing the end of its life. It also wouldn't surprise me if the Unbound becomes the most popular pack in Hyperlite's backpacking line, even outshining the Southwest and Windrider backpacks, because the hipbelt is easier to tighten and fit and the pack is more functional with no added weight gain. Disclosure: Hyperlite Mountain Gear donated a backpack for review. SectionHiker never accepts payment for gear reviews or editorial coverage. When you buy through affiliate links on our site, we may earn a small commission at no extra cost to you. Help us continue to test and write unsponsored and independent gear reviews, hiking and backpacking FAQs, and free hiking guides. Thanks for the review. Could you easily get a bear canister into it? Yes, of course. Anyone you want, vertically. It’s a 55L pack. But here’s a jedi tip – pack your food/smellables in a plastic bag inside your pack and carry the empty canister under the Y strap on top of the pack. At night, put your food into the bear canister. This makes it much easier to carry a bear canister because it won’t be top heavy and throw you off balance without losing pack volume or increasing gear weight. I like that Jedi tip, thanks!

item.title: ‘Fabulous museums and no queues’: five of the best under-the-radar city breaks in Europe
item.description:
Source: The Guardian Travel Score: 3.43
Nantes, France As dilemmas go, it’s an unusual one: saddle up a giant squid or board a submersible for a voyage to the bottom of the ocean. In the end, I find myself drawn to a fierce-looking merhorse and tentatively take the reins. High above, my daughter glides by on a flying fish, metallic fins flapping, while her Dad is battling stormy seas at the helm of a huge conch shell. A ride on the Carrousel des Mondes Marins (marine worlds carousel) – a three-storey steampunk merry-go-round inspired by Jules Verne’s novel Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Sea – is one of the highlights of a visit to Nantes. A surreal fairground ride, a work of art and a homage to the city’s most famous son. It’s also a lot of fun. On the banks of the Loire, 30 miles from the Atlantic ocean, Nantes is a city whose fortunes were built on the sea. As a young boy growing up near the docks in the 1830s, Verne dreamed of being a ship’s captain, but it wasn’t to be. Instead, he embarked on a series of journeys of the imagination, channelling his wanderlust into novels such as Around the World in 80 Days and Journey to the Centre of the Earth. The last of Nantes’ shipyards closed in the 1980s, but Verne’s unique vision provided the inspiration for a radical art and regeneration project, Les Machines de l’Île, that has breathed life into the abandoned quays and warehouses of the Île de Nantes, the river island that was home to the city’s docks. This is now the stomping ground of the Grand Éléphant, a 12m-high mechanical pachyderm that carries passengers on tours of the island, spraying bystanders with water from its trunk. I’d seen photos but nothing prepares you for the thrill of turning a corner and seeing the real thing lumbering towards you. You can learn about the magic behind the machinery at the nearby Galerie des Machines, where the creators bring a mechanical menagerie of strange creatures to life. The Verne connection also inspired the name of the city’s summer arts festival, Le Voyage à Nantes, which transforms streets, parks and public spaces into an open-air art gallery from July to September. Our visit coincides with the festival’s opening weekend, and the squares and avenues of the elegant Graslin district are busy with DJ sets, food stalls and people checking out the new artworks. In the Place Graslin, a beautiful square built – like much of Nantes – from chalky-white tuffeau stone from the Loire valley, some kind of cataclysmic eruption has been conjured up in front of the opera house. Huge ammonites appear to have been forced up from beneath the earth, engulfing cars in a mountain of rubble, their doors wide open, radios playing, as though abandoned in haste. Just yards away, children are playing in the dancing water fountains of the square, while the white-aproned waiters of art nouveau brasserie La Cigale weave through the pavement tables delivering seafood platters to diners unfazed by the apocalyptic scene before them. Titled Fossil Opera, the artwork is a commentary on consumerism and the fleeting nature of human endeavour, and is one of about a dozen site-specific installations that have appeared in the city, as if by magic. Even outside the summer months, there is plenty to discover in France’s sixth largest city. Each year, a handful of the festival installations are selected to become permanent fixtures, which has resulted in an impressive collection of contemporary public art, from Les Anneaux, a series of 18 giant steel rings on the Quai des Antilles, which frame views of the Loire and light up at night, to Tadashi Kawamata’s Belvédère de l’Hermitage, a viewing platform inspired by a swallow’s nest, which juts over a sheer cliff. All of these cultural highlights, old and new, are linked by the Ligne Verte, a 12-mile (20km) green line painted on the pavement. We follow the trail through the Passage Pommeraye, an exquisite 19th century glass-roofed shopping arcade; past the imposing Château des ducs de Bretagne, a moated 15th-century castle; stop off at the excellent Musée d’arts de Nantes, which houses an impressive collection of international art spanning seven centuries; and finish up at the peaceful Jardin des Plantes, a charming (and free) botanical garden which is home to a handful of modern art installations and a good cafe. From here it’s a short stroll to the Lieu Unique, a cultural space and concert venue in the factory that once produced the city’s beloved buttery LU biscuits. And there’s more to come. The Jardin Extraordinaire is a newly created garden and climbing wall in a disused granite quarry in the Bas‑Chantenay district. The exotic planting, waterfall and paddling pools were inspired by descriptions in Verne’s novel, The Mysterious Island. The nearby Chantenay docks have been colonised by studios, music spaces and the Little Atlantique Brewery, housed in a 19th-century former oil mill. Opposite the quarry, a derelict industrial building is being transformed into a new riverside cultural hub, the Cité des Imaginaires, which will eventually provide a home for an expanded Jules Verne museum. It’s an ambitious project: creative, unconventional and looking to the future. I’m sure Jules Verne would approve. Joanne O’Connor The trip was supported by Le Voyage à Nantes. Oceania Hôtel de France, just off the Place Graslin, has air‑conditioned doubles from €101 room-only Winter’s Journey, a seasonal festival of concerts, temporary light installations, artworks and gastronomic events, runs from 21 November to 3 January. Basel, Switzerland Unless you’re a professional who makes their way to the Art Basel fair every year, chances are Switzerland’s third largest city will have passed you by – or rather you will have passed it by. Basel is one stop before Zurich on the fast train from Paris, but to whiz through would be a mistake. For art and design lovers, it is the perfect city to explore on a long weekend. Basel bills itself as “the city of art and culture on the Rhine”, and it lives up to its boast. Stroll around the charming old town and marvel at the cathedral before enjoying a cold beer at one of the many cafes. If temperatures soar, you might want to join local people with a dip in the Rhine. Once you’ve done all that, you need to engage with the area’s art offerings. Within the city, the Kunstmuseum holds more than 300,000 works spanning eight centuries, with big hitters such as Monet, Van Gogh and Warhol, while Museum Tinguely is home to the work of the idiosyncratic Swiss sculptor Jean Tinguely and his dada-esque machines. But the two real draws are on the outskirts of the city. Fondation Beyeler in the suburb of Riehen is home to an impressive collection of modern and contemporary art, and always has a blockbuster exhibition (currently Pierre Huyghe) to check out. A short bus or train ride across the German border in Weil am Rhein is the Vitra Design Museum, home to one of the world’s largest permanent exhibitions of modern furniture design. Before you admire the furniture collection, take a walk around the campus, where you can marvel at the main museum building designed by Frank Gehry; the Vitra Schaudepot – which houses the furniture collection – designed by Herzog & de Meuron; Zaha Hadid’s former fire station; and Tadao Ando’s conference centre. There is a beautiful garden by the Dutch designer Piet Oudolf, and the recently added Doshi Retreat for a moment of quiet reflection designed by the Indian architect Balkrishna Doshi, his first completed project outside India and the last he worked on before he died in 2023. That’s half the day gone, so time to head inside. In lots of ways, exploring the Schaudepot is like walking through a giant doll’s house, with the rooms filled with instantly recognisable furniture icons from the 19th century to today, including works by Verner Panton, Le Corbusier, Alvar Aalto and Charles and Ray Eames. The museum also puts on temporary exhibitions. And if all of that has exhausted you, head to the VitraHaus Café, which serves a delicious lunch. Max Benato The Volkshaus, a boutique hotel in the old town, has doubles from 152 swiss francs (£138) room-only Lübeck, Germany Unless you’ve read Buddenbrooks, Thomas Mann’s epic family saga, you may not have heard of Lübeck. But in the middle ages, this port city in Germany, 70km north-east of Hamburg, was one of the richest and most powerful places on Earth. Today, despite the best efforts of the RAF to destroy it in 1942, it remains a beautifully intact medieval gem. The old town is a Unesco world heritage site. It sits on an island in the centre of the city, encircled by the rivers Trave and Wakenitz, and the water is a good place to start exploring. My boyfriend and I hired an electric boat (€49 for up to six people) and spent an hour circumnavigating and gazing at its distinctive seven church spires. Back on dry land, we set off on a guided walking tour, starting at the imposing – if wonky – Holsten Gate. We took in the five red brick churches the spires belong to (two have doubles), and climbed one of them, St Petri’s viewing tower, for a panoramic view. We also stopped at the 800-year-old town hall on the marketplace. But just as fascinating was what lies behind the gothic splendour. At one time, there were 180 hidden alleyways and courtyards threaded through the old town, and about 80 remain. These labyrinthine lanes were built behind wealthy merchants’ mansions to house the poor. Today, the restored cottages are sought-after and the flower-filled, cobbled alleys are charming to explore. To better understand Lübeck’s past, we visited the European Hansemuseum in the old castle monastery. It tells the story of the Hanseatic League, the powerful trade network that stretched from England to Russia and gave Lübeck (“the Queen of the League”) its wealth in the middle ages and its status as a free city state right up to 1937. In a nearby palace, the Museum Behnhaus Drägerhaus displays 19th- and early 20th-century German and European art, including work by Edvard Munch, who visited Lübeck and painted its salt warehouses. Just round the corner is the Günter Grass-Haus, where the writer regularly stayed (he died in Lübeck in 2015). We visited in June during the HanseKulturFestival, when the quarter around St Jakob’s church was full of live music stages, food stalls and outdoor bars. The next festival isn’t until 2028, but there are annual museum, theatre and literature nights, and popup live music in the summer. Lübeck has three natural open-air swimming areas, one on the island. And the seaside isn’t far away – we had a day trip to Travemünde, a historic resort town with miles of sandy beach, taking a scenic river ferry there (90 minutes) and a 20-minute train back. In town, the medieval Schiffergesellschaft (Seafarers’ Guild) is now a traditional Hanseatic restaurant, with long communal tables. Alongside North Sea fish and Holstein meat dishes are vegetarian versions of labskaus, a sort of hash. Sadly, we couldn’t visit Buddenbrookhaus, the museum dedicated to the novel, as it is being renovated. It is expected to reopen in 2030 – which gives you plenty of time to read Mann’s 864-page doorstopper. Like Lübeck itself, it is worth the effort. Rachel Dixon The trip was provided by germany.travel and luebeck-tourismus.de. Accommodation was provided by Liho Lübeck, doubles from £73 room-only Parma, Italy Parma is just far enough off Italy’s main travel routes to discourage the huge crowds of tourists that flood the likes of Venice and Florence. Most travellers reach this tranquil Italian gem by flying into Milan or Bologna, followed by an hour’s train ride. It is definitely worth that extra effort, as I discover a city that ticks every box for a weekend getaway: fabulous museums and frescoed churches without long queues or the need to book a timeslot in advance; friendly, affordable trattorie and osterie showcasing a feast of local food and wines; and, if you time it right, the chance to catch an opera composed by locally born Giuseppe Verdi in the intimate Teatro Regio. The historic centre of Parma is small and easily explored on foot, taking me past an array of architectural masterpieces. I kick off at the grand Piazza Duomo, dominated by the imposing 900-year-old romanesque cathedral. Everyone’s eyes are drawn up to the ornate cupola, decorated with a captivating illusionist fresco by local Renaissance artist Antonio da Correggio. Next to the cathedral stands the early gothic Battistero, an octagonal baptistery whose bare, minimalist exterior contrasts with an incredible explosion of colours from the 13th- and 14th-century paintings that cover the interior. Then, tucked away behind the Duomo, I come upon the entrance of the medieval Monastero di San Giovanni Evangelista, whose cloisters and garden are a peaceful oasis. Entry to the monastery and cathedral is free. Parma’s big must-see is the monumental Palazzo della Pilotta, a baroque complex of palatial museums, a library and remarkable 400-year-old theatre, all included in a single €18 entry ticket. Just by the Parma river that slices the city into two, the palazzo was built by the Farnese family, whose patronage created most of the city’s Renaissance monuments. The Teatro Farnese, made almost entirely of wood, is rarely used as a venue today, but a visit remains an incredible experience. I leave most sightseeing time, though, for the Pilotta’s landmark Galleria Nazionale di Parma, a treasure trove of old master paintings. It may not quite rival the collection of the Uffizi, but I enjoy the chance to just turn up without booking in advance and quietly appreciate works by Leonardo da Vinci, Fra Angelico, Canaletto and Tintoretto without being surrounded by crowds. Sightseeing is only part of Parma’s attraction, however, as this is one of Italy’s food capitals. I walk into the rustic, raucous OsteMagno bar, where everyone is tucking into tagliere – wooden boards piled with razor-thin slices of cured ham, the famous prosciutto crudo di Parma, artisan salami and crumbly aged parmigiano reggiano cheese, accompanied by a glass of the local’s favourite tipple, fizzy red Lambrusco wine, which is a lot more drinkable than I expect. This is not a city to seek out chic, gourmet restaurants, but rather one of the many traditional trattorie such as Da Antonia, whose eponymous owner has overseen the cucina for more than 50 years, or the 120-year-old Trattoria Corrieri, serving up generous plates of homemade pasta for less than €15. John Brunton Palazzo Dalla Rosa Prati has doubles from €80 room-only Santander, Spain Often dismissed as little more than a ferry terminal – somewhere to stop overnight if you want to take your dog to Europe or lower your carbon footprint – the port city of Santander is undergoing something of a cultural renaissance. It’s already blessed with a spectacular bay facing the Cantabrian mountains, wide sandy beaches, grand, colonnaded plazas and superb food, but the opening of new art spaces and museums in the coming months will put the Cantabrian capital firmly on the weekend-break map. Leading the way on 8 September is Faro Santander – a new cultural centre in a grand historical building housing a 1,000-piece art collection belonging to Banco Santander, including works by Velázquez, Goya, Titian, Rubens and Picasso. Different parts of the collection will be shown at different times. With its ornate white facade facing the bay, the Pereda building was previously the bank’s headquarters, but has been transformed into a striking, 21st-century museum space by Pritzker prize-winning British architect David Chipperfield. Santander’s moment in the spotlight will extend into 2027 when Madrid’s Reina Sofia Museum opens its first outpost, set in a similarly grand neo-Renaissance building just a few metres away from Faro Santander. The museum will house the Archivo Lafuente, with paintings, sculptures and manuscripts, including major collections on dadaism and the Spanish civil war, as well as art from Spain, North America and Latin America. Faro Santander and Archivo Lafuente will form two points on a kind of “art triangle”, along with architect Renzo Piano’s 2017 Centro Botín contemporary art centre just over the road. With a bijou but impressive permanent collection, including works by Matisse, Juan Gris, Joaquín Sorolla and Mark Rothko, the Centro Botín sits on the waterfront like a giant, stilt-mounted, 60s alarm clock sawn in half. Spaniards cottoned on to Santander’s charms long ago, and the seafront is lined with elegant fin-de-siècle villas built when well-heeled Madrileños discovered that the city’s Atlantic breezes were the perfect respite from the Spanish capital’s infernal summer. More than 100 years later, while Britain was experiencing its own heatwave, I followed their lead. Temperatures were in the balmy high 20s as I ambled past toddlers building sand castles and teenagers frolicking in the surf on El Sardinero beach, just 15 minutes by bus from the city centre. The centre itself is wonderfully walkable and there’s an unhurried, laid-back vibe in the streets, grand plazas and narrow alleys near the gothic cathedral, lined with bars serving pinchos – the Cantabrian equivalent to tapas. After tucking into tender, grilled squid, laced with gutsy garlic and olive oil, at Mesón Rampalay on a leafy square, I spent a fascinating couple of hours at Mupac – the Museum of Prehistory and Archaeology of Cantabria, just a few minutes’ walk away from Faro Santander. The museum, which is home to one of Spain’s most important prehistoric collections, features excellent interactive displays, and in 2027 it is moving to a brand new, multimillion-euro building. By next year, it seems, Santander will be not just the capital of Cantabria, but a capital of culture too. Eddi Fiegel The trip was provided by Faro Santander. Abba Santander, near the Centro Botín, has stylish doubles from €66 room-only

item.title: You can now go through TSA without a plane ticket at these airports
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 6.28
You can now go through TSA without a plane ticket at these airports The Transportation Security Administration now wants you to visit the airport without a plane ticket. Twenty-five years after the Sept. 11 terrorist attacks changed airport security and largely put an end to non-ticketed visitors meeting loved ones at the gate, the TSA is rolling out a new program welcoming non-ticketed visitors at 13 airports. The program, called Gateside by TSA PreCheck, invites non-travelers with TSA PreCheck status and Known Traveler Numbers to apply for an airport day pass and use the dedicated TSA PreCheck lanes for expedited entry to the airport. "This new program makes it easier to return to the gate for welcomes and send-offs, meet friends during a layover, and enjoy dining and shopping along the way," TSA said in the program announcement, adding that the program brings back "the moments that once defined air travel." The program could be particularly useful for people who want to help family members navigate the airport. Parents could accompany children all the way to their departure gate, while family members could escort older relatives through security or meet them at the gate when they arrive. How it works Gateside by TSA PreCheck is free and is open to TSA PreCheck members and those with Known Traveler Numbers. To use the program, you'll need to apply one to three days before your planned visit, log in using your Login.gov account (or create one), enter your personal information on the form and wait for approval. Kids are welcome to join you, but be sure to enter their information on your reservation. Once approved, you'll need to bring a Real ID or other acceptable form of ID to a PreCheck lane at the airport and be prepared to log in to the application portal to show the TSA officer your approval status. Keep in mind that TSA says screenshots or printouts of your approval status won't be accepted for this program. For now, the Gateside by TSA PreCheck program is only available at 13 airports, with more promised by TSA in the coming months. If you don't have TSA PreCheck or know that your membership will soon be renewed, here's the TPG guide to everything you need to know about TSA PreCheck and some ways to get free or discounted TSA membership. Airports rolling out Gateside by TSA PreCheck - Mesa Gateway Airport (AZA) in Arizona - John Glenn Columbus International Airport (CMH) - Dallas Fort Worth International Airport (DFW) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - Wichita Dwight D. Eisenhower National Airport (ICT) in Kansas - Indianapolis International Airport (IND) - Harry Reid International Airport (LAS) - Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) - Bill and Hillary Clinton National Airport (LIT) in Arkansas - Will Rogers International Airport (OKC) in Oklahoma - Eppley Airfield (OMA) in Nebraska - San Diego International Airport (SAN) - Salt Lake City International Airport (SLC) Gateside by TSA versus other airport gate pass programs At least 20 airports already welcome non-ticketed guests to apply for gate passes to visit the non-secure side of the airport. These programs go by different names at each airport; for example, there's the Hopkins Hang Out Pass at Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) and the Wingmate Pass at Philadelphia International Airport (PHL). These programs differ from Gateside: While they do run an applicant's name through the TSA database, anyone can apply for a pass, and no PreCheck membership is required. And for these gate pass programs, using the TSA PreCheck lanes to enter the airport is prohibited. Related: The best credit cards for TSA PreCheck and Global Entry Some of those gate pass programs also differ in that applications for same-day access are often permitted, the application windows can be much longer, and screenshots and printouts of approved passes are often allowed. Here's a list of airports with their own gate pass programs: - Albuquerque International Airport (ABQ) - Cleveland Hopkins International Airport (CLE) - Kansas City International Airport (MCI) - Louis Armstrong International Airport (MSY) - Philadelphia International Airport (PHL) - Seattle-Tacoma International Airport (SEA) - Detroit Metropolitan Wayne County Airport (DTW) - Nashville International Airport (BNA) - Palm Springs International Airport (PSP) - San Antonio International Airport (SAT) - Tulsa International Airport (TUL) - John Wayne Airport (SNA) in California - Ontario International Airport (ONT) in California - Capital Regional International Airport (LAN) in Michigan - Tri-Cities Airport (PSC) in Washington - San Francisco International Airport (SFO) - Orlando International Airport (MCO) - Shreveport Regional Airport (SHV) in Louisiana - San Diego International Airport (SAN) - Tampa International Airport (TPA) Note that two of the above airports — SAN and DTW — are also on the Gateside by TSA PreCheck list. We checked with the airports to see whether anything about their gate passes will change. Matt Morawski, director of communications and external affairs at DTW, said the DTW Destination Pass is available to anyone who meets the program requirements and has a valid government-issued ID. "We do not anticipate that the Gateside by TSA PreCheck program will have any impact on our DTW Destination Pass program," Morawski said. "We're pleased to continue offering this safe and convenient option for our customers." As for SAN, the airport's public information officer, Nicole Hall, said: "While both programs offer a similar experience by allowing access to the gate area without a boarding pass, they operate independently of one another, and there are some differences." She noted that TSA's Gateside program is only available to TSA PreCheck members, while the SAN Pass program works with TSA to approve applicants to use the normal (non-PreCheck) TSA security checkpoint line. "The timeline for requesting passes also differs between the programs," Hall said. "Our SAN Pass Program allows applicants to apply for the SAN Pass as early as seven days prior to their visit date and as late as the day of the visit." Bottom line Gateside by TSA PreCheck brings back an airport experience that largely disappeared more than two decades ago: the ability to accompany loved ones all the way to the gate even when you aren't flying yourself. Beyond meeting friends during layovers or taking advantage of airport dining and shopping, the program could be particularly valuable for families who want to accompany children or older relatives through the airport. And unlike existing airport visitor-pass programs, eligible Gateside visitors get the added benefit of using TSA PreCheck lanes to get through security.

item.title: New York to Dusseldorf, nonstop? All-biz carrier La Compagnie will give it a try
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 5.17
New York to Dusseldorf, nonstop? All-biz carrier La Compagnie will give it a try New York City-based travelers will have a new business-class option to Germany next spring. The all-business-class airline La Compagnie will launch service between Newark Liberty International Airport (EWR) and Dusseldorf Airport (DUS) on April 23, it announced Monday. The carrier will offer five weekly flights, operating on Mondays, Tuesdays, Thursdays, Fridays and Sundays. La Compagnie will fly an Airbus A321LR with 76 lie-flat, business-class seats in a 2-2 layout on the new EWR-DUS route. All La Compagnie flyers have access to its lounge, Lounge&Co, at EWR and the DUS Sky Lounge at DUS. "La Compagnie is bringing a clearly defined product to our airport: nonstop, comfortable and designed for people who want to cross the Atlantic efficiently and in a relaxed way," Lars Redeligx, CEO of Dusseldorf Airport, said in a statement. Filling a gap from New York DUS, a large business and industrial center in northwestern Germany, lacks a regular nonstop to New York City. Only Condor offers limited seasonal flights in September and October, schedule data from aviation analytics firm Cirium shows. "Dusseldorf represents a natural next chapter in La Compagnie's development," Christian Vernet, CEO of La Compagnie, said in a statement. "At the heart of one of Europe's most dynamic economic regions, with strong international businesses and long-standing ties to the United States, North Rhine-Westphalia is well suited to our unique all-business-class model." Prior to the COVID-19 pandemic, DUS boasted regular daily flights to New York City. Lufthansa flew to EWR from at least 2004 until 2018, when its budget subsidiary, Eurowings, took over the route, Cirium data shows. Eurowings suspended flights in 2020. And now-defunct Air Berlin flew from New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) to DUS from 2008 until its shutdown in 2017. La Compagnie's EWR-DUS route complements its existing flights from EWR to Milan Malpensa Airport (MXP), Nice Cote d'Azur Airport (NCE) and Paris Orly Airport (ORY). Tickets on the new route start at $2,428.50 one-way, according to the airline's website. That compares to $2,313 one-way on United Airlines from EWR to Frankfurt Airport (FRA) in April 2027.

item.title: How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.84
How to get more out of every all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards All-inclusive vacations can simplify trip planning, and IHG Hotels & Resorts makes it easy to discover, compare and book a growing range of participating all-inclusive resorts across destinations worldwide. Booking through IHG can add even more value to the experience. With IHG One Rewards, members can earn and redeem points at participating all-inclusive properties. That means a beach vacation can help fund a future trip or reduce your out-of-pocket cost if you redeem IHG points for your stay. After all, one of the biggest appeals of an all-inclusive vacation is knowing that many of your meals, drinks and activities are included in your stay. But by booking a participating all-inclusive stay through IHG, you may also be able to earn points, work toward elite status and enjoy select IHG One Rewards benefits during your stay. Here's what to know about getting more out of an all-inclusive vacation with IHG One Rewards. IHG has a growing all-inclusive portfolio IHG Hotels & Resorts has expanded its all-inclusive portfolio to give travelers more ways to discover and book resort experiences across a range of brands, destinations and stay types, all through the hotel loyalty program you already know and trust. Iberostar Beachfront Resorts are a key part of IHG's all-inclusive offering, with participating resorts in beach destinations across Mexico, the Caribbean, Europe and Africa. For example, if you're planning an all-inclusive trip to Mexico, you might look at Iberostar Selection Riviera Cancún or JOIA Paraíso by Iberostar. If the Caribbean is calling, Iberostar Selection Bávaro Suites in the Dominican Republic may be worth considering. And if you're thinking about Europe, Iberostar Jardín del Sol Suites in Mallorca might be a good fit. But IHG's all-inclusive options go beyond Iberostar Beachfront Resorts. For example, Holiday Inn Club Vacations Grand Residences All-Inclusive and Holiday Inn Club Vacations The Royal Sands All-Inclusive are notable options in Mexico. And if you're interested in an all-inclusive vacation without leaving the U.S., the voco Sandpiper All-Inclusive Resort in Florida is worth considering. Of course, the best all-inclusive resort for your trip depends on who you are traveling with and what you want from your vacation. Some resorts are better suited for families who want pools, activities and kids clubs. Meanwhile, other resorts are more appealing to couples, friends and multigenerational groups that want to package their stay, dining and activities together. That's one reason it can be useful to start your search on IHG's website or app. You can look for participating all-inclusive resorts by destination and compare options. Plus, booking through IHG ensures your IHG One Rewards number is attached to your reservation. Earn IHG points on all-inclusive stays One of the best reasons to book an all-inclusive stay through IHG is that you can earn IHG points. IHG members earn 10 points per dollar spent on qualifying stays at participating IHG hotels and resorts, including Iberostar Beachfront Resorts and Holiday Inn Club Vacations resorts. Plus, travelers with IHG elite status can earn even more through status bonuses as follows: | IHG elite status tier | Base points on qualifying stays | Status bonus on qualifying stays | Total points earned on qualifying stays | |---|---|---|---| | Member | 10 points per dollar spent | None | 10 points per dollar spent | | Silver Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 20% | 12 points per dollar spent | | Gold Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 40% | 14 points per dollar spent | | Platinum Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 60% | 16 points per dollar spent | | Diamond Elite | 10 points per dollar spent | 100% | 20 points per dollar spent | Earning points can be especially valuable on an all-inclusive stay. Since these stays often cost more than a typical hotel night, a qualifying all-inclusive resort booking could earn you a significant number of IHG points. To earn IHG points on your all-inclusive stay, book through an eligible method such as the IHG website or app and confirm your IHG One Rewards number is attached to your reservation. This is important, as your stay may not qualify for points or IHG One Rewards benefits if you book through another source (including most online travel agencies). Redeem IHG points for all-inclusive stays You can also redeem IHG points for reward nights at all-inclusive properties that participate in the IHG One Rewards program. To redeem IHG points for an all-inclusive stay — including those at Iberostar Beachfront Resorts — go to IHG's website or app, log in to your account and search for your destination, dates and number of guests. Be sure to set your rate preference to "Reward Nights." From there, you can compare properties. On the results page, you'll see the starting nightly award rate and some flags that let you know if the property is all-inclusive or adults only. If you click a specific property, you can see the available room types. Note that some room types may carry a higher nightly award rate. Be sure to click "Reward Nights + All Inclusive" for the room type and rate you select to confirm what's included in the rate. It's important to enter the correct number of guests, including children, when searching for your all-inclusive vacation, as IHG adjusts reward-night pricing based on factors such as guest count and dining plan. For example, a two-night stay at Iberostar Selection Cancun in Mexico might cost 90,000 points per night for two adults but 135,000 points per night for two adults and two children. And at some resorts, such as Iberostar Waves Cristina in Spain, you can choose from breakfast-only, half-board and full all-inclusive award rates, each priced accordingly. If you have an eligible IHG One Rewards credit card, you may be able to get even more value from your points at participating IHG properties. The fourth Reward Night is free when you redeem points for any stay of four or more nights. You'll automatically see the discounted award rates at participating properties if you're logged into your account, have an eligible card and search for a reward stay of four nights or longer. Plus, eligible Cardmembers have an annual Free Night that can be enhanced with points to access hotels above the 40,000-point redemption threshold. Get IHG elite-night credits and benefits on all-inclusive stays Qualifying all-inclusive stays can also help IHG One Rewards members work toward elite status and milestone rewards. Plus, IHG One Rewards members can enjoy select benefits during qualifying all-inclusive stays at participating IHG hotels and resorts and participating Iberostar Beachfront Resorts. Even if you don't have elite status with IHG, you can access member rates, Wi-Fi access and 2 p.m. late checkout, subject to availability at participating hotels. IHG Platinum Elite and Diamond Elite members may be eligible for benefits such as early check-in, room upgrades and a welcome amenity at check-in, subject to availability. And if you have an annual lounge membership that you earned through the milestone rewards program, you can use the Star Prestige facilities when available at participating Iberostar Beachfront Resort properties. All these benefits can be especially useful at a resort. A late checkout can give you a few more hours at the pool before an evening flight, while an early check-in can make a morning arrival less awkward. And a room upgrade can make a special trip feel even more spectacular. Just keep in mind that many elite benefits are subject to availability and may vary by brand, hotel and stay type. Bottom line All-inclusive vacations are appealing because they can make travel simpler, but booking an all-inclusive stay through IHG can add another layer of value. Through IHG Hotels and Resorts, travelers can discover, compare and book all-inclusive resorts in a wide range of vacation destinations. And IHG One Rewards members can earn points on qualifying paid stays, redeem points for all-inclusive stays and enjoy member or elite benefits along the way. Whether you're planning a family beach trip, a couples getaway, a friends trip or a multigenerational vacation, it's worth checking IHG's all-inclusive options before you book.

item.title: Frontier plans first South America service, adds 3 former Spirit routes
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.76
Frontier plans first South America service, adds 3 former Spirit routes Frontier Airlines is getting ready to fly to South America for the first time. The Denver-based budget airline on Thursday announced nonstop service to three cities in Colombia. The trio of routes from Orlando International Airport (MCO) will mark the first time Frontier has sent its planes to the continent. It will also be a clear move to pick up routes abandoned by former rival Spirit Airlines, which had a significant presence in Colombia prior to its collapse earlier this year. Among the routes: nonstop service to the Colombian capital city of Bogota, along with new flights to Medellin and Cartagena. Read more: Spirit is gone. Can other budget airlines survive? "We believe there is strong, unmet demand for low-cost travel between Orlando and Colombia, and we look forward to offering affordable flight options between these two magnificent destinations," Tyri Squyres, Frontier's vice president of public and consumer affairs, said in a statement announcing the news. Read more: Frontier wants to be an airline you want to fly. Will first class and new perks do the trick? Frontier's 3 new Colombia routes Here's the full rundown of the new international service Frontier announced: | Route | Launch date | Frequency | |---|---|---| | Orlando to Jose Maria Cordova International Airport (MDE) in Medellin | Dec. 10 | Daily | | Orlando to El Dorado International Airport (BOG) in Bogota | Dec. 14 | Six times per week at the start; daily after March 6, 2027 | | Orlando to Rafael Nunez International Airport (CTG) in Cartagena | Dec. 19 | Weekly | Picking up where Spirit left off All three of those new Frontier flights were routes once served by Spirit. The now-defunct budget airline had been America's top ultra-low-cost carrier in Colombia and in South America. So, Spirit's collapse left a clear void for consumers looking to fly to the region on a budget airline. TPG's Summer Hull: An ode to Spirit Airlines — Yeah, they were all yellow It's worth watching to see whether Frontier makes further moves to acquire former Spirit routes in Latin America. Frontier executives have said the airline would take a more measured approach in picking up service abandoned by its former competitor. At the same time, the airline isn't done adding former Spirit routes to the mix — even though it has been several months since its big yellow planes were grounded. "There are opportunities to pick off markets that they've obviously exited, now, over the coming year or two," Frontier CEO James Dempsey told me in July. Worth noting The reveal of Frontier's first-ever service to South America comes days after the airline confirmed it was fully exiting America's largest market. The carrier plans to bid farewell to New York City's John F. Kennedy International Airport (JFK) next month. Related reading:

item.title: American and Hyatt are winding down their enhanced loyalty partnership
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.49
American and Hyatt are winding down their enhanced loyalty partnership American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt launched a partnership in 2019. My favorite part of this partnership was reciprocal earnings: Hyatt elite members could earn 1 bonus point per $1 spent on qualifying American Airlines flights, and American elite members could earn 1 bonus mile per $1 spent on qualifying Hyatt stays. Unfortunately, the programs ended reciprocal earnings on Dec. 31, 2024. And now, they've announced plans to end their enhanced loyalty partnership. American and Hyatt are ending their enhanced partnership Press releases from both American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt on Sept. 9 state the programs "have mutually decided to not continue our enhanced relationship." However, both programs say they are "committed to preserving the benefits members can earn through the current earning year in each program (including providing the standard time to select an award after it has been earned)." Specifically, American AAdvantage and World of Hyatt members will see "no interruption in earning, selecting and redeeming their eligible benefits" for "the remainder of each program's current earning year." What happens to current American-Hyatt benefits Nov. 15 will be the last day to link your AAdvantage and World of Hyatt accounts. But if your accounts are linked by Nov. 15, AAdvantage members can continue earning World of Hyatt awards through Loyalty Point Rewards through Feb. 28, 2027, and World of Hyatt members can continue earning AAdvantage awards through Milestone Rewards through Dec. 31, 2026. As a reminder, American's Loyalty Point Rewards program offers members World of Hyatt benefits at select milestones reached within an elite-qualifying year. At some milestones, you'll get perks automatically, while at other milestones, you'll get one or two choices of perks. - 100,000 Loyalty Points: Get World of Hyatt Discoverist status - 175,000 and 250,000 Loyalty Points: Choose World of Hyatt Explorist status - 400,000, 550,000 and 750,000 Loyalty Points: Choose a World of Hyatt Category 1-4 free night award - 1,000,000, 3,000,000 and 5,000,000 Loyalty Points: Choose a World of Hyatt Category 1-7 free night award I wouldn't, and haven't, chosen any of these perks as Loyalty Point Rewards since there are more valuable options. As such, I'm not particularly sad to see these options removed as of March 1, 2027. However, if you reach a Loyalty Point Rewards tier on or before Feb. 28, 2027, you'll still get the standard amount of time to select your reward and then enjoy or redeem it. American currently gives members until March 31, 2027, to select 2026 Loyalty Point Rewards. If you select Hyatt free night awards, they'll expire 180 days from the date they are issued in your World of Hyatt account (be sure to check the expiration date once the free night award is in your account). Meanwhile, the Hyatt Milestone Rewards program lets members choose American Airlines perks at select milestones: - 20 qualifying nights or 35,000 base points and 30 qualifying nights or 50,000 base points: Choose 2 Preferred seat coupons on American Airlines - 40 qualifying nights or 65,000 base points and 50 qualifying nights or 80,000 base points: Choose 2 Main Cabin Extra seat coupons on American Airlines - 70, 80 and 90 qualifying nights: Choose AAdvantage Gold status - 100, 110, 120, 130, 140 and 150 qualifying nights: Choose AAdvantage Platinum status If you reach one of these Milestone Rewards tiers on or before Dec. 31, 2026, you'll still have the standard amount of time to select your rewards and enjoy or redeem them. Seat coupons typically expire 365 days from when they were issued to your AAdvantage account, while AAdvantage status selected as a milestone reward expires on March 31 of the following full year. So if you select an AAdvantage status as a milestone reward on Dec. 1, 2026, your status will be valid through March 31, 2028. We'll also likely see the end of the ability to redeem American miles for Hyatt free-night awards and redeem Hyatt points for AAdvantage Status for a Day. But perhaps the most painful part of this partnership ending for many members will be the end of the status fast tracks for members of both programs. Bottom line American and Hyatt's partnership has already become less valuable since reciprocal earnings ended at the end of 2024, and I won't personally miss most of the current cross-program reward choices. However, I'm sad to see the status fast-track benefits disappear, as they could offer significant value to eligible members of both programs. If your AAdvantage and World of Hyatt accounts aren't already linked, it's worth doing so by Nov. 15. That will let you continue earning the current cross-program rewards through the end of each program's earning year. And even after the enhanced partnership ends, AAdvantage members will still be able to choose to earn 500 miles instead of World of Hyatt points on eligible Hyatt stays.

item.title: Have a travel problem? Here's how to write an effective complaint letter
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.43
Have a travel problem? Here's how to write an effective complaint letter Last December, Scott Tallal redeemed 68,500 American Airlines AAdvantage miles for a business-class ticket from Harrisburg International Airport (MDT) to Los Angeles International Airport (LAX) via Chicago O'Hare International Airport (ORD). Unfortunately, when he arrived at the airport for his flight, he learned that it had been canceled. Helpful agents rerouted him, but in the process, they downgraded him to economy. No worries, they told him. American Airlines would refund the difference in miles between the two classes since it was an involuntary downgrade. Six months later, despite numerous calls and emails to American Airlines customer service, Scott's points were still missing. In his last written correspondence with the airline, an agent informed him that his complaint had been extensively reviewed. According to her, American Airlines did not owe him a refund in miles or cash, and the airline considered his complaint closed. That's when Scott sent his request for help to TPG. A gaggle of gripes After I spoke to him and reviewed his paper trail, I had good news: American Airlines did owe him the refund he had been expecting. The Department of Transportation requires it, in fact. But it took me a while to untangle. So what went wrong? Scott had made one of the most common mistakes travelers make when writing a complaint: overcomplicating things. In an effort to convey the full extent of his inconvenience, Scott had submitted a laundry list of grievances. He included a lengthy narrative about previous flights, other cancellations, partner airline experiences, delays and other extraneous information. That turned what should have been a straightforward request into a complicated maze that customer service agents could not follow. In fact, when I first reviewed Scott's complaint, even I had difficulty determining what had happened and what he was asking American Airlines to do. Not surprisingly, when customer service agents — or even a consumer advocate — cannot easily identify the problem, there is little chance of a positive outcome. If you cannot pinpoint the issue, you cannot offer a solution. After I delivered his complaint to my executive contact at American Airlines in a concise, easy-to-understand format, though, Scott quickly received his miles. I review hundreds of consumer complaints each month. Many involve legitimate grievances that customer service agents and even company executives have rejected. In many of these cases, the complaint should have been approved. But the traveler made one or more common — and mostly correctable — mistakes when presenting their request. Here are the top reasons valid complaints fail and how to give yourself the best chance of finding a resolution to your problem. Make sure you're sending your complaint to the right company Even the best travel complaint letter can succeed only if a traveler delivers it to the correct entity. Unfortunately, that isn't as easy as it sounds in 2026. Recently, I received a request for help from Shane McCormick, who thought he had paid Costco Travel $6,000 for two cabins aboard Royal Caribbean's Ovation of the Seas. He was angry about the company's inability to provide what it had promised at the quoted price. Instead of two cabins, his family had been assigned just one when his itinerary came through. So what had happened? When I reviewed his paper trail, a surprising detail emerged. McCormick had not actually been corresponding with Costco Travel. Google search results had misdirected him to a scam call center posing as Costco Travel. All of McCormick's emailed complaints had been sent to the fraudsters, who had very little interest in correcting his mistaken belief — or fixing his problem. Those bad actors were only interested in spending the $6,000 they had convinced him to send them. For several years now, scammers have been flooding the internet with fake customer service centers posing as major airlines and cruise lines. And those human agents are always available and eager to receive your complaint and "help" you fix the problem. Before calling a number or emailing a grievance, it is crucial to make sure you have the company's correct contact information. Never rely on search results to find it. Instead, visit the official website of the business you are trying to reach. Check the URL in your browser to confirm. Downloading the company's app is also another reliable way to find real contact information for a cruise line, airline or hotel. If you need help locating customer service contacts or consumer-facing executives to escalate a problem beyond the frontline, my advocacy organization, Consumer Rescue, maintains a free directory that I continually update. Keep your complaint concise One of the best ways to give your complaint letter a fair chance of succeeding is to keep it concise. Earlier this month, I received a request for help from a United Airlines customer whose EU 261 claim was rejected. He sent me an eight-page missive that he had already submitted to the airline. It read like a court presentation, complete with labeled exhibits and complicated legal jargon. This traveler was surprised that his manifesto had not produced the outcome he had hoped for. He shared his suspicion that no one at United Airlines had actually read his magnum opus. I agreed. Travelers should always keep in mind that the company representative receiving the letter is likely reviewing dozens of complaints every day. You want that person to be able to scan your message and quickly figure out what happened and how to help. You can do that by keeping your complaint brief and factual. Start with the problem. End with the desired resolution. Be realistic about what you ask for. Never send a complaint that extends beyond one page. If the company needs more information, it will ask. Don't "bury the lede" in your complaint "Don't bury the lede" is a foundational rule of good journalism, and the same concept applies when writing a grievance. An effective travel complaint catches the customer service agent's attention and immediately conveys the reason for the letter. I know from my case files, however, that travelers often compose complaints that begin long before getting to the actual problem. They hide the pressing issue hundreds — and sometimes thousands — of words into the narrative. That's a mistake. Most customer service agents likely will not ever reach that far in an individual complaint. Even worse, AI programs are now reviewing and responding to many emailed grievances. These systems often limit how much text they will process. If your critical information is not near the top, the bot may never even consider it. Remember, your goal is to make the problem simple to understand and instantly clear. An easy-to-read, bullet-point list showing what happened and the resolution you are requesting often works best. If you use AI, don't forget common sense and fact-checking Increasingly, consumers are leaning on AI programs to help them compose complaint letters and the results are mixed. These programs can help travelers create professional-looking complaint letters free of typos and grammatical errors. However, AI is also known to invent laws and regulations and encourage travelers to escalate minor grievances into catastrophic, and sometimes sinister, events. In the worst cases, AI creates problems where none exist. Celebrity Cruises customer Cherie Johnson turned to AI after she and her husband were denied boarding a transatlantic cruise aboard Celebrity Equinox. The couple arrived in Lisbon, Portugal, ready to begin their much-anticipated vacation. Instead, the crew told them they needed Brazilian eVisas to board. That was something they did not have. Even before Equinox sailed away without them, Cherie began asking AI who was to blame and whether they really needed those visas. Google Gemini instantly agreed with her suspicion that they did not need visas. According to the AI bot, Celebrity had made a grave error by preventing the couple from boarding. It cited "Brazilian Decree 86715/1981," which Gemini claimed allowed cruise passengers to use the ship as a visa-free transit zone as long as they remained onboard while docked in Brazil. The AI agent also told Cherie that Celebrity was legally required to inform passengers of all documentation requirements before the cruise. But it was all an AI hallucination. Cruise ships are not visa-free immigration zones, and there is no Brazilian decree that makes them so. Cherie sent the AI-created "proof" to Celebrity Cruises' legal department and accused the crew of wrongfully denying her boarding and keeping her money. She included an itemized chart of all the things she expected the cruise line to reimburse her for beyond the cost of the cruise. The grand total exceeded $16,000. Celebrity was not swayed by the confident accusations in Cherie's letter. Despite the AI's certainty that the cruise line had made a mistake refusing to let the couple board the ship, it was wrong and Celebrity knew it. As a result nearly all her letters were simply ignored. By the time Cherie sent me a request for help she had been unsuccessfully trying to convince Celebrity for four months that it owed her $16,000. She hoped I could shine a light on what had happened and succeed in proving the cruise line's mistake. The task of telling her the truth and hopefully ending her futile battle fell to me. AI had misled her by citing an outdated legal doctrine that didn't apply to her situation. The cruise line had not made a mistake in her case. Travelers are responsible for having the documents required for their international flights and cruises. This is written into the terms and conditions of every cruise line and airline that I know of. To ensure you don't end up in the unpleasant situation this couple did, visit the State Department's website. There, you can verify what you need for entry to all countries on your itinerary. Before asking AI to help with your travel complaint, make sure you understand its limitations. These programs can confidently provide false information — especially if your questions suggest the answer you want to hear. Always independently verify the "facts" AI provides. And never sign your name to a complaint letter until you have thoroughly researched every claim it contains. Don't file a credit card dispute before appealing to the company first The Fair Credit Billing Act (FCBA) allows consumers to dispute credit card charges involving billing errors or unauthorized transactions. But a chargeback should not be your opening move. I see consumers misuse this important protection every day — sometimes with devastating consequences. First, ask the company with which you have an issue to try to resolve your problem. Follow its complaint process and give it a reasonable opportunity to investigate. Do not simultaneously file a complaint with the company and a dispute with your credit card issuer. Once a chargeback is underway, the company will typically allow that process to play out instead of continuing to negotiate with you. If you lose the dispute, the company will have very little motivation to reopen your case — even if your original complaint was legitimate. By then, you may also have weakened your chances of getting help from a consumer advocate. The proper order of events is simple: Exhaust your options with the company first. Consider a credit card dispute only after those efforts fail and only if your claim qualifies under the FCBA. Don't insult the company or declare "I'll never be your customer again" Telling a company you're done with it and will never give them business again is counterproductive. Think about it: If you've written off the company, why shouldn't it write you off too? Your complaint letter should be cordial, clearly explain the facts and propose a reasonable resolution. Yet so many complaint letters I receive begin with some version of: "I will never use your services again. Now give me the goodwill gesture I'm asking for." Surely, once the emotion is removed from the situation, most travelers can see the problem with that approach. In nearly every case, the traveler feels mistreated by a company they have been loyal to. They do not really want to never be its customer again. They want to be heard and have their problem handled properly. However, by telling a company that you will never patronize it again, you disincentivize it from helping you. Before sending this type of letter, take a breath and think about what you really want. Maybe even close your browser for the night. In the morning, start again and explain what the company can do to keep you as a valued customer. Do not threaten legal action In the age of AI, this is becoming increasingly important to underscore. AI seems to love escalating minor problems into legal battles. But consumers should understand that once they send a legal threat to an airline, cruise line or other travel provider, they had better be prepared to follow through. The problem is that ordinary travelers are being encouraged to make legal threats without any factual basis. As a professional mediator and TPG's ombudsman, I always begin by attempting a cordial resolution. Most legitimate travel complaints can be resolved with a friendly overture to the company backed by clear facts. But if you open your complaint with a threat to sue or announce that you have involved a lawyer, your letter will likely be forwarded directly to the company's legal department. At that point, frontline customer service may no longer be willing or authorized to help you. I have seen consumers threaten legal action over disputes involving as little as $25. Companies recognize these empty threats for what they are, and those complaints often land in a virtual garbage can. If you genuinely want the company's help, leave the legal threats out of your complaint. Make your complaint clear A concise complaint is not necessarily a clear one. Make sure your message explains what went wrong, when it happened and what you are asking the company to do about it. Include your confirmation or reservation number and any evidence that directly supports your claim, such as a receipt, cancellation notice, or written promise from a company representative. Leave out unrelated documents and details that make the problem harder to follow. Before sending your complaint, ask someone unfamiliar with the situation to read it. If that person can't quickly explain what went wrong and what you want the company to do, the customer service agent probably won't be able to either. Over at Consumer Rescue, I have published a free resource page that includes a template for an effective complaint letter along with a variety of sample letters. The bottom line Writing an effective complaint letter doesn't have to be difficult if you keep a few things in mind. The letters that receive the most favorable response follow the three C's. They are: - Cordial - Concise - Clear But don't forget one more essential ingredient: a reasonable proposed resolution. Travelers often weaken legitimate complaints by asking for far more than the situation warrants. Asking a company to correct its mistake or reimburse a documented loss is reasonable. Demanding a full refund, substantial additional compensation and a pile of loyalty points for a relatively minor problem probably is not. The goal of a complaint is to make you whole — not to provide a windfall. Customer service agents are much more likely to help when they can quickly understand what happened, why you believe the company is responsible and what you are asking to be made right. Leave out the insults, legal threats, lengthy backstory and anything else that distracts from your central problem. You may not receive exactly the outcome you want. But keeping your complaint cordial, concise and clear — and ending with a fair proposed resolution — gives it the best chance of reaching someone who can, and wants to, help. If you have a problem with a cruise line, airline, car rental company, vacation rental or credit card company, send your request for free help to ombudsman@thepointsguy.com. I'll be happy to try to help or offer advice that may allow you to resolve the problem on your own.

item.title: We visited the New 7 Wonders of the World on 1 ticket — here's how
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 4.36
We visited the New 7 Wonders of the World on 1 ticket — here's how Editor's Note Members of our video team just visited all seven New Wonders of the World — from Machu Picchu in Peru to the Taj Mahal in India — and one special type of plane ticket made it possible. The Oneworld airline alliance offers a Round The World (RTW) ticket that lets you visit (almost) as many countries as you like, all on one itinerary at one price. Check out the full video here — and keep reading to learn how to book your own round-the-world adventure. What is a round-the-world ticket? Oneworld's RTW tickets offer hundreds of destinations in 170 countries and territories, with three types of fares: - Oneworld Explorer: The price you pay depends on the number of continents you visit, with up to 15 flight segments on one ticket. - Global Explorer: The fare depends on the distance you travel, with a total cap of 39,000 miles. However, this includes additional partner airlines like Aer Lingus and WestJet. - Circle Pacific: Only includes continents that border the Pacific Ocean. The cost of a ticket starts around $3,600 for a three-continent journey in economy class. To cover all seven Wonders, two members of our intrepid team took RTW tickets in business class. Between them, they covered six continents and traveled on seven different Oneworld airlines. Maximizing rewards on your ticket Since there's no way to book these tickets with miles, here are our top tips to maximize your rewards on a cash booking. First, you should be able to purchase RTW tickets directly with individual airlines. If you do, make sure you're using a credit card that offers bonus points or miles on airfare purchases. Start by planning your itinerary through Oneworld's site and then call your favorite Oneworld airline (such as American) to book and pay. This way, your transaction will code as an airline purchase, and you'll earn bonus points and any other perks your card might offer. Check out our favorite airline cards for maximizing your RTW ticket purchase. In addition, since these are cash tickets, you'll able to earn miles and credit toward elite status for each flight. Your best option is likely to pick your preferred program — like American AAdvantage or Alaska Atmos Rewards — and add that frequent flyer number to your ticket. Maximizing rewards on your journey Trip expenses don't end after you step off the plane. Our team had to budget for tours and tickets for each of the New Seven Wonders of the World, as well as ground transportation from the airport, and they used the credit cards already in their wallets to help offset these costs. Check your Chase Offers and Amex Offers for targeted savings at tour booking sites like Viator. Or consider redeeming points for tickets through your credit card travel portal. Select American Express cards offer monthly Uber Cash on U.S. Uber rides and Uber Eats orders. Meanwhile, eligible Chase cardholders can unlock bonus points and monthly in-app credits with Lyft. At a minimum, be sure to pay with a card that earns bonus points on general travel to maximize your rewards on tours, tickets and transportation — and make sure you're not paying any pesky foreign transaction fees. Bottom line If you're hoping to book your own round-the-world journey, check out these sample itineraries for inspiration. Alternatively, you can chart your own course with Oneworld's handy tool. Let us know which continents you're dreaming of in the comments!

item.title: Spacious suites and fine wines: A review of United's new Elevated Polaris business class
item.description:
Source: The Points Guy Score: 3.15
Spacious suites and fine wines: A review of United's new Elevated Polaris business class Quick take: United's new "Elevated" Polaris business class represents a sophisticated step forward for the airline. Hopefully the closing privacy doors will be certified soon. Pros - There's decent award availability for United cardholders. - Seats are spacious and have closing doors. - Upscale food and beverage service with pre-order is available. Cons - Privacy doors need to be certified before they can be used. - Wi-Fi isn't free and is slower than Starlink. - The sound systems in the seats seem to have a few bugs. TPG got the first peek at United's swanky new "Elevated" Polaris business class in March when the airline showed off the fancy new suite-style pods at an event in Los Angeles shortly after flights went on sale. Senior aviation reporter Sean Cudahy was also among the first to actually fly in the new suites when he boarded the inaugural flight from San Francisco to Singapore in April. Sean actually flew in the enhanced "Studio" version of the suites, which are in the bulkhead row and cost a premium. So I took it upon myself to be TPG's guinea pig and fly the standard version of the seat on my own way from Singapore to San Francisco a couple of weeks ago. The new Elevated Polaris feels like a timely step forward for the airline, with amenities and other soft touches that loyal United flyers have come to expect. Here's what it was like flying nearly 16 hours in United's new business class and how to book it for yourself. How much does it cost to book United's Elevated Polaris business class? The cost of a long-haul, business-class ticket in United's new Elevated Polaris business class depends on the route, dates and whether you are flying round-trip or one-way. My one-way flight from Singapore Changi International Airport (SIN) to San Francisco International Airport (SFO) cost me 90,000 United MileagePlus miles plus $74.23 in taxes and fees instead of a paid fare of $4,148. That yielded me a value of about 4.5 cents per mile, soundly beating TPG's September 2026 valuation of United miles. It was free to choose a regular Polaris seat, but upgrading to a Studio seat would have cost $599 in advance. However, the price dropped to $499 when I checked in. Other passengers must have taken that offer since the five empty Studios I could see on the seat map had filled in by the time we departed. My 90,000-mile award ticket was the lowest level I could find for this route for the entire next year. What's more, it was only available to me because I am a United cobranded credit card holder. Without a United credit card or United Premier status, I would have needed a whopping 250,000 miles. The best way to increase your number of United miles quickly — and to unlock that preferential redemption rate — is to apply for one of the following cobranded credit cards: - United Gateway℠ Card (see rates and fees): 2 bonus miles per dollar spent on United purchases - United℠ Business Card (see rates and fees): 2 bonus miles per dollar spent on United purchases - United Club℠ Business Card: 2 bonus miles per dollar spent on United purchases - United℠ Explorer Card (see rates and fees): 3 bonus miles per dollar spent on United purchases - United Quest℠ Card (see rates and fees): 4 bonus miles per dollar spent on United purchases - United Club℠ Card (see rates and fees): 5 bonus miles per dollar spent on United purchases The information for the United Club Business has been collected independently by The Points Guy. The card details on this page have not been reviewed or provided by the card issuer. The good news is, there seems to be plenty of availability on this route, especially in the direction I flew, for that same 90,000 miles — even if you tag on another leg to your final destination within the U.S. Checking into and boarding United business class United Polaris business-class passengers can enjoy the following services at the airport. | Priority check-in | Yes | |---|---| | Luggage allowance | Two checked bags up to 70 pounds (32 kgs) each | | Lounge access | Yes | | Does the airline participate in TSA PreCheck? | Yes | | Priority boarding | Yes | My flight departed from Singapore Changi's Terminal 2. There were dedicated check-in lines for economy and Premier Access, which I could access thanks to my business-class ticket. I checked my bag, cleared immigration in a matter of minutes, and then made my way to Singapore Airlines' business-class KrisFlyer Lounge. I only spent a few minutes there getting a coffee since it was rush hour and nearly every seat was taken, but you can expect a variety of seating areas and an extensive buffet with live cooking stations for items like egg dishes and soup. Just over an hour before departure time, I made the 15-minute walk to the gate, which was just opening up for security checks. Boarding began right on time, 55 minutes before departure, and I was the first on board. How comfortable is United's Elevated Polaris business class? You can currently find United's Elevated Polaris cabins aboard a handful of newly delivered Boeing 787-9 Dreamliners. Each plane features an enormous premium section spanning the front half of the aircraft, with a total of 64 Polaris seats, including eight premium Studios. The business-class section of the plane is split into two large cabins, each with eight rows of four seats. Here's a quick look at the layout. | Number of seats | 64 (8 Studios and 56 regular seats) | |---|---| | Cabin layout | 1-2-1 | | Seat recline | 78 inches fully flat | | Seat width | 21 inches | | Screen size | 19 inches | All the seats along the sides of the plane are angled out toward the window, so you're not really looking at other passengers. What's interesting is that in the forward cabin, the center seats are angled toward one another with their seatbacks farther apart, while in the back cabin, the center seats have their seatbacks closer to one another and their footrests toward the aisle. For that reason, those back seats might be better for companions traveling together. All the center seats have huge privacy partitions that can be raised, though. | Best seats for solo travelers | Best seats for couples | |---|---| | A and L seats along the sides | Rows 9-17 F and D seats | The biggest evolution of this new Elevated Polaris product is the fact that the seats have substantial sliding doors for privacy, so you can cocoon yourself away from the activity on the aisle. Unfortunately, the plane I was on had only been delivered recently, and the doors had not yet been certified, according to the crew, so they were locked in the open position. I guess I'll just need to test them out on another flight! Jokes aside, I found the footprint to be roomy and provide plenty of privacy. The new Polaris seats also look more sophisticated than their predecessors, thanks to a moody palette of textured graphite-gray exterior shells with navy-blue interior walls, silvery-gray seating upholstery with accent cross-stitching, faux-marble shelving and caramel-colored woodgrain paneling. The aesthetic feels more sultry and elegant than the old Polaris' cheerier sky-blue and brushed-chrome combination. The Studios comprise the four seats in the two bulkhead rows and have a roomier footprint, larger entertainment screens than the regular seats, an ottoman that can double as a companion's dining perch and some extra amenities and food and beverage options on board.
